539d56b377e8.text: By — Marcia Dunn, Associated Press Marcia Dunn, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/watch-nasa-launches-crew-13-to-international-space-station Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: NASA launches Crew-13 to International Space Station Science Oct 1, 2026 4:54 PM EDT CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — Four astronauts rocketed into orbit Thursday on a space station mission that will stretch until spring, among them a Canadian whose wife will give birth while he's away. SpaceX launched commander Jessica Watkins and her crew for NASA after a three-week delay to fix their Dragon capsule's leaking fuel system. Thick clouds threatened all morning to halt the countdown but in the end, the skies cleared enough to allow for a safe liftoff. READ MORE: International Space Station marks 25 years of nonstop human presence in orbit Although their stay at the International Space Station will last a long six months, the flight there promised to be the quickest yet for Elon Musk's company: a mere eight-hour transit with an arrival well before bedtime. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. With the late morning liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Watkins became the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit. A geologist who worked with NASA's Mars rover Curiosity a decade ago, Watkins is making her second trip to the space station following a lengthy stay in 2022. "Thanks for an amazing ride," Watkins radioed after reaching orbit. The others are newcomers to space: NASA's Luke Delaney, a retired Marine; Canada's Joshua Kutryk, a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force; and Russia's Sergey Teteryatnikov, a former submariner. They will replace four astronauts who have been living at the orbiting laboratory since February. This was the 13th crew launched by SpaceX for NASA, not counting 2020's test flight. All four embrace their Crew-13 designation that pays homage in their mission patch to Apollo 13. The harrowing 1970 moonshot ended with the astronauts' safe return. References to the number 13 abounded Thursday. Watkins and her crew rode to the launch pad in black Teslas bearing plates that read "Lucky 13." What's more, they carried up a small crocheted golden dragon named Lucky with a four-leaf clover around its neck. "We figured it wouldn't hurt to bring a little of our own luck just in case, but clearly we don't need it," Watkins said from orbit, noting they were "four of the luckiest humans on or off planet Earth." Kutryk will become the fourth man to become a father while orbiting Earth. Wife Heather is due to give birth to their third child in late November. The Canadian Space Agency promises plenty of support for the entire family when the big day comes. "A lot of life-changing things can happen over six months," NASA manager Dana Weigel said on the eve of liftoff, noting that the space agency will do its best to keep Kutryk looped in to his family. In 2004, NASA provided a radio link between space station astronaut Mike Fincke and his wife's delivery room during the birth of their daughter. Five years later, Randy Bresnik, commander of next year's Artemis III mission, dialed in to his wife's hospital from orbit. The happy news traveled more slowly for Austrian astronaut Franz Viehbock. His daughter was born a few hours after he launched to the Soviet Union's Mir space station in 1991. He was not informed until the next day. SpaceX, meanwhile, is on a roll. Three hours after Crew-13 blasted off, SpaceX launched a Falcon rocket from California with more than 100 mini satellites. Another Falcon was set to soar late Thursday night from Florida, with a classified satellite for the National Reconnaissance Office. All this comes the same week that the company's massive Starship reached orbit for the first time. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. It's been a difficult few years for Nike.
The largest sportswear brand on the planet, named after the ancient Greek goddess of victory, has been losing of late. Losing sales, losing customers and losing ground to its rivals.
The one-time industry disruptor is now the establishment and in the middle of a tricky turnaround plan aimed at clinging on to market dominance.
Nike's latest financial results show signs a turnaround strategy put in place by company veteran Elliott Hill, who was coaxed out of retirement two years ago to lead the firm, is working - but the pace of change is more marathon than sprint.
However, its recovery has been dented by the loss of football star Kylian MbappÃ©, who ended his 20-year association with the brand last week to join fast-growing Swiss rival, On.
The Real Madrid striker's departure raises the question of whether Nike can remain the top logo for not just elite athletes, but also the fans that idolise them.
To be clear, Nike is still a mega brand and popular the world over. But missteps have seen hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value as its share price tumbled by 75% over five years.
Last month, Nike was ejected from the S&P 100 stock market index of the biggest blue-chip firms in the US.
So what's gone wrong? And can Hill turn things around?
Matt Powell, a veteran analyst and adviser in the sports retail industry, reckons Nike has made "several strategic errors" which have been difficult to reverse, including cutting ties with retailers to sell only direct to customers online and making limited editions items more available.
"The more broadly available those shoes became, the fewer people were interested," Powell says.
Other self-inflicted wounds he suggests include spending research and development cash on digital operations rather than new products.
"They really shut down their innovation on product. Someone jokingly said they were trying to turn Nike into eBay."
That jibe was aimed at John Donahoe, the former eBay boss behind Nike's online direct-to-consumer sales pivot, before he made way for Hill.
Donahoe's four years at Nike coincided with the company's share price plunge.
His tenure saw sales initially soar, driven by pandemic restrictions that boosted online shopping, but subsequent cost-of-living pressures curbed customer spending.
As demand weakened overseas in key markets like China, Nike announced cost cuts and redundancies.
Its digital distraction allowed newer footwear firms on top of the trends to snap at its heels. Shop shelf space previously occupied by Nike was replaced by brands such as On and Hoka.
This was a stark warning to a company that prided and built itself on innovation.
Nike was the firm that signed a deal with a rookie called Michael Jordan in the mid-1980s at a time when the company wasn't a major player in basketball and still mostly known for its running trainers.
The gamble - spending its entire basketball budget on Jordan before he had even competed in the NBA - made Nike what it is today.
The company built a shoe brand around him - Air Jordan. The red and black colours broke NBA rules, but Nike used it as a marketing stunt and paid the fines.
In years that followed Nike partnered with generational talents Tiger Woods, Serena Williams and Cristiano Ronaldo, who all donned the Swoosh on their way to golf, tennis and football greatness.
While the brand retains partnerships with long-retired Jordan, plus Williams and Ronaldo - Woods ended his association in 2024.
"[I'm] not saying that what they did wasn't great, but it was in the past," said Tim Derdenger, an academic in marketing and strategy. "It's not the future and it's not the current and that is what drives apparel sales today."
Nike's books still boast top athletes, ranging from Rory McIlory to Vinicius Junior.
However, it has now lost its biggest footballing star in MbappÃ©, who had been with Nike since he was nine years old, along with World Cup winner Lamine Yamal.
Yamal suggested his move to Adidas gave him the chance to stand out from Nike's star-studded roster, while MbappÃ© said On would see him "surrounded by innovators who dream of the same things I do".
Was that a parting dig at Nike?
Derdenger suggests MbappÃ©'s move had parallels to Jordan's decision decades earlier to choose Nike over Converse and Adidas due to the opportunity for the athlete to become synonymous with one brand.
"Athletes have egos and those egos want them to be a part of something big and that they're the ones that are helping drive that change, that growth."
Nike down but not out
For all the "doom and gloom", Nike will stay number one, according to Powell - millions worldwide, including young people, remain loyal - but its mistakes have dented its dominance.
"Will Nike be the gorilla they once were? I don't think so. Can the brand come back to growth and profitability? Yes," Powell says.
"When you shut down innovation, you don't turn it back on and it goes right back to full speed," he adds.
Powell thinks Nike's turnaround plan, called "Sport Offense", will start to show positive signs next year.
Hill said Nike had "more work to do" on its sportswear, Jordan brand and in China as the company announced quarterly revenues of $11bn, which undershot analysts' expectations.
The company said it expected revenues to decline by "high-single digits" in the financial year ahead, adding that it planned to make savings of $2.5bn by 2031, some of which will result in job losses.
Last year the company launched a spin-off campaign to its iconic "Just Do It" slogan aimed at younger generations with the line "Why Do It?"
Young people, and future sporting stars, may ask themselves: Why Nike?

BIRMINGHAM, Ala.—It’s time to act. It’s long past time.
That was the case made by lawyers for the Southern Environmental Law Center, who filed a petition Wednesday in Jefferson County Circuit Court asking a judge to force local health officials to act on a 2023 air permit renewal application for ABC Coke, the nation’s largest producer of foundry coke.
SELC lawyers filed the petition on behalf of the Greater-Birmingham Alliance to Stop Pollution, an environmental nonprofit better known as GASP. The filing argued that Dr. David Hicks, the county’s health officer, has failed his “statutory, nondiscretionary duty to take action” on the renewal application, resulting in the facility legally operating without an up-to-date permit.
“Communities should not have to wait indefinitely for the protections the law requires,” GASP Executive Director Jilisa Milton said. “The people of Tarrant and surrounding communities have lived with ABC Coke’s pollution for generations.”
Foundry coke is a dirty, high-carbon fuel produced by burning coal at extreme temperatures.
By Thursday afternoon, just a day after the court filing, the Jefferson County Department of Health had notified SELC that it was moving forward with the permitting process, according to a representative from the environmental nonprofit.
“It’s unfortunate it took us filing a lawsuit for JCDH to do its job, but at least we’re one step closer to ABC Coke having a renewed permit,” SELC said in a statement. “We’ll continue to watch this process very closely and demand accountability for communities surrounding [the facility].”
ABC Coke, owned by Drummond Coal, has long polluted the air in Tarrant, a community abutting north Birmingham. The company agreed to pay a $775,000 civil penalty in 2019 over alleged Clean Air Act violations related to the release of benzene, a cancer-causing chemical that can also trigger other health problems.
Representatives for ABC Coke did not respond to a request for comment.
The company applied for a renewal of its air permit in 2023, records show, but health officials did not issue a draft permit until January 2026. Since then, the agency’s public progress has stalled, a delay that SELC and GASP say has prevented residents’ concerns from being addressed.

“Defendant’s failure to timely act has deprived and continues to deprive the public, including GASP and its members, of procedural and substantive rights under the Clean Air Act and Air Rules,” the petition stated.
The Jefferson County Department of Health did not respond to a request for comment, but in a September 2026 letter to SELC, Hicks wrote that his agency “respectfully disagrees with the assertion that it has failed to fulfill its obligations under applicable law.”
The department, he wrote, was waiting on a “regulatory assessment” by the Trump administration’s Environmental Protection Agency before taking action on the application.
“Accordingly, JCDH does not believe litigation is necessary or appropriate at this time,” Hicks wrote. “JCDH remains committed to carrying out its regulatory responsibilities and will continue to keep the permitting process moving forward consistent with those responsibilities.”
A representative for the EPA did not immediately answer questions about the assessment referenced by Hicks.
Lawyers for the SELC have said there is no requirement that EPA conduct such an assessment.
“Unless JCDH moves forward and submits a proposed permit to EPA for its official 45-day review, EPA could sit on the current draft permit indefinitely, depriving GASP and the surrounding communities of the substantive benefits of an updated permit and their procedural rights to challenge said permit, if necessary,” SELC wrote to Hicks on Sept. 30.
The Trump administration has already rolled back initiatives meant to help communities facing industrial air pollution, including in Birmingham and Tarrant. In 2025, for example, the administration announced it would grant a two-year exemption to coke oven operators from a Biden-era federal rule requiring fenceline air quality monitoring and improved workplace practices at coke oven facilities across the country. SELC and GASP are challenging the exemption in court.
That fenceline monitoring has shown elevated levels of benzene at several coke oven facilities. Monitoring programs in Indiana, Pennsylvania and Alabama recorded benzene levels as high as 14 times the occupational exposure limit recommended by the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists.
At ABC Coke in Alabama, monitoring equipment recorded benzene levels more than 60 percent above that threshold limit, raising cancer risks in the mostly Black areas of north Birmingham and Tarrant by as much as 1.7 cases in every 10,000 people.
Those are risks that should compel local health officials not to delay final action on ABC Coke’s permit, according to GASP’s Milton.
“They deserve action,” she said, “not delay.”

85ad898550c0.text: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike's attorneys said she was "in critical condition" and "receiving life-saving care" Thursday, a day after she survived an execution attempt during which the state administered two doses of the lethal injection drug. A death penalty expert told the Associated Press that Pike's survival after receiving the execution drug was unprecedented. The latest: State and federal elected officials are pressing for public accountability after the second failed execution this year. Gov. Bill Lee ordered a independent review of the Pike execution attempt. On Thursday morning, he told reporters there were "very few answers" about what had gone wrong. U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the frontrunner to succeed Lee as governor next year, blasted the "botched process" in a statement and pushed for the state to "bring back the electric chair." Pike's attorneys told reporters Thursday that Lee's pledge to launch an investigation did not go far enough. They urged him to commute her death sentence. What they're saying: Attorney Randy Spivey, who was inside the prison during the execution attempt, said prison officials spent about an hour trying to establish IV access. He counted at least seven needles used in Pike's left arm alone. Pike complained of sharp pain during the lethal injection. Spivey said he noticed her right arm turning purple, especially after the second round of chemicals. He said the lawyers had also been told of blistering and burning around the injection sites. Between the lines: Federal public defender Stephen Ferrell said the lawyers had warned courts months earlier about medical problems with Pike's veins that made it harder to establish an IV. Zoom in: The attorneys also said they weren't able to quickly reach their colleagues or court officials responsible for overseeing the execution. Spivey said it took seven minutes and passage through six locked doors to get to a telephone so he could reach the rest of Pike's legal team. Ferrell said an emergency telephone number provided for the Tennessee Supreme Court went to voicemail. The state's response: Lee called the latest failed execution "a tragedy" on Thursday morning. "It's deeply disturbing to me that that has happened in this state," he told reporters, according to Reuters. The big picture: This isn't the first time Tennessee's prison officials have faced scrutiny for their approach to the death penalty. After a 2022 execution was halted over failures to properly test the drugs , Lee paused all executions so the state could investigate and overhaul its lethal injection protocol. Executions resumed last year. But more problems surfaced in 2026. Tennessee prison officials abruptly stopped another inmate's execution in May after staff had difficulties finding a vein for an IV line used in the lethal injection. Critics blasted prison officials for disregarding Pike's concerns that there might be similar problems during her execution. Zoom out: Pike was convicted and sentenced to death for the 1995 beating death of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Her legal team does not contest her guilt. Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, traveled to Nashville this week to witness the execution. "It was a mess," she told NBC News early Thursday. "They went to try to execute her, and she didn't die." Martinez vented her anger with the governor and prison officials: "They f----- up."

A judge in Nova Scotia, Canada, has dismissed the sexual assault case against Trailer Park Boys actor Mike Smith.
The trial was set to begin in provincial court in Dartmouth on Thursday, but after the Crown provided no evidence against Smith, the actor's attorneys requested the case be dismissed.
The 54-year-old actor, who plays the character Bubbles on the Canadian sitcom, was charged last year for an alleged sexual assault in 2017.
Prosecutor Bryson McDonald told reporters outside court that the Crown offered no evidence in relation to the charge "based on the Crown's ongoing assessment that the prosecution standard has no longer been met".
McDonald would not go into further detail about the standard not being met or why, but said his office has been in regular communication with the complainant throughout the process.
There is a publication ban in place protecting the identity of the complainant.
The complainant said in a statement to Canadian broadcaster CBC that the trial was dismissed because she is "unwilling to sacrifice my mental health" by testifying.
Trailer Park Boys Incorporated, the company behind the show, said in a statement that because the charge against Smith was dropped, the actor will resume his responsibilities with the company.
Smith's attorney also said his client is "pleased that this matter is now behind him and is ready to move forward".
In February, Smith pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual assault.
Set in a fictional trailer park in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia, Trailer Park Boys follows the adventures of three longtime friends and petty criminals.
The Canadian mockumentary series first began airing in 2001 before ending in 2007, but was later revived by Netflix. Season 13 is expected to be released in the coming months.

After six years and an unprecedented botanical operation, Edinburgh's famous Palm Houses are back.
The historic glasshouses at the Royal Botanic Garden have been closed to the public for vital restoration work.
Hundreds of plants had to be temporarily moved while repairs were done on the 19th century buildings - the vast majority of them surviving the experience.
But members of the public are once again able to enjoy the redesigned space.
The shutdown had to happen because the buildings had become leaky and rusty and needed a complete overhaul.
Glass house curator Sadie Barber is delighted that, after years of disruption, the palm houses are once again being used for their intended purpose - to protect rare and and endangered plants, and to allow people to enjoy the space.
The plants were decanted to temporary homes, and then carefully moved back into the renovated space. Sadie says this has been a great achievement that wasn't without risk.
"I think whenever you move a plant and you take it out of the ground and then you stick it in a pot, it's going to suffer or it's going to get under stress.
"So there was a bit of trepidation when we picked up the biggest plants, moved them to another place, and left them there for a number of years.
"We've done really well. It feels like a huge achievement getting all these plants back in here and having them actually so well placed.
"The glasshouse team have done an enormous job, a really exceptional job of getting the plants looking like they belong.
"So it's great to see them actually thriving already."
The buildings have undergone a huge amount of work. More than five thousand panes of glass have been replaced, and the once corroding ironwork has been repaired and repainted.
Stone work has been renovated and a partition wall between the two houses has been knocked down to create a light and airy space which shows off the historic architecture and living plants.
Prof Julia Knights is the Regius Keeper of the Botanic Garden. She says they have a wide range of plants and species, many of which are endangered.
"We've got palms, conifers, ferns, begonias, all of those families, plants are hugely important in our living collection and many of them are extinct in the wild," she said.
"So what the palm houses are doing is helping to protect so many of these species, and many of them of course have medicinal properties for human health.
"So if we don't save these we are also potentially not helping to save humanity, so it's super important."
Whilst most of the plants were saved in the process of moving, there was one major casualty - the Sabal palm tree which was over 200 years old. It had grown too tall for the glass house and had to be cut down and couldn't be stored.
But some seedlings were kept, and so its legacy has not been forgotten. One of the Sabal palm's descendants is growing in its place.
David Knott, the director of horticulture at the Botanic Garden, said: "Hopefully, because we've planted it in this glass house which is a bit taller than where it was previously, hopefully it will last a bit longer than the previous one did."
He is happy to see the new one growing in place of the old giant tree.
"There was no way that we were actually going to ever be able to transplant the Sabal palm. And that was probably one of the hardest, most poignant parts of the whole process."
David Knott hopes the people of Scotland will welcome the return of the glass houses.
"For many people in Edinburgh and throughout Scotland and throughout the world, the palm houses in Edinburgh really are one of the most iconic features of the Botanic Garden here.
And we hope when we reopen, we will be able to welcome people and they'll be able to enjoy the space as it was always intended to be."
Sadie Barber says there are signs that the plants are enjoying their new home.
"You can see new growth coming out of some of those plants that are now in the ground. One thing people will notice is little new croziers coming in, coming up from the fern crowns.
"When you see that unfurling you know a plant is happy. And if you look around there's just so much life. It's been an enormous job, but a really well done job. So we are overjoyed"
The restoration keeps the palm houses looking much as they were intended, but using modern techniques and materials which should guarantee the future of these much-loved buildings.

a03e60480fce.text: By — Steve Douglas, Associated Press Steve Douglas, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/what-to-know-about-the-man-city-scandal-and-charges-against-the-premier-league-soccer-team Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about the Man City scandal and charges against the Premier League soccer team World Oct 1, 2026 6:06 PM EDT It's a years-long controversy that has gripped English soccer and beyond: Did Manchester City's ownership engage in large-scale rule-breaking in an effort to transform the team into a global superpower and serial title winner? The answer, the Premier League says, is yes. In a stunning verdict announced Tuesday, the Premier League published a statement confirming City was guilty of almost all of the 115 charges leveled against the Abu Dhabi-controlled club for alleged breaches of financial rules in the world's most popular league for much of the last two decades. READ MORE: Manchester City captures Premier League title "This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history," said Richard Masters, the league's chief executive. There are likely to be seismic ramifications when sanctions are eventually handed out to City, with a whole range of punishments on the table — including expulsion from the Premier League. And what will happen to City's squad of superstars that includes Norway striker Erling Haaland and Argentina midfielder Enzo Fernandez, signed this month for $169 million? Here's a closer look at the case that everyone in soccer is talking about: Leaks, emails and an unprecedented number of charges In February 2023, the Premier League went to battle against its own champion team in unprecedented fashion, releasing a long statement detailing a list of 80 alleged breaches of its financial rules by City from 2009-18, the first nine seasons under Abu Dhabi ownership as the club tried to escape the shadow of great rival Manchester United. The violations included failing to provide accurate financial information and submitting inflated figures for sponsorship deals out of Abu Dhabi; hiding payments that supplemented salaries of managers and players; and breaching financial rules established by the Premier League and UEFA, European soccer's governing body, aiming to keep clubs financially stable by not spending beyond their means. The league also accused City of 35 more breaches relating to its alleged failure to cooperate with the investigation from December 2018. The charges stemmed from purported internal emails from City published by German outlet Der Spiegel which, it claimed, detailed schemes by the club to allegedly cover up true sources of income in a bid to comply with financial fair play regulations. The information published by Der Spiegel was unearthed by the "Football Leaks" website, whose founder is Rui Pinto — a Portuguese computer hacker. The verdict: 'Sham' contracts, lying witnesses and secret funding of $1 billion The announcement the soccer world was waiting for came Tuesday — and it was explosive. City was guilty of all the financial breaches in the 2009-18 period and the majority of the charges of non-cooperation, the league said. Standing out in the findings was the revelation that City arranged what the league described as "sham" contracts with commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than 830 million pounds ($1.1 billion) by the Abu Dhabi ownership. The commission also said that some witnesses called by City to the hearing gave evidence "they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest." "By its conduct the club clearly intended to circumvent" Premier League rules, the commission added. City has long maintained its innocence — and still does The club did not dispute the authenticity of any initial published emails but said they were "out-of-context materials purportedly hacked or stolen from City Football Group" and that it was an "organized and clear" attempt to damage City's reputation. When the Premier League announced its charges in 2023, City said it was "surprised" by the allegations and that it welcomed an investigation by an independent commission "to impartially consider the comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that exists in support of its position." City chief executive Ferran Soriano again referenced that "irrefutable evidence" in an internal video to club staff — obtained by broadcaster Sky News — that detailed why he felt the verdict was wrong. Soriano said the Premier League's case against City was "based on a single false accusation: that the owner's personal money was somehow and secretly put into the club via some sponsors from Abu Dhabi. This is just not true." In a separate statement issued by the club, City called the commission's findings an "opinion" that "contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe." City would be appealing against the verdict and will be "relentless" in attempting to clear its name," the statement said. Points deduction? Relegation? The next steps in the case The Premier League said sanctions will be decided in a separate, confidential hearing held by the same independent commission at an unspecified date. It also depends on the completion of the appeal that City needs to lodge by Friday. According to Rule W64 of the Premier League handbook, there is a range of sanctions available to the commission, from a fine, to a points deduction to expulsion from the league. For context, Everton was given a record 10-point deduction in 2023 — later reduced to six — for overspending in one financial period (three years up to the end of the 2021-22 season). City's charges are much, much wider — and unlike Everton, include a refusal to cooperate. An appeal by City will lead to a three-person Appeal Panel being set up. Sky Sports has reported that City could go to the High Court in London if it feels the process in the case

3393149222c4.text: By — Ken Sweet, Associated Press Ken Sweet, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/new-trump-proposal-would-require-tax-filers-to-disclose-citizenship-status-to-irs Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter New Trump proposal would require tax filers to disclose citizenship status to IRS Politics Oct 1, 2026 5:51 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — The Trump administration would require U.S. taxpayers to disclose their citizenship and work authorization status to the IRS as part of a proposed change to the annual tax form that nearly all workers file each year. Administration officials argue the new requirement will help the federal government stop immigrants lacking permanent legal status from collecting federal benefits they are not eligible for, potentially saving taxpayers up to $2 billion. But taxpayer and privacy advocates say the data could be used to help find and deport those people. WATCH: DOJ deploys tactic to strip naturalized Americans of citizenship "It could be used as an immigration enforcement tool and that is probably the reason why they are doing this," said David Bier, director of immigration studies at the libertarian-leaning Cato Institute. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Most Americans will see it as a new checkbox that gives the government even more information on taxpayers. But those living in the country illegally face a more complicated choice: Declare on a tax return that they are not authorized to live in the U.S. or lie on the return, which is a felony. Some may stop filing their taxes altogether. "It's dragging the IRS into this administration's immigration policies," said Nina Olson, executive director for the Center for Taxpayer Rights. The IRS posted its draft 1040 form for 2026 in late August. It includes the question, "At the time you file your return, are you, and your spouse if filing jointly, a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, or an alien lawfully authorized to work in the U.S.?" There are "Yes" or "No" checkboxes for both the filer and their spouse. A draft of a second form, known as Schedule 3-A used to claim refundable tax credits, asks a similar question. The questions are not optional. Every tax filer must certify under penalty of law their immigration or citizenship status to the IRS to file their return. The Treasury Department says the new question is meant to keep immigrants lacking permanent legal status from taking advantage of refundable tax credits, such as the Earned Income Tax Credit or the Additional Child Tax Credit. These are credits for which low- and middle income workers and families may qualify that often result in a refund back to the taxpayer. In a statement, a Treasury Department official said the information will be "subject to a variety of privacy, disclosure and other legal protections." The statement did not say whether the information will be shared with immigration enforcement agencies. WATCH: How Trump's immigration crackdown made it harder to become a U.S. citizen Despite not being authorized to live and work in the U.S., immigrants that do not have permanent legal status do pay taxes. A 2024 report by the National Taxpayer Advocate found 3.8 million tax returns where a taxpayer used an Individual Tax Identification Number, or ITIN. While an ITIN can be issued for a variety of purposes, undocumented workers who cannot obtain a Social Security number are among those who use them. IRS data show that taxpayers who filed those nearly 4 million returns paid $14.4 billion in income taxes and $6.5 billion in Social Security and Medicare taxes. A valid Social Security Number, not an ITIN, is required to qualify for the Earned Income Tax Credit. The IRS checks Social Security Numbers against Social Security Administration records for each claim of the EITC. Because of this process, Olson said she believes the new proposal is unnecessary. "Your citizenship or residency status is not information the IRS needs to process a return. It's not even information the IRS needs to process these tax credits," she said. "The IRS already has Social Security data on taxpayers, as well as ITIN information. It already has what it needs to process a return." Immigrants lacking permanent legal status are generally not eligible for federal benefits after Congress overhauled federal welfare programs in the mid-1990s. A tax filer needs to be a U.S. citizen or a green card holder to claim the EITC or CTC, with some limited exceptions. But some immigrants in the U.S. who presently qualify for some of these credits would not under the new policy. This would include people covered under the Obama-era Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, those with temporary protected status and temporary workers in the country under H1-B visas. The Trump administration argues in its proposal that the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act, the law that governs who is eligible for benefit programs, should be applied to refundable tax credits as well. The research paper published this week estimates that 671,000 people, including 309,000 children, will lose the Earned Income Tax Credit under this policy. Another roughly 1.1 million people, including 574,000 children, will lose the Additional Child Tax Credit. Most of the children that would lose eligibility to these credits are U.S. citizens, according to these researchers at Boston University, Columbia University and the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, because one or more of their parents' citizenship or immigration status. The Trump administration has tried to use the IRS to implement its immigration policies before. Last year, the Treasury Department agreed to share confidential taxpayer information of immigrants with U.S. Immigrat

77a0a1af687b.text: By — Dave Collins, Associated Press Dave Collins, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/california-helicopter-crash-kills-2-people-leaves-2-hospitalized-and-1-missing Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter California helicopter crash kills 2 people, leaves 2 hospitalized and 1 missing Nation Oct 1, 2026 5:34 PM EDT A medical helicopter transporting a patient crashed off Catalina Island near Los Angeles, killing two people and leaving two hospitalized, authorities said Thursday. Rescuers continued searching Thursday for a fifth person who was aboard the aircraft and went missing after the Wednesday night crash. WATCH: Are helicopters safe? Aviation expert weighs in on factors behind notable crashes The Coast Guard, area firefighters and divers with the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department were among emergency personnel who worked through the night, Coast Guard Capt. Stacey Crecy said at a news conference. "We're still doing an active search for the person who's missing and then in addition to that, the divers and the remote operated vehicle are going to get a look at more of the wreckage and hopefully if there's a sunken fuselage … we're hoping to get a better picture of that this morning," Crecy said. The cause of the crash was not immediately clear. Crecy said the helicopter went down shortly after takeoff and hit the water a short distance from the island. Authorities were working on identifying the victims, she said. "We believe that the medical aircraft was transporting a person off the island for additional medical care on the mainland," Crecy said, adding that she did not have more information on the transport or the patient. According to preliminary information released by the Federal Aviation Administration, the pilot and a cabin crew member were killed. Another cabin crew member was seriously injured and a passenger had minor injuries, the FAA said. The crash came 11 days after a firefighting helicopter went down and killed two pilots in Yosemite National Park in California, and two weeks after a news helicopter crashed in Los Angeles, killing two people. First responders were called to the crash shortly before 8 p.m. Wednesday and pulled four people from the water. Two were pronounced dead at the scene, and two, in stable condition, were brought to hospitals on the mainland, the Los Angeles County Fire Department said. Firefighters on the island were able to get to the scene quickly by boat, Crecy said. The National Transportation Safety Board said it is investigating and identified the helicopter as a Eurocopter EC-135-P2. NTSB staff were expected to arrive on the scene later Thursday. The aircraft will be brought to a secure facility for evaluation, a board spokesperson said. Authorities said the helicopter was submerged in 240 feet (73 meters) of water off Catalina, which is located about 22 miles (35 kilometers) off the mainland of Los Angeles County. The helicopter landed on the island shortly after 7 p.m., following a 24-minute flight from an airport in Oceanside, California, according to the flight tracking service Flightradar24. The helicopter was operated by REACH Air Medical Services of Sacramento, California. "At this time, we are gathering information and coordinating with emergency responders and authorities," the company said in a statement. "Our thoughts are with the families, loved ones and colleagues affected by this tragedy. We are focused on supporting our team and everyone impacted during this incredibly difficult time." The company said it was unable to share additional details, out of respect for the people involved and the ongoing emergency response. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 47fc8c6e4281.text: By — Michael Casey, Associated Press Michael Casey, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/judge-denies-motion-asking-for-lindsay-clancy-to-be-found-not-guilty-due-to-lack-of-evidence Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge denies motion asking for Lindsay Clancy to be found not guilty due to lack of evidence Nation Oct 1, 2026 7:09 PM EDT EDITOR'S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. BOSTON (AP) — The judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder case on Thursday refused to declare her not guilty, turning down a defense motion that had argued there wasn't enough evidence to prove she was responsible for killing her three children. During Clancy's first trial, which ended Sept. 4 with a deadlocked jury, her defense argued that she was not criminally responsible because of a mental disease, specifically a rare condition called postpartum psychosis. As such, the defense didn't dispute that the 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse carried out the killings at her family's Massachusetts home in 2023. However, in a hearing earlier this week, Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington tried to persuade the judge that prosecutors had not offered any proof that Clancy did it. Prosecutors argued there was plenty of evidence, calling Reddington's claim "laughable." WATCH: In return to court, Lindsay Clancy's lawyer now questions whether she killed her children Prosecutors have yet to decide whether they will put the case in front of a jury for a second time. They could choose to retry her on first-degree murder charges or seek to try her only on lesser charges, including second-degree murder or manslaughter, or drop the case entirely. In his ruling Thursday, Judge William Sullivan noted that for the purposes of his decision, he was required to analyze the evidence in the light most favorable to prosecutors — and that it was up to the jury, not the judge, to decide whether to believe expert witnesses for the defense who testified that Clancy was not responsible for her actions because of mental illness. "There was evidence introduced, both physical and circumstantial, that would permit a rational trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of the charge of murder," Sullivan wrote. At the first trial, prosecutors acknowledged that Clancy had mental health problems that included months of treatment and a stay in a psychiatric hospital, but argued that she knew what she was doing when she strangled the children — the youngest just 8 months old — then tried to kill herself. Sullivan had declared a mistrial with the jury split 11 to 1 in favor of acquitting Clancy of murder charges. In Tuesday's hearing, Reddington suggested the entire case "was based on speculation" and listed shortcomings in the prosecution's case. There was almost no police investigation, he claimed, and significant questions revolving around Clancy's condition outside the night of the killings and her lack of memory of what happened. At the trial, jurors heard testimony that Clancy said she heard voices instructing her to kill 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan Clancy. Her DNA was found on exercise bands used to strangle them. Before the trial, Reddington himself filed a motion in which he said Clancy was willing to stipulate, in writing, to her involvement in the children's deaths. "For the first time, the defendant is arguing that there is no evidence she did this," Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham told the judge. "I'd suggest to you the entire record is voluminous as to information supporting the fact that she did this." Clancy remains charged with murder and is expected to stay at a psychiatric hospital until her case is resolved. Clancy could have been sentenced to life in prison if convicted of murder. If acquitted, the judge could have ordered her confined to a mental health facility. Her former husband, Patrick Clancy, who discovered the children's bodies, has said in interviews that he forgives her. The livestreamed trial generated intense public interest and drew attention to maternal mental health after childbirth. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 648a9a193402.text: By — Nicolas Garriga, Associated Press Nicolas Garriga, Associated Press By — John Leicester, Associated Press John Leicester, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/student-protests-grip-france-as-prime-minister-lecornu-calls-crisis-meeting Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Student protests grip France as Prime Minister Lecornu calls crisis meeting World Oct 1, 2026 6:43 PM EDT PARIS (AP) — France's prime minister convened a crisis meeting Thursday and canceled ministers' trips to focus on the nationwide spread of protests, some violent, by high school students venting about under-resourced schools, long hours and other complaints. The demonstrations erupted in Paris-region schools last week and have snowballed, with police making hundreds of arrests in clashes with the young protesters. Authorities have reported many dozens of injuries, including from hurled objects but also, in some suspected cases, from police riot-control projectiles. The protests are quickly blowing up as a hot topic in the election campaign to replace President Emmanuel Macron, who is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term next May. They are also heightening pressure on the government beset by France's growing financial problems, and overshadowing the release on Thursday of its proposed cost-cutting budget for 2027. At a Paris high school where students barricaded an entrance, 18-year-old Salama Gargouri said protesters want to target "overloaded schedules, the system, the teachers, people who don't listen to us, the university application process." High school students in France often start classes at 8 a.m. and remain at school until late afternoon. "Older people say, 'Kids, go to school from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. every day.' But you don't know what that does mentally," said Janna Tahari, another Paris high school student. Arson, thrown projectiles and other violence on the margins of some protests have caused mounting injuries and recriminations. The interior minister has issued orders for police to break up blockades that prevent pupils from attending classes and to put a stop to violence and vandalism. Juliette Estiville, a high school Spanish teacher, said that the repression of the protests led her to join the students. "So, I'm here just to provide protection, to form a barrier between the police and the students," she said. "And indeed, today went well, it's going well, but I really think that the teachers who come to the blockades are really just there to protect our young people." Education Minister Edouard Geffray said Thursday's violence included a school set on fire and staff doused with gasoline. He said he issued instructions that classes be held remotely when blockades or damage to schools put students at risk. "Violence will not deprive our students of their fundamental right to education," Geffray said in a post on X. Far-left presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon has denounced the government response as repressive. His critics have accused Mélenchon's party of inciting violence and using the unrest to score points ahead of the presidential election. The office of Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said he asked ministers to cancel any planned official trips in the coming days, to enable authorities and police to focus on dealing with the demonstrations. Samuel Petrequin in Paris contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 1ecdde15091a.text: House Democratic leadership is pointing to the colossal spending by President Trump's super PACs in their behind-the-scenes efforts to get members to pay their dues to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee , Axios has learned. Why it matters: DCCC dues have fueled heated infighting among House Democrats in recent months, with several proposals emerging to force members to cough up more money. Some House Democrats want to require colleagues to pay their dues before seeking committee leadership roles, as The Washington Sun first reported . But other lawmakers, particularly in the Progressive and Black Caucuses, are "furious" about these suggestions, said a senior House Democrat, who told Axios that "members ... don't like threats." Driving the news: "While our case to the American people is strong, our Frontliners and candidates face ugly daily attacks from the right as MAGA Inc. unloads its coffers," DCCC chair Suzan DelBene (D-Wash.) wrote in an email to House Democrats obtained by Axios . "We need the resources to fight back and support our battleground colleagues and candidates in these final weeks," she added. DelBene ended the email with a plea for dues payments: "I urge everyone to make a dues contribution today. Let's make sure we don't have any regrets on Election Day." Between the lines: While several House Democrats noted to Axios that DelBene routinely urges members to pay their dues — in emails and at caucus meetings — some clocked a more urgent tone than usual. One lawmaker described the email, which was sent out on Wednesday, as "slightly more aggressive about shaming people" about not paying their dues than past entreaties. By the numbers: A pair of super PACs linked to MAGA Inc. have emerged as two of the top spenders on congressional races nationwide despite launching in September. No Going Back PAC and Safety and Affordability PAC have respectively spent $50 million and $38 million on ads in House races, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact. That makes them the fourth and fifth largest outside ad spenders in the country, after Democrats' House Majority PAC and Republicans' Congressional Leadership Fund and American Action Network. The intrigue: DelBene's email included the final version of House Democrats' August dues report, a draft copy of which was first reported by The Sun. The report shows significant progress from April, with leadership going from 28 members who have paid 100% or more of their dues to 66. Still, the August report lists 100 House Democrats as having paid 25% or less of their dues, including 38 who have paid none at all — though about half are swing-district members exempt from dues payments.

db8217b00912.text: Democratic House leaders are being pressured by their members over the lack of Black candidates receiving top-level party support in the final weeks of the 2026 midterms, Axios has learned. Why it matters: With 33 days to go, Democrats are torn between triaging their resources and satisfying all corners of their party's diverse but fractious racial coalition. Zoom in: Some Black lawmakers have taken their concerns to Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and DCCC chair and Rep. Suzan DelBene (D-Wash.) about the lack of Black candidates on the DCCC's " Red to Blue " list, according to a senior aide to a House Democrat. Congressional Black Caucus Chair Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.) spoke personally with DelBene about the lack of Black candidates on Red to Blue, according to two sources familiar with the matter. The intrigue: The dearth of Black representation was a hot topic of conversation among legislators at the Congressional Black Caucus' annual conference in D.C. in September, three people told Axios. "Members were openly talking about it, and they were pissed," said one Democratic operative. "Red to Blue" provides fundraising and staffing assistance to contenders in swing districts. The intrigue: Their push comes as some legislators argue that Democrats should do more to support Black candidates in the wake of a recent Supreme Court ruling that could threaten Black representation in Congress. Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), a CBC member, told Axios that "with the CBC under attack through gerrymandering and voter suppression, it's essential that the party invest in Black candidates." In particular, she urged the DCCC to help Justin Pearson, a Black candidate running in a long-shot bid for Tennessee's 9th House District. "Justin Pearson is an exceptional candidate who has proven that coalition-building and community-centered campaigns can make strides — even with the odds stacked against him," she said. "He is exactly the type of candidate the DCCC should be investing in." Yes, but: Other CBC members say the party must be hard-nosed about its spending in 2026's final stretch, and that Black candidates such as Pearson and Raymond Smith in North Carolina's 3rd District are simply in territory that is too favorable to Republicans to warrant a serious investment. "Jeffries, CBC PAC, DCCC, etc. can absolutely not be poor fiduciaries and spend money on races that are not attainable," one House Democrat told Axios in a text. Added this lawmaker: "We need to make sure, next cycle, that we do a better job of recruiting Black candidates ... in actual Red to Blue seats. Not seats we wish were Red2Blue." Some Democrats acknowledge that Pearson and Smith are facing an uphill battle in red districts. However, they argue, the DCCC has other ambitious races on its "Red to Blue" list that Cook Political Report rates solidly Republican and likely Republican, respectively. The big picture: Jeffries was asked at a press conference on Wednesday about the lack of Black candidates in the "Red to Blue" program. Jeffries said it is "largely a result of, you know, the primary process — there were in fact not a lot of candidates who stepped forward in these competitive districts." He also defended the DCCC's record of supporting frontline Black candidates, such as Reps. Emilia Sykes (D-Ohio) and Jahana Hayes (D-Conn.). "When I came into Congress, I think there were 38 members of the Congressional Black Caucus. Right now, there are 62," he said. "That's because the DCCC has actually partnered with the Congressional Black Caucus political action committee to grow the number of members of the CBC in districts that are overwhelmingly white." What they're saying: "The CBC is in lockstep with Leader Jeffries," said CBC PAC spokesperson Chris Taylor in a statement. "At his direction, the DCCC has backed our shared commitment to recruiting and investing to elect Black candidates and reach Black voters with real investment. Together, we will deliver the Democratic majority and make Hakeem Jeffries Speaker." "We have enjoyed a strong partnership with the CBC PAC," said DCCC executive director Julie Merz in a statement. It noted that the group "began investing in talking to and organizing Black voters in key districts earlier than ever this election cycle." Between the lines: This is not the first time the DCCC has caught heat from House Democrats' internal factions this year for its strategic decision-making. Members of the Congressional Hispanic and Progressive Caucuses raged at the House Democratic campaign arm in June for spending $135,000 against a CHC- and CPC-backed primary candidate. What's next: The DCCC's "Red to Blue" slate is ever-evolving, and there have been rumblings in Democratic circles in recent weeks that some Black candidates may soon be added to the program. Jeffries said Wednesday that there "emerging opportunities in places throughout the South that we're closely monitoring." A source familiar with the DCCC's planning said it expects to expand the battlefield further.

eab5a61b07f7.text: By — Amy Sherman, PolitiFact Amy Sherman, PolitiFact By — Louis Jacobson, PolitiFact Louis Jacobson, PolitiFact Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/a-fact-checked-guide-to-trumps-talking-points-and-falsehoods-at-midterm-rallies Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A fact-checked guide to Trump's talking points and falsehoods at midterm rallies Politics Oct 1, 2026 7:41 PM EDT This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. President Donald Trump is hitting the campaign trail to support Republican candidates in toss-up races that will determine which party controls Congress for the final two years of his presidency. PolitiFact listens to Trump's public remarks every day. Although there is always room for surprising new lines, he tends to repeat boasts about his achievements and attacks on Democrats. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Here's a list of more than two dozen go-to Trump statements and how they square for accuracy, drawing from his Republican National Convention midterm speech, subsequent speeches and interviews, and his Sept. 16 North Carolina rally. Jump to a section for our analysis of his claims on affordability, taxes and tariffs, artificial intelligence, immigration, military activities and the Iran war, energy and gas prices, voting and elections, crime, the White House ballroom, campaign promises and democratic socialism. Affordability, taxes and tariffs We have "$22 trillion coming into this country" in foreign investment — midterm convention speech False. The number Trump cites is almost double the $11.2 trillion listed on the White House's website. The website's tally should be viewed with caution. It includes aspirational, multi-year goals for sprawling projects on AI infrastructure, semiconductors, energy, quantum computing, biotechnology and manufacturing. Some examples involve future purchases or sales of products, rather than capital investments. Some listed pledges from countries in the Middle East aren't plausible when compared to those countries' gross domestic product, such as the United Arab Emirates pledging an amount equal to three years of the country's entire economic output. Americans' "401ks are up about $46,000." — remarks in Ireland Mostly False. The stock market has notched notable increases during Trump's second term, but a $46,000 rise is not supported. Fidelity Investments data shows that between Dec. 31, 2024, and March 31, 2026, the average increase in 401(k) balances was $9,454. Fidelity hasn't updated its data since March, but the S&P 500, a broad market gauge, was up 20% between the end of March and mid-September, and if that jump is fully applied to the figure, it would increase the value to only about $11,300. "More Americans are working today by far than ever before." — speech to the United Nations General Assembly Half True. Employment in August was at a record high of more than 159 million workers — largely driven by population growth. Two other statistics for working people aren't at record levels. The labor force participation rate and the employment-population ratio for workers ages 25 to 54 are relatively high by historical standards, but they've fallen slightly on Trump's watch. Both metrics were higher during the latter part of Biden's term. "The prices are coming down, not only of food but just about everything else." — in Oval Office remarks Mostly False. Through August, overall, prices increased by about 4.7% since Trump began his second term, and groceries have risen by about 3.4%. By mid-September, gasoline was up 41% from January 2025, when Trump began his second term, a spike driven by the Iran war. Fuel oil and natural gas have risen as well. Electricity was up by more than 8%. READ MORE: Most Americans blame Trump for high prices as his economic approval hits new low, AP-NORC poll shows Coffee, ground beef and chicken breast were also up during this period. Car prices, eggs, bacon and bread prices were down. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act is the "largest tax cut in American history." — remarks in Ireland Mostly False. When factoring in the bill's extension of Trump's 2017 tax cuts, the tax savings from Trump's 2025 law rank third among tax cut laws since 1980, following bills signed in 1981 by Reagan in 1981 and in 2012 by Obama. Trump's 2025 legislation means "no tax" on tips, overtime and Social Security. — remarks in Ireland There's a bit more to know about the bill's tax breaks for tipped workers, workers receiving overtime and older Americans. For one, the breaks expire in 2028, unless Congress extends them. Tips: The law gives most workers a tax break on some tipped income. Households earning less than $150,000 (for a single filer) or $300,000 (for joint filers) would receive tips tax-free; above those levels, the tax reduction would be partial. Overtime: The law covers people who work overtime under the Fair Labor Standards Act, which requires time-and-a-half pay for weekly hours worked over 40. The break does not apply to overtime that is not required under the law, such as overtime paid under more stringent state laws. In addition, the law makes tax-free the incremental increase in pay from working overtime — the "and a half" portion — so it won't eliminate taxation on all the money people receive from working overtime. Social Security: The bill falls short of a full repeal of Social Security taxation. The bill gives an additional $6,000 tax deduction to people ages 65 and older. This does not mean all Social Security beneficiaries receive a tax cut (because some of them are under 65). Some people get the tax break without receiving Social Security (if they are over 65 and not collecting benefits yet). These deductions come on top of existing tax deductions fo

1b5bc5f56561.text: Mortgage rates spiked to their highest level in nearly three years, continuing their climb above the 7% threshold. Why it matters: Housing sales were already slow due to a lack of inventory and elevated rates, creating a risk that the market could further its freeze. Zoom in: The weekly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.28% as of Thursday, Freddie Mac reported . That's up 0.94 points from a year ago, and up 0.25 points from last week. Mortgage rates closely track 10-year Treasury yields, which have risen by over 1.25 percentage points since the start of the Iran war in February. The impact: Mortgage applications are plunging. The Mortgage Bankers Association reported Wednesday that applications during the week ended Sept. 25 fell 6% from a week earlier. With rates at their highest point since November 2023, home buyers are beginning to turn to adjustable-rate mortgages. ARMs made up 10.3% of mortgage applications in the most recent period, marking the highest point since October 2025, according to MBA. "Affordability and borrower demand have weakened in recent weeks as the higher-rate environment continues to put pressure on both prospective homebuyers and homeowners looking to refinance," MBA CEO Bob Broeksmit said in a statement. What we're watching: There are early signs that rising rates could put downward pressure on prices as sellers look to attract buyers. "Softer market conditions and greater affordability pressures have contributed to increased pricing pressures across many of our markets," KB Home senior VP William Hollinger said last week on an earnings call, noting the home builder had "made pricing adjustments." Reality check: Rates may not remain elevated for long. "We expect the situation to improve next year, as energy prices drop back and the aggressive Fed tightening cycle which has been priced into money markets does not fully materialise, causing mortgage rates to retrace most of their recent increases," Capital Economics senior North America economist Thomas Ryan wrote Tuesday. Capital Economics projected that 30-year fixed mortgage rates would average 6.25% by the end of 2027.

ce76d8f81164.text: The initial investigation into the attempted hijacking of the FlyDubai flight from the UAE to Israel found that the co-pilot went through religious Islamic radicalization in recent months, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News Thursday. Why it matters: Netanyahu's remarks, confirmed by an Israeli intelligence official and people who worked with the co-pilot, strengthen the possibility that the incident was a terrorist attack. Driving the news: The investigation is being led by the Saudi security services, which have been interrogating the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the other pilot while the plane was en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The United Arab Emirates has formed a team to investigate the incident. "The investigation includes examining all circumstances and motives surrounding the incident, including any possible connection to terrorist activity or intent, and whether it involved prior planning or direction," a spokeswoman for Emirati Foreign Minister Afra Alhameli said in a statement . Behind the scenes: An Israeli intelligence official said the Mossad and Shin Bet spy agencies are also investigating. "The Omani co-pilot went through a process of religious radicalization in recent years. We don't know yet if he is a 'lone wolf' or whether he was sent by someone to conduct an attack," the official said. The intrigue: On Wednesday, Israel's Channel 16 reported testimony of another FlyDubai pilot who knew the Omani co-pilot. According to the report, the co-pilot worked for the company for only eight months and was more religiously observant than most of his co-workers. What he's saying: President Trump told reporters Thursday he has reason to believe Iran was involved in the foiled hijacking. "Based on what I'm hearing is yes, but we're working on it right now," he said. Israeli officials say they currently don't have indications of Iranian involvement, by they haven't ruled it out. The Saudi Ministry of Interior said in a statement that UAE officials took part in the interrogation of the pilot and co-pilot. Both have been transferred to the UAE for further interrogation, per the statement. What to watch: One of the things that will be investigated is how an Omani national was assigned as a pilot on a flight to Israel. According to security protocols agreed to by the UAE and Israel, crew members from countries that don't have diplomatic relations with Israel can't serve on flights to Israel.

cb1bf3ba82e5.text: The relentless rise in long-term interest rates is starting to have effects on more parts of the economy, Kansas City Fed president Jeff Schmid told Axios Thursday. "You're starting to see some friction in some of the long-market users of credit," he said, pointing to multifamily housing and commercial lending. "Even on the mortgage rate side, it's starting to affect home prices, which is how the price of credit works relative to valuation," Schmid said at a conference on investing in rural America hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond in Asheville, N.C. The big picture: Schmid spoke alongside Richmond Fed president Tom Barkin and Boston Fed president Susan Collins, who weighed in on the forces driving the rise in borrowing costs. "I think you're seeing this trillion-dollar AI buildout, and I think it's not surprising that rates go up if you've got a lot more demand out there," Barkin added. Collins said AI investment is also helping drive the solid economic growth that has persisted despite higher borrowing costs. "I think it does have broader effects, not just in particular sectors," Collins said. But it "remains to be seen" whether investment will continue at its current pace, she added. The intrigue: Schmid likened the Fed's challenge of separating strong demand from supply-driven inflation to a seven-layer dip — one of his favorite foods. "The beauty of a seven-layer dip is you have equal amounts of beans and sour cream," Schmid said. Right now, with AI and data centers, "there's too much beans in that dip," he added. "And not enough chips!" quipped Barkin.

9a303b8b4d65.text: The U.S. military in recent weeks sent two additional Patriot missile batteries to protect oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, two U.S. officials and one regional source said. Why it matters: The U.S. wanted to reassure both allies that it would protect their key energy facilities in case President Trump decides to resume major combat operations against Iran. Trump said on Thursday that he's considering renewing a bombing campaign in the coming weeks. "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer," he said. Flashback: In early August, when Trump was considering launching a massive attack that included strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure, the leaders of both Saudi Arabia and Qatar lobbied him not to do it. They expressed grave concern that Iran would strike their oil and natural gas facilities in retaliation. U.S. officials said the pleas were a key reason Trump decided not to attack and move instead toward an economic pressure campaign. Behind the scenes: Last month, the U.S. military sent one additional Patriot battery to Saudi Arabia to protect a key oil facility. Another Patriot battery was sent to Qatar to protect a natural gas facility. The U.S. will need Saudi Arabia to allow it to use the country's airspace if major combat operations resume. But the Saudis are unlikely to grant permission if they feel oil facilities won't be protected. A spokesman for U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), Capt. Tim Hawkins, declined to comment. Reality check: Patriot batteries and especially their interceptors have become a highly sought-after commodity since the war in Iran started. The U.S. military transferred batteries and interceptors to the Middle East from other regional commands, raising concerns about readiness in other parts of the world. State of play: The U.S. military is sending more warships, fighter jets and troops to the Middle East ahead of a possible resumption of the war. A U.S. official said the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and its strike group left San Diego "quietly" on Sunday heading to the region. It's expected to arrive in the Middle East around mid-November. The Roosevelt will join the USS George H.W. Bush, which has been in the region since March, and the USS George Washington, which was sent from Japan during the summer and has been in the region for only about a month. "This means the Middle East region could potentially have up to three aircraft carrier strike groups. This is much more firepower," the U.S. official said. But another U.S. official said it hasn't been determined whether the Roosevelt will replace one of the aircraft carriers currently deployed to the Middle East or whether it will be additional. Zoom in: The Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group, which includes three amphibious ships carrying thousands of Marines from the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit, left for the region on Monday, a U.S. official said. It is expected to arrive in the Middle East by the end of November and join another Amphibious Group and Marine expeditionary unit that have been deployed to the region over the last few months.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general as a special prosecutor in investigating the alleged gang rape of a woman at Cornell University.
The woman has alleged she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house. The case, which stems back to 2024, was reopened after the woman filed a civil lawsuit last month that thrust the allegations into the national spotlight.
"New information has raised serious questions about how this case was handled, and I've lost faith in the Tompkins County DA's ability to fairly oversee it," Hochul said.
Hochul's announcement removes Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten from overseeing the case.
The BBC has contacted Van Houten's office.
He has defended his office's previous decision not to file charges in the case, arguing they were not given enough evidence to meet the legal threshold.
Van Houten reopened the case after the civil lawsuit and said much of the information released in recent weeks about the case was not passed to his office.
"The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued," Hochul said in a statement.
The attorney general will, if warranted, prosecute any offences found by her investigation and present evidence to a grand jury, the governor said.
James, the state's chief legal officer, said on X that she stood ready "to lead a process guided by the facts and the law".
"The Governor has entrusted my office with this investigation, and we do not take that responsibility lightly," James added.
Hochul and James are scheduled to provide an update on the investigation on Friday morning local time.
The woman at the centre of the case, identified anonymously as Jane Doe in court documents, filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university in September.
She alleged that she was drugged and raped by seven men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.
She claimed that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men, who have now become known as the Cornell Seven.
The case was initially referred to Van Houten, the top prosecutor in the county, in 2024.
Van Houten said his office did not bring charges at the time because he had only seen a statement from Doe implying the incident was consensual and that she had not been drugged.
This week, his office announced it would be reopening the case - less than two weeks after Doe filed her civil lawsuit.
Cornell has said it provided evidence to the district attorney's office from its own investigation, including a Snapchat group chat in which fraternity members discussed a "free" sexual encounter with Doe on the night of the alleged assault.
Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, has accused the district attorney of repeatedly changing his story amid news coverage of the case.

Australia's online safety regulator has found "significant gaps" in how popular gaming platforms protect children online.
In a new report it found inconsistent approaches in how Steam, Roblox, Fortnite and Minecraft implement child safety measures as research shows nine out of 10 children aged 8 to 17 in Australia have played online games.
"Australian children have a right to play online without being exposed to predators, sexual extortionists, violent extremist content or other harmful material," eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant said.
Weak safety on platforms allow "predatory adults" to make contact with children before grooming them, she said, for sexual exploitation or radicalisation.
The report found that Valve - the US gaming giant that owns Steam and Steam Chat - was the only provider that did not use a type of technology widely used by the industry to detect and remove known harmful content.
Valve also did not "proactively" use tools to detect child sexual exploitation or violent material in chats, with current systems mainly flagging scams, the report found.
Roblox, along with Valve, were noted in the report as using only internal datasets to train language detection systems and for not regularly retraining these models.
"We expect these services to lift their game to identify and combat serious harms such as child sexual exploitation, sexual extortion and material and activity which promotes, incites or instructs violence," Inman-Grant said.
Minecraft and Fortnite, which does offer child accounts, generally let users self-declare their age, the report highlighted, meaning anyone who said they were adults could access "higher-risk communication features".
Steam also relied on users self-declaring their age but the report acknowledged the platform had recently introduced age checks using credit cards, and that Roblox had put in stronger age checks since last December.
Another issue raised by the report was the inconsistent manner in which the four gaming platforms shared information and participated in industry initiatives.
Mojang Studios, developer of Minecraft, and Roblox shared industry expertise in combating child sexual exploitation as well as violent extremism online, but Valve did not.
Elsewhere, Fortnite maker Epic Games failed to share instances of breaches with other platforms under a global programme that was designed to combat online child sexual exploitation and abuse.
The report was based on information collected by Australia's eSafety Commission on how the platforms were protecting users from serious online harm between October 2025 and March 2026.
Australia has made global headlines in recent years for its stance on online safety, after it introduced its world-leading social media ban for under-16s last December - which did not include gaming platforms - and a more recent push to force tech giants to offer users a chance to opt-out of social media algorithms.
Valve, Fortnite, Roblox and Microsoft - which owns Minecraft - have been contacted for comment.
