Drive the Pacific Coast Highway, spearfish alongside Great White sharks, surf in Santa Cruz, dive for lobster, cast a line or set a crab pot: California is defined by its 840-mile coastline. Managing the miles of beach, reef and cliffsides that define the state is a complicated and controversial process and has long left out Indigenous Californians.
But this fall, the California Fish and Game Commission will vote on a set of tribal petitions to amend the state’s network of marine parks, marking a potential shift in the state’s management of marine resources.
California’s coastline is home to 125 marine protected areas, a system of underwater parks established to protect and enhance biodiversity in the state. After over a decade of use, data shows that the network is working to enhance biodiversity and climate resiliency, but for years the state has agonized over the next steps it should take to manage the network.
In 2023, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and Fish and Game Commission allowed the public to submit petitions for change—a process which drew criticism from all sides, much of it over fishing access and ecological benefits. Of the 20 petitions received, five are tribally led or co-led and seek to protect heritage sites, specific species and tribally important ecosystems. The tribal petitions are significant because tribes were left out as formal stakeholders when the Marine Life Protection Act, which guides the network, was passed in 1999.
While all of the petitions—tribally led or otherwise—are subject to the same level of scientific scrutiny, the tribal petitions represent a new thread of government-to-government consultation between tribes and the state of California in the management of marine resources. “ I suspect my fellow commissioners will give real deference to what the tribes are looking for and what their concerns are,” said Eric Sklar, president of the California Fish and Game Commission.
Conflicting Recommendations
The commission’s members will consider evaluations from two state agencies, both the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, which manages marine protected areas, and the Ocean Protection Council, which sets policy priorities for the network, as well as public comments, in casting their final votes.
Importantly, the recommendations from the department and council have drawn attention, since they differ in what next steps they suggest the commission take.
Of the five tribal petitions, three propose establishing new marine protected areas outright, while two request tribal harvest exemptions for specific species without the creation of a new protected area. For these tribal “take,” or fishing exemptions, both the council and department generally agree that the measures should be approved.
“Traditional harvest has so much more behind it,” said Rachel McCain, Natural Resource Department director for the Tolowa Dee-ni’ Nation. “It’s tied to culture and life ways and existence and identity. It’s way deeper than just catching fish.”
The Nation has requested that true smelt, which have been in decline for years, be limited to tribal take only within the Pyramid Point State Marine Conservation Area near the Oregon border.
But other requests for change are not as cut and dry. The Department of Fish and Wildlife recommends denial of the newly proposed tribal marine protected areas, while the Ocean Protection Council recommends approval of all but one proposal.
“ OPC’s recommendations reflect the best available science wherein they are very seriously considering how it is that they can make the MPA network more resilient to the impacts of climate change and protect some of the state’s most vulnerable habitats, like persistent kelp forests,” said Sandy Aylesworth, director of the Pacific Initiative, Nature, at the Natural Resources Defense Council. “And then CDFW’s recommendations, on the other hand, really read as if they are interested in entrenching decisions of the past.”
The conflicting recommendations reflect, in part, how the agencies serve different purposes. The department is tied to an evaluation framework established by the Fish and Game Commission in 2009, which outlines scientific metrics and ecological spacing that a protected area should meet. The council, on the other hand, is tasked with evaluating the network on far more flexible policy priorities to advance the Marine Life Protection Act.
The council’s recommendations are “intended to complement the comprehensive evaluations that the Department of Fish and Wildlife conducted under a separate set of questions and criteria,” said Jenn Eckerle, executive director of the Ocean Protection Council. The council, she said, approached its evaluations through a precautionary principle, considering worsening climate scenarios.
“… Our MPA network is one of the most effective conservation tools for safeguarding biodiversity and building climate resilience and protecting our $51 billion coastal economy and so it’s through that lens that we assessed the petitions,” she said.
Still, the differing recommendations have caused some confusion among stakeholders, especially in what new marine protections would look like. The department did not simply recommend denial of the new tribal marine protected areas, but suggested the state explore an entirely new designation under state parks, called “State Marine Cultural Preservation Areas.” This designation would require an entirely new process outside of the department’s purview, and caught tribal stakeholders off guard.

Two major challenges could complicate efforts to restore the Chesapeake Bay.
First, a new executive order from President Donald Trump revoked the longstanding framework for coordinating federal efforts to protect the bay. Second, seven Virginia tribes withdrew from formal participation after the Chesapeake Bay Program partnership denied them the signatory status they sought.
The new executive order replaces an Obama administration directive that created a broad federal framework for protecting and restoring the Chesapeake Bay. It named the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency as the lead agency for coordinating and overseeing federal efforts, and gave specific responsibilities to other participating federal agencies.
The new directive is narrower in scope. It directs federal agencies to focus funding and staff on projects that produce measurable improvements in water quality, particularly reductions in nutrient and sediment runoff. It argues that the previous order lacked clarity on implementation, citing stormwater management fees as an example of policies that placed an undue burden on residents and provided little or no benefit to the Bay’s environmental health.
The directive comes at a crucial moment for the Bay program and its partners. At its December 2025 meeting, the partnership approved a revised Bay Watershed Agreement that extended the region’s long-delayed pollution cleanup deadline to 2040.
At the meeting, the Chesapeake Executive Council, which makes policy decisions for the partnership between federal and state governments, and the District of Columbia, also directed staff to work with the Indigenous Conservation Council to bring tribal nations into the partnership.
Alison Prost, senior vice president for advocacy and restoration of the nonprofit Chesapeake Bay Foundation, said the 2009 order provided a clear roadmap by instructing agencies to develop strategic plans on bay restoration.
“The Trump executive order creates confusion,” Prost said, adding that “we need to figure out what the executive order means moving forward.”
In a statement, Maryland’s congressional delegation reacted sharply to the development, calling it “shortsighted and harmful” to the Bay communities. The statement said that removing that federal support could undermine the health of the Bay and the businesses and communities that depend on it. “Make no mistake: the Chesapeake Bay is a national treasure. And we will continue to fight for it.”.
Leila Duman, the Maryland Department of Natural Resources’ Chesapeake and Coastal Bays restoration officer, said the Clean Water Act, Chesapeake Bay Watershed Agreement and various Chesapeake Bay Program decisions and frameworks established over the last 17 years remain unchanged by Trump’s executive order. As a result, she said, the order should not affect Maryland’s restoration funding, planning or pollution reduction targets.
Jon Mueller, former vice president for litigation at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, said Obama’s order gave the EPA responsibility for overseeing federal agencies’ plans to meet the Bay’s pollution limits. Mueller warned that rescinding Obama’s order could eliminate federal coordination and accountability and undermine climate-adaptation planning and implementation.
Mueller said that eliminating stormwater fees, also known as “rain taxes,” would leave local governments hard-pressed to fund runoff-control measures while meeting their legal obligation to reduce pollution. Failure to meet those requirements “exposes them to enforcement actions by EPA, the state and citizens,” he said. Losing that funding would also leave communities more vulnerable to heavier rainfall driven by climate change, with more homes and businesses flooded and streets closed.
The EPA defended the order, saying it would focus federal efforts on measurable water-quality improvements while maintaining the agency’s obligations under the Clean Water Act.
But the agency did not specify whether the Federal Leadership Committee, annual action plans and progress reports would continue under another authority or be replaced. It also did not explain how agencies would decide which programs qualify for continued support or whether they would disclose funding and staffing decisions publicly.
Separately, the partnership faces a breakdown in its relationship with seven federally recognized Virginia tribes, whose representatives have withdrawn from formal engagement after negotiations failed to deliver the full partner status they asked for.
At a 2025 meeting, the Chesapeake Executive Council, the Chesapeake Bay Program’s decision-making body, committed to bringing tribes into the Bay partnership and directed staff to develop a roadmap for including tribal nations in future agreements.
Those recommendations, including pathways for formally including tribes as signatories to future Bay agreements, were due by July 1. But the program leadership missed the deadline and pushed the question to December. Instead, the negotiations came to a head unexpectedly in an early September meeting.

Richardson said she felt “the door was slammed in our face” after more than a year of work, including efforts to bring Indigenous knowledge into the program. The Signal Interview
In a little more than a decade, Octopus Energy has grown from an outlandish idea into Britainâs largest energy provider. It now powers 12 million homes in eight countries, manages wind and solar farms from Scotland to South Korea, manufactures heat pumps, installs smart meters, leases out 50,000 electric vehicles, and supplies technology to utilities around the world.
The tentacles of this âOctoverseâ all lead back to Greg Jackson, a founder-CEO who has built his 13,000-person company without bonuses, HR or IT teams, or a succession plan.
Beyond the walls of the companyâs London headquarters, which is filled with thousands of its plushy pink octopus mascots, Jacksonâs empire may look like an unwieldy one. It is not, he insists: âThe thing thatâs connecting it all is the underlying insight: that the technologies of electrification can deliver tremendous cost savings, but only if you build a new system.â And building that new system requires using every tool at his disposal.
âThereâs a scene in the movie Apollo 13 where the astronauts are stranded and theyâre going to die unless the solution is found. And on the ground, Mission Control assembles â¦ everything there is on the space station, like duct tape and bits of piping, and they say, this is all weâve got to save their lives,â he explains. âIn any business, you choose your constraints, and then how you assemble the stuff you have to create the outcome you want.â
Octopusâ job is âto take all these ingredients and say, how can we outcompete the old world of energy with better products and services with better value?â Jackson says, before reaching back to the beginning of that old world for another analogy.
âWhen [Thomas] Edison first started building electricity businesses, he didnât just have to innovate, fund, and build centralized electricity generation, which he did. He also had to invent the grid and distribution model. He also had to invent or sell the products that use electricity, from lightbulbs to music players. And if I look at what weâre doing, itâs almost trivial in comparison.â
How to run a 13,000-person company with no HR department
The growth of Octopus, which had revenues of Â£13.7 billion last year and a valuation of $9 billion at its last fundraising, poses a challenge for its irrepressible founder: how to transmit to thousands of employees the energy that has powered him since he dropped out of school at 16 to write video games.
Jackson no longer knows each staff member by name, but he still runs his company by the same rhythms with which he started it. Each Monday starts with a gathering of senior executives to review performance data from the previous week. That helps maintain âpace and alignment,â Jackson says. Each week ends with âfamily dinner,â a Friday afternoon all-hands event at which the company recaps its latest innovations, achievements, and challenges.
The Friday sessions began over beers with a small founding team, and Jackson âdiscovered that it was the best way of reminding you how great your colleagues were, and re-energizing you on the big picture.â Livestreams have since replaced in-person drinks. But the gatherings help Octopus âstart the week left-brain, end it right-brain,â Jackson says, and help him explain to staff what they need to do next âand maintain the energy to feel great about it.â
The company has no intranet or staff newsletters, he adds, so if people donât tune in to âfamily dinner,â they wonât know whatâs happening. Less is more in internal communications, he says: âThe more information you put out there, the less it gets read. What you want to do is make sure the stuff that goes out there is canonical and consumed.â
Octopus also has no central human resources department, devolving people management responsibilities to individual teams unless legal staff need to step in. Still a private company, it gives equity to every employee, but it pays no bonuses outside a few sales roles. Jackson says this is because heâs determined to focus people on the companyâs success, rather than their own individual advancement.
Similarly, Octopus sets no divisional performance targets, to keep each division from promoting whatever will make them look best at the expense of others, he adds.
âThe most important thing for us is to build trust among our team, so they wake up every morning thinking, âHow do I drive the companyâs mission?â Not, âHow do I get myself promoted?ââ
Hands-on leadership, from the cockpit to the customers
Even as Octopus has grown to span industries as diverse as renewable power generation and software licensing, Jackson says his job has barely changed. The CEOâs role is still to understand customers and industry economics; set the vision for where the company needs to go; and build a team with the expertise and innovative impulses to get it there.
For a pilot, the view from the cockpit window of a small Cessna is not that different from that of an Airbus A380, he says: âThe difference comes when you look back.â If Octopus became a more complex organization, âthen Iâd get drawn more into wandering down the aisle of the plane than looking forward out the window,â he reasons. âThe bit that really matters for me is being in the cockpit, looking forward, however many people weâve got behind us.â So Jackson is constantly checking that his headcount is not growing faster than Octopus is adding new customers, as he looks to avoid diseconomies of scale and guards against the spread of bureaucracy. Yet he is equally anxious about ensuring that he is not losing touch with customers as their numbers run into the millions.Â
Octopus was built on a proprietary technology platform called Kraken, which now has an $8.7 billion valuation and will soon spin out as a standalone company with its own listing. Kraken gives Jackson and every member of his staff a âsingle viewâ of everything that is happening in the company, from customer service to pricing, energy trading to finance.

An Indian pilot who was attacked by his co-pilot on an Israel-bound Flydubai plane has received a call in his hospital bed from India PM Narendra Modi.

Immigrant advocates are grappling with the Supreme Courtâs decision to allow the Trump administration to move forward with third-country deportations, which will leave the policy in place for months while they wait for the court to rule on it.
Trina Realmuto, lead counsel for the plaintiffs that challenged the policy at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, called it a âdevastating result.â She warned migrants could be sent to countries âwhere they may face persecution, torture, imprisonment, or other grave danger.â
The Trump administration has signed deals with various countries to accept deported migrants, many of them in Africa. Burundi was the latest to announce it will accept migrants.
The Supreme Courtâs unsigned order this week lifted a ruling requiring migrants receive notice of â and a chance to challenge â their deportation to countries where they have no personal ties.
The high court will hear oral arguments on the case, but not until December, meaning a decision will come next year.
The Department of Homeland Security celebrated this weekâs move, with the agencyâs general counsel declaring it âa bad day for criminal illegals and open borders activists alike.â
The arrangements have drawn mounting scrutiny, most recently after migrants deported to Equatorial Guinea were held at gunpoint and beaten.
Congressional Democrats are vowing to investigate the deportations if they take control of the House or Senate â or both â in Novemberâs midterm elections.
â Adrian Elimian

224a6189359f.text:
Ashleyâs view
The tech industry is facing strange headwinds in Washington after meeting with President Donald Trump and senior administration officials this week and signing a âmorally bindingâ accord on AI.
The meeting with Trump was largely successful for all of the companies involved. But now these same firms have to navigate maintaining ties with the president while placating Democrats who could very well control both houses of Congress next year. Thatâs not to mention what could be a massively consequential midterm election, fueled by AI anxiety among voters, that could test the bounds of their power.
âCompanies are going to have to make it more specific, on how theyâre going to operationalize it,â Chris Lehane, OpenAIâs chief global affairs officer, told Semafor about the new White House accord on âSuper Intelligenceâ signed by the leaders of several top firms and Trump this week, including OpenAI President Greg Brockman.
âWeâve certainly approached this believing â¦ itâs also in our self-interest to make sure that people feel that we are actually building things safely and deploying responsibly,â Lehane said, adding that OpenAIâs support for certain state-level AI bills and its hopes for a federal bill will remain the same.
âThatâs almost either a democratic market force, or the actual market forces themselves. Like, if youâre making cars, youâre going to want to make sure the cars are safe, or people arenât going to buy your cars, whether there are regulations or not,â he added.
Know More
Before lawmakers departed Washington to focus on campaigning ahead of the November elections, AI companies were still in active discussions on Capitol Hill. Theyâre trying to influence forthcoming bills and determine where they can find consensus with lawmakers, a tech industry source and a source who works on AI policy told Semafor.
Companies know that the midterms are likely to mean a Democratic-run House and possibly a Democratic-run Senate, and with that will come more momentum to pass AI legislation â and likely more scrutiny of their operations, particularly for firms that have demonstrated ties with the Trump administration. âThereâs a world where people are smarter and smarter about these issues, and bills are going to be introduced imminently that are much better than what weâve seen,â the AI policy source told Semafor.
After the election, legislating is an obvious place to go, given the public and many lawmakers in both parties want to see something done, the tech industry source told Semafor.
Considering where the Trump administration was a year ago â that is, attempting to ban state-level AI bills â progress toward federal AI policy is slow, but itâs inching forward, the tech industry source said. The FTC also kicked off its own AI inquiry, which may not yield much in the end, but nevertheless represents a signal from the administration that regulators are prepared to use existing laws to go after any companies that they suspect have hurt consumers.
Still, the White Houseâs pro-AI posture is unlikely to fundamentally change, and Trump will remain the most important voice on it until the end of his term. Groups that are pushing for data center expansion and industry-friendly laws have plenty of money and resources, plus their own complicated financial ties to the AI and tech companies themselves.
Anthropic may be experiencing the most whiplash since the surreal AI summit: Days after a federal court upheld its designation by the Pentagon as a supply chain risk, CEO Dario Amodei dined with Trump at the White House.
The administration has repeatedly painted Anthropic as the face of a pro-AI safety movement that is âwokeâ and composed of âdoomersâ â too focused on AIâs harms and trying to gin up fear for ulterior motives.
âI think theyâre going to try to walk this tightrope for two years,â the person who works on AI policy told Semafor. âTheyâre in a weird place. [Undersecretary of Defense] Emil Michael hates you, and is tweeting about you every day. Nonetheless, the government seems to find you indispensable to their operations.â
Sarah Heck, a policy lead at Anthropic, posted on X following the White House meeting: âYou canât do safety from second place.â She shared a video clip of Amodei applauding the accord while saying AI still has very real risks and how companies address them is still under discussion.
On Thursday, Heck added: âTo be clear, Iâm talking about the US and its allies here: We canât ensure AI is developed safely unless the US is in the lead.â

Under normal circumstances, Cornell University is a beautiful place to study at this time of year. Autumn leaves bring pops of colour to its stately buildings, which are set against the backdrop of the rolling hills of upstate New York.
But students and faculty members say the investigation into an alleged gang rape that took place on these grounds two years ago has cast a "dark cloud" over the campus - stirring anger, concern over fraternity culture, and a backlash against the university's handling of the situation.
Students and staff at the Ivy League university spoke to the BBC, some on condition of anonymity, saying the tension on campus had become palpable since the 2024 case resurfaced in recent weeks.
At a student assembly on Thursday, which was organised to allow students to voice their concerns, many called for drastic change at the university.
Others labelled the perceived lack of justice a "disgrace" and said they felt ashamed of the prestigious university, which has defended its handling of the case.
"We deserve to know that our institution values our safety more than its reputation," undergraduate Sophia Riley Sim told those at the gathering.
Sim said she had been too upset by the case to attend classes for the past week.
The accuser at the centre of the alleged gang rape, known anonymously as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell on 16 September, saying she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in 2024.
She claimed that Cornell had failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved in the incident. The men have been dubbed the Cornell Seven.
Cornell has already agreed to an independent investigation into the rape allegation.
The university has also defended its handling of the issue to date, external, saying it conducted an "extensive investigation" that lasted several months following the report of the incident, and that it followed applicable federal civil rights law.
Shortly after Thursday's student assembly at Cornell, New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced she had appointed the state attorney general, Letitia James, as special prosecutor in the case.
She said she had "lost faith" in the Tompkins County district attorney, who was previously leading the investigation. James therefore takes over the case from Matthew Van Houten.
Van Houten's office initially concluded that the evidence did not meet the legal threshold to bring charges - before reopening a criminal investigation last week in light of the new civil complaint, a move that Cornell supported.
The upcoming "Justice for Survivors" protest, planned at the university for 5 October, is being advertised in flyers all over campus. It calls on Cornell to take action against alleged rape culture.
Student organisers are calling for Cornell to expel and revoke the degrees of the alleged perpetrators of the rape, rewrite policies around sexual assault punishments, initiate an external investigation of the university and mandate prevention training for campus police.
As part of its account of its prior investigation of the case, Cornell says: "At its conclusion, the hearing panel issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell."
Cornell says it is legally prevented from publicly disclosing specific disciplinary outcomes about disciplinary students, adding that "we recognise that this legal limitation can be frustrating".
Across campus, the case has stirred anger.
One fourth-year student recalled that it had been hard to live there in 2024, in the aftermath of the incident, as rumours began spreading about Jane Doe.
Now, two years on, she told the BBC how she and her friends felt "overwhelmed" and "disappointed", comparing the atmosphere on campus to a "dark cloud". Cornell, she believes, mishandled things.
She wants the administration to admit what she sees as its mistakes, calling the lack of transparency disheartening.
She also asked why multiple men in a group chat for members of Chi Phi - the fraternity group at the centre of the allegations - did not speak up. A chapter of the fraternity was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.
Students and community members also used Thursday's student assembly meeting to vent their frustrations and disappointment.
"I am very disgusted to be here, to be paying this institution to be here," freshman Eliana Dolven-Miller said. "There was a lot of anger in that room, I was very angry."
Eeshaan Chaudhuri, the student assembly chair, opened the meeting by saying that the campus stood "with victims of sexual violence".
"We don't tolerate it here on campus, and I think I can speak for every single one of us, and I can say we're absolutely ashamed of the events that happened on our campus," Chaudhuri said.
The student group has also raised a resolution calling on the university to release a written account of how it handled the alleged sexual assault, including what evidence was gathered and whether and when the university referred the matter to campus police.
A faculty member said the mood on campus was "dismal". Staff were not trained therapists, she said, so it was hard to know how to navigate these discussions with students.
It was an "incredible situation that was soâ¦ I just don't understand," she said, adding that she was unsure if the university should have gone further, and adding that this was not the first time a fraternity group had had problems on campus.
Some of the freshmen, or first-year students, who spoke to the BBC had only arrived at Cornell last month.
A young woman said she and her friends had been discussing the allegations again that morning. Her friend said it had been difficult for him to come to an Ivy League university feeling excited about the future, only to see this story dominate the news.
Students were not OK about what happened to Jane Doe, he said.
Cornell alumni have also given their views.

27b019c05e96.text: No industry has ever documented its own foreseeable risks as loudly as AI. Imagine a plaintiff's lawyer reading the public warnings of Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: They told the world it was dangerous. They told the world it was moving too fast. Then they unleashed it and sold it to your kid. No industry has ever taken so much copyrighted work and left behind so much proof. Imagine a plaintiff's lawyer reading OpenAI's own files to a jury: They trained on a pirated library. They renamed it to something blander. Then they deleted it when the headlines got hot. Why it matters: AI's origins, use and future will be picked apart in countless epic court fights, with a historic paper and public statement trail to tap. Every significant invention — be it social media, automobiles, electricity or capitalism itself — gets disrupted and eventually shaped by the courts. AI, with its tentacles into every part of industry and life, will experience this at scale. The big picture: The fights are no longer theoretical. They're underway, in discovery and headed toward juries. Early verdicts and settlements capture the risk for the biggest players. 🤖 Chatbots are being treated as products, not speech. Unlike social media companies, they likely can't hide behind Section 230 , which protects platforms from liability for what users post — not what the platform itself creates. 📖 Copyright is a massive problem. Anthropic already paid the biggest copyright settlement in history, $1.5 billion to authors and book publishers, and now music publishers and news media want a piece. 💻 Agents gone wild. What happens when they do damage — and it was foreseeable and foreseen? ⚖️ Discovery gone wild. AI leaves LOTS of receipts (and, ironically, makes it easier for the lawyers to comb through them, too). Product liability turns on two words: foreseeable and knew. Punitive damages turn on whether you knew the danger and shipped anyway. This is where all these memos and warnings could really backfire. Candor is good for safety but terrible for litigation. The companies that warn most honestly create the most discoverable evidence of foreseeability. Expect general counsels to push hard to tone down the candor. It's the rational legal move. ⚠️ The intrigue: The liabilities won't be limited to AI companies. Any corporate user of powerful AI systems that unleashes rogue agents, even without intending to do harm, would face substantial penalties as well. "It's not if, but when," said Miriam Vogel, a former senior Justice Department official who now leads EqualAI. "An algorithm will do what it's told to do. The more power and capability it has, the more access it has, the more it will do anything in its power to achieve a goal." That will create another layer of litigation as companies fight back. The CTO of a top Wall Street hedge fund who spoke to Axios after the notorious OpenAI/Hugging Face hack said his first call, if his firm's systems are breached, will be to his general counsel. President Trump, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and former FTC chair Lina Khan have all argued that AI companies are responsible for making sure their products are safe. If not, a wave of lawsuits awaits. The other side: There's a school of thought that AI companies might escape the worst liability, despite their frankness about things they and their products might have done wrong. One way to see it, and the argument lawyers will undoubtedly make, is that the labs spoke about dangers frequently, and took pains to protect users and mitigate harms. The bottom line: For all the fights in Washington about whether or not Congress will act, the U.S. legal system may be the ultimate, and most powerful, regulator of the AI industry. Bradley Olson, Axios managing editor of AI & tech, contributed reporting. 📈 If you're a CEO or on a CEO's team: Ask to join Jim's new weekly Axios C-Suite newsletter.

e583d6e66d73.text: A small cadre of elite AI researchers is wielding extraordinary influence inside OpenAI and other leading companies, challenging executives, shaping policy and complicating negotiations with Washington. Why it matters: As a safety crisis has unfolded across the industry, it's an open question who is doing more to shape the national AI debate — top researchers or the executives they report to. The researchers, some of whom are among the most highly paid and sought-after scientists in the world, are outspoken online and have repeatedly clashed with company strategy. The big picture: The situation has the makings of a grassroots uprising, where any potential deal the companies may strike — with the Trump administration, one another, or even globally — will also have to pass muster with their top scientists. Behind the scenes : OpenAI, Anthropic and others at the frontier of AI aren't like other companies. Many began years ago as idealistic research labs with scientific cultures that prized openness and collaboration. To function, and to continue to build better and better models, the companies need highly specialized machine learning researchers and scientists to push the frontiers of what's technologically possible. The trouble is , the best of those researchers are in extraordinarily short supply. Last year's talent wars drove compensation packages into the hundreds of millions of dollars for the most elite, giving top researchers enormous leverage over their employers. Perks include favorable vesting schedules for their compensation and largely freewheeling policies that allow them to share triumphs, trash rivals and offer their perspectives about the AI race frequently on X. AI CEOs must prioritize safety and embrace regulation to retain top research talent, an OpenAI investor told Axios. Zoom in: OpenAI President Greg Brockman scrapped plans to donate another $25 million to a pro-AI political group that some researchers had openly criticized. Researchers and employees say they helped push OpenAI from resisting regulation — and candidates who supported it — toward working more closely with lawmakers in several states. The company recently backed a transparency bill in Illinois and, at the 11th hour, an independent auditing bill in California. "We have a lot of debate inside OpenAI, and that's a good thing, but what ultimately drives our policy positions is what we're seeing in our own technology and how quickly its capabilities are advancing," an OpenAI spokesperson said. Yes, but : OpenAI signaled Thursday that there are limits to how much dissent it will tolerate, firing three employees for allegedly mishandling sensitive information. The employees broke the "deep level of trust" needed to keep systems safe, the company said. Friction point: In Washington, the unusual dynamic has frustrated policymakers who see AI companies as inconsistent on regulation — opposing proposals at some points and supporting them at others, sources tell Axios. OpenAI is "no longer seen as or acting as a leader in driving policy," one source close to the administration said, arguing researchers have "neutered" the company. A White House official said OpenAI has been an incredible partner and pointed to the recent accord the company signed with the president. Zoom out: It's not just OpenAI. Researchers also complicated Anthropic's efforts to strike a deal with the Pentagon after a clash between the company and senior administration officials earlier this year. Employees at OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have signed high-profile letters at pivotal moments between companies and the government, including more than 1,000 who backed the viral "pacing the frontier" petition. In a remarkable show of internal solidarity, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned and publicly blasted the company's safety practices — only to have several colleagues still inside Anthropic endorse his concerns. Reality check : Executives have also adapted as political backlash to AI has grown and safety incidents have drawn more scrutiny, sources close to the companies say. With some level of regulation seen as inevitable, companies have focused on molding the rules as favorably as possible rather than simply resisting them. The bottom line: In the debate over AI safety and regulation, some researchers have become nearly as influential in setting the terms as OpenAI's Sam Altman or Anthropic's Dario Amodei.

93e51f61c07c.text:
Matthewâs view
Saudi Arabiaâs recently appointed stock market regulator has had a whirlwind few weeks. Mazen Al-Sudairi is leading an overhaul of the Capital Market Authorityâs rules, one of the kingdomâs biggest revamps since it opened its stocks to foreign investors in 2015.
That shift, from shunning so-called âhot moneyâ to courting foreign capital, was essential to boosting the marketâs global importance and bringing in foreign cash to help fund Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salmanâs economic transformation program.
Bankers and lawyers here in Riyadh worry, though, that the latest effort, rather than fueling a revival of the Tadawul, may hamper it.
Saudi stocks â which saw a multiyear bull run end in 2022 â have rebounded since the Iran war broke out and outperformed peers in the region thanks to the kingdomâs ability to export crude. But the index is still down 3% since Feb. 28, while the MSCI Emerging Markets Index rose 6% in the same period. Overall, falling valuations, compounded by the war, have added to the poor sentiment and put off new listings. The government needs a thriving market to offload its domestic portfolio and recycle the capital into new ventures.
Investors had anticipated a recovery on promised changes to foreign ownership limits. Instead, the regulator turned its attention to listing rules, aiming to attract mature, well-run companies onto the stock exchange â quality over quantity.
The proposals are under consultation and could change before they are finalized, but critics (none of whom would go on the record, fearing reprisal) warn that requirements such as hard underwriting, which forces banks to take on more IPO risk, could delay deals already in the pipeline. Smaller banks may not be able to participate in the process and even large ones may initially be wary of untested new rules.
Therein lies the CMAâs dilemma: By weeding out listings that arenât ready for public markets â and many werenât, based on the performance of many recent IPOs â the regulator could end up depressing IPO activity and ultimately dragging down valuations, instead of restoring confidence among local investors sitting on underperforming portfolios.
Notable
- Saudi Arabiaâs stock market regulator is investigating the poor performance of recent IPOs, including looking into the advice given by investment banks as it tries to kick-start new listings, Semafor reported.

How to move 1,300 plants for Kew's Palm House mega makeover
The world-famous Palm House at the Royal Botanic Gardens Kew in London is about to undergo a massive makeover.

Senate Republicansâ top super PAC is making a tactical change, pausing its ad campaign in North Carolinaâs Senate race and launching a new one in Kansas.
Senate Leadership Fund is plowing seven figures into Kansas to help incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall against Democrat Adam Hamilton. After spending more than $30 million in North Carolinaâs Senate race, the super PAC is putting further spending there on hold. A Trump-aligned group also has no further spending on the books past this week either, according to Ad Impact.
âSLFâs job is to maintain the majority and this move reflects the most effective and efficient use of resources to do exactly that,â said a person familiar with the plans. The group also recently boosted its spending in Senate races in Ohio and Iowa.
The move to shore up Marshall and put North Carolina on the back burner reflects a shifting Senate battleground map â and Republican Michael Whatleyâs struggles in North Carolina against former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper. Another GOP group cut millions in North Carolina ad reservations last week and some Republicans have been urging their allies to concentrate on other Senate races.
In Kansas, Hamilton is running surprisingly close to Marshall, who is seeking a second term in a state where a Democrat hasnât won a Senate race in nearly a century.
The new SLF ad hits Hamilton as a âtwo-face extremistâ and is aimed at eroding his centrist credibility with voters, dinging him on his immigration record and linking him to Democrats like Kamala Harris and Hillary Clinton and calling him âtoo-extreme for Kansas.â
Senate Republicans currently hold 53 seats, including North Carolina and Kansas, and can afford to lose up to three seats to keep the majority.

The US jobs market saw a sharp slowdown in September, with employers adding just 29,000 jobs in the final update before the midterm elections.
Headcounts were little changed in major sectors from tech to retail as hiring fell significantly from August, according to figures from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).
Meanwhile, the unemployment rate rose slightly from 4.1% in August to 4.2% in September.
The figures signal a cooling US economy, which experts said reduced the likelihood of a series of further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.
The 29,000 jobs created in September was down from a figure of 133,000 in August, according to revised BLS figures for the month.
The BLS report stands in sharp contrast to President Donald Trump's insistence that America's economy is booming and it is the "hottest" nation in the world
The disconnect is likely to present significant challenges as the president and his fellow Republicans hit the the campaign trail with just a month to go before the midterm congressional elections.
According to an AP/NORC poll released on Thursday, just 17% of Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall.
Both are new lows for Trump, surpassing the lowest mark for Democrat Joe Biden during his presidential term. They also represent a flashing warning sign for his party with early voting in some states already under way.
There have been some indications that the president understands that his views of the American economy are out of step with those of most Americans.
"I've done a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing," he said at a White House event earlier this week.
These latest job figures have only added to the challenge facing Trump.

7dc9ef8aa7d3.text: Pope Leo XIV called Friday for the church to form an alliance with artists to protect human creativity during an era of AI-generated content. Why it matters: Though he has acknowledged the technology's potential benefits, the pope continues to warn that AI progress cannot come at the expense of human dignity. The statement comes after the New York Times reported on Anthropic's efforts to confer with religious scholars to infuse religious morals into Claude. What he's saying: "In this era of artificial intelligence, it is becoming urgent to distinguish human art from what machines produce," the pope wrote on X. "There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others. Algorithms lack the spark of humanity." Leo said the Catholic Church is calling for "an alliance with artists and cultural institutions to safeguard our humanity." Zoom out: Leo has spoken out against AI before, specifically around how the technology could influence and potentially harm humanity. In the first encyclical of his papacy, he said there was a need to "disarm" the technology to prevent it "from dominating humanity." In May, the pope established a Vatican commission on AI to coordinate the church's policies and work around the technology. Last week, he warned of a "paradise of machines" invading and taking over our daily activities. He also said that recent warnings from AI researchers should be "taken seriously." "We have to keep working. We can't sit back and pretend nothing is going to happen," he told reporters in late September. Flashback: The late Pope Francis also warned that AI potentially risked reducing humans into data points.

It is a piece of wisdom that all French leaders take care to heed: young people on the street equals trouble.
Since the student protests of May 1968 â memorably described by President De Gaulle as chienlit (bed defecation, in other words chaos) â every government has run scared of angry French youth.
Why? Because youth movements are unpredictable and shapeless, often with no clear structure to negotiate with. Because when they protest, other groups join in.
Also: because as they're young, the public tends to sympathise. And because if the police mess up and cause injury or worse, then the consequences are incalculable. And presidential elections are only months away.
For all these reasons, when la jeunesse en colÃ¨re (angry youth) is at the barricades governments tread very carefully indeed.
Right now, French teenagers are at the barricades and if they are not visibly angry (the mood is more excitement), they certainly have the government of President Emmanuel Macron in what Le Monde called on Friday "the cold sweats".
A movement that started nearly two weeks ago in the low-income Seine-Saint-Denis area of northern Paris has in the last few days spread across the country.
On Thursday â the high point so far â hundreds of lycÃ©es (where 15-18 year-olds finish their schooling) were being blockaded. On Friday, the situation had improved but around 400 lycÃ©es were closed in order to protect staff and students. Universities are beginning to join in.
Violence has erupted. On Thursday the main hall of a lycÃ©e in Nantes was destroyed by fire. Smaller fires too numerable to mention were lit at school entrance gates around the country. The cost of the damage is millions of euros.
According to Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray, 65 teaching staff including 40 school heads have been injured. "Most of the staff who were hurt said that the people they were facingâ¦ were not their own pupils," he said.
In addition, the government says that around 300 police and firefighters have been treated for injuries, and some 2,000 people â mainly minors â taken into custody. For their part, student groups say they have a long list of people injured by police. Two teenagers have serious eye injuries and one has lost many of his teeth.
The problem would be hard enough if it was just a question of meeting the protesters' demands. But there is another dimension â a political and social one â which makes this student crisis far more dangerous than in the past.
The demands do exist, even if they remain vague. They are about money â the lack of it â and the need for more teachers, smaller classes and better buildings.
On such matters, many in France would agree with the teenagers. Certainly using protest to demand money from government is such a national habit that even governments agree it's legitimate. And of course, things are indeed getting worse in the education system â because money is so tight.
This week Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu published his draft for next year's budget. The motif is "More cuts â and this time we're serious!"
Whether or not he manages to remove â¬54bn (Â£46bn) from state spending, as he promises, remains open to question.
But it is surely obvious that the era of public largesse to defuse social unrest in France is now in its twilight. Students demanding an extra school nurse or insulation in the dining-block are likely to be disappointed.
But that is the lesser of the worries.
The far greater fear is that these student protests are being manipulated by the hard left â and that the violence of recent days is a foretaste of what awaits a dangerously polarised society in the year of elections that is coming.
For the right and centre, there is no doubt that behind the student trouble lies the cunning hand of the France Unbowed party (LFI) and its popular presidential candidate, Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon.
LFI leaders have regularly appeared next to the students â notably in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis whose mayor Bally Bagayoko was criticised for saying that "violence can sometimes be legitimate."
An internal report prepared for the Paris police department which was leaked to the media analysed the opening of the movement in Seine-Saint-Denis. It concluded that students were being "egged on by far-left elements from students unionsâ¦ and political groups such asâ¦ LFI."
It said the tensions "could be part of a flame-kindling strategyâ¦ aimed at imposing their ideas ahead of the national elections".
In support of its conclusion, the report's writers cited the presence of protesters who are not themselves lycÃ©ens, the vagueness of the demands, the flying of Palestinian and Algerian flags, and the use of tactics â like calling for supplementary protests at police-stations - that come from the radical-left playbook.
The LFI strongly denies doing anything more than lending its natural support to a movement it regards as legitimate. On Thursday MÃ©lenchon called on students to avoid violence "which only serves our enemies' interests".
But his opponents believe that the 75-year-old veteran â who stands a good chance of making it to the second round of the presidential elections in May, probably against the hard-right's Marine Le Pen â knows exactly what he is doing.
Polls show he has massive support â some 40% -- among 18-24 year-olds in France, and that this is concentrated in the populous, high-immigration city suburbs where his talk of a "new France" and "creolisation", to reflect France's changing language and population, are highly appreciated.
But young people are also the biggest abstainers in French elections, so the strategy â as the elections approach â will be to give constant reminders to this part of the population that the LFI is at their side, and that their vote can count.
Whether this will be enough to ensure victory for MÃ©lenchon is another matter. He must surely take seriously the polls which all show him losing massively in a run-off against Le Pen.
If that happen

Reporter Michael Graczyk has covered nearly 500 executions carried out in Texas, continuing even after his 2018 retirement from The Associated Press.
He remembers two instances where needles popped out before reinsertion for successful execution - but never one in which an inmate survived.
That's what happened this week in Tennessee, when 50-year-old inmate Christa Pike remained breathing and audibly snoring after two separate doses of pentobarbital, the barbiturate used in the state's lethal injection protocol.
Graczyk, 76, says he wasn't entirely surprised to hear of the anomaly - and had actually thought about the possibility during his decades-long career as a Texas journalist.
"It seems to me it was just a matter of time," he told BBC News.
Tennessee's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of pentobarbital-filled syringes in case the person being put to death does not die after the first set, according to AP, but does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.
Governor Bill Lee halted executions in the state after Wednesday night's failure, ordering an independent review into procedures. Botched executions have come under scrutiny over the past decade, since a shortage of the drugs used led some states to change the formula, or procure drugs from more questionable sources. Some states even brought back death by firing squad as an alternative.
Pike is now in hospital where she is receiving "life-saving care", according to her lawyer.
It's not uncommon for lethal injections - the most frequently used form of capital punishment in the 27 US states where the penalty is legal - to be "botched". The Death Penalty Information Center, a think-tank that does not take a stance on the death penalty, lists 64 botched executions since 1982, 51 of them lethal injections. In at least seven of those cases, the executions were halted because the IV line could not be set.
But Graczyk has never seen an execution fail after the injection was delivered.
"That has never happened here," Graczyk said of the Lone Star State.
Graczyk, who covered a wide range of topics for the AP during his 46 years with the news service, considers his prolific attendance at executions to be an important part of the job.
"There is no [greater] authority, power, or whatever you want to call it, that state or federal government has over us than the power to take our life," he said.
There have been 1,683 executions in the US since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre. which is when the US Supreme Court re-instated the death penalty. Texas has carried out by far the most of any state, with 602 executions. In 1982, it became the first state to use lethal injections to execute people.
"I always thought it was important for someone who has no stake in the outcome of a case to be there and to see the law being carried out and to make certain that it is done properly," Graczyk said.
"That someone is there to see it and tell others: Here's what I saw. Here's what happened."
He feels a particular responsibility to remember victims in his coverage and it's especially disheartening when he writes a story about an execution that doesn't make big news.
"I feel bad for the victims in the case," he said. "They are the forgotten folks. They always have been."
"Today, all the emphasis is on the inmate in Tennessee," he said. "No tears are being shed, other than the victim's immediate family, for the victim â¦ and I understand that's the business we're in, but it doesn't mean it's right."
Pike's victim was Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old originally from Florida who loved to roller skate, smile and help others, according to descriptions given by her friends and family. Slemmer was tortured and killed by Pike, then 18, and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, after they met her at a job training camp.
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was present in Tennessee on Wednesday for the execution attempt, telling NBC News afterwards that it "was a mess".
Texas, where Graczyk lives and works, does not allow observers in the execution chamber when the IV is being inserted, he said.
"So when we get into the chamber, the inmate's already hooked up."
In a lethal injection execution, the IV would typically be inserted in the crook of the person's arm, Graczyk said. But if that didn't work, sometimes it would go into the top of their hand, their leg, neck or other sites.
During successful executions, Graczyk said inmates become "visibly unconscious after just a few seconds". They are usually pronounced dead 20 to 40 minutes after the fatal dose is given, he said.
He still remembers the death of Jonathan Nobles, who was executed by lethal injection in Texas in 1998. He'd been handed the sentence after his conviction for the brutal 1986 stabbing murders of two Austin women, Kelley Fraquhar and Mitzi Johnson-Nalley.
Nobles sang "Silent Night" as his last words.
"He gets to 'Round yon virgin' and he stops talking," Graczyk told BBC News. "That's how long it took for the drug to kick in so he wasn't conscious anymore."
That scene has stuck with Graczyk for nearly 30 years.
"To this day, when I'm in church on Christmas, and the choir is singing Silent Night, and all the congregation is joining in Silent Night and they're all, you know, in the spirit of the season and the joy of the season, and I'm thinking of this execution, I'm sure I'm the only one in that congregation that is having that kind of recollection."
When people hear about his career covering executions, he said, they are usually curious.
"Most people don't get to watch someone die," he said.
But when people ask him about what he has witnessed, he tells them "it's not the only thing I did or do or have done".

2ccb16db9cf8.text: By — Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/disappointing-29000-jobs-added-in-september-as-unemployment-ticks-up Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Disappointing 29,000 jobs added in September as unemployment ticks up Economy Oct 2, 2026 9:48 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. employers added a disappointing 29,000 jobs and the unemployment rate ticked up last month, the government reported Friday, a month before voters go to the polls in pivotal midterm elections at a time of discontent over the high cost of living and the state of the economy. Hiring dropped from a revised 133,000 in August, the Labor Department reported. The unemployment rate rose to a still-low 4.2% from 4.1% in August, READ MORE: U.S. unemployment claims dip to the lowest since mid-July Economists had expected September payrolls to come in at 90,000. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Labor Department revisions also shaved 60,000 jobs off combined July and August payrolls. Average hourly wages were up just 3% last year from a year earlier — smallest year-over-year gain since May 2021. The U.S. job market has proven resilient in the face of a series of shocks — trade wars, persistent inflation, high interest rates and a conflict with Iran that has driven energy prices higher. Friday's jobs report is the last one that will come out before the Nov. 3 elections that will determine whether President Donald Trump's Republicans maintain full control of Congress. READ MORE: Trump keeps heralding an economic boom, but even a solid jobs report is causing problems for him Futures for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq composite added to their gains after the data was released, while Treasury yields moved lower. The yield on the 10-year Treasury was 5.17%, down from 5.24% a day earlier. The U.S. job market has recovered from a dismal 2025, but ordinary Americans remain unhappy about the economy and the high cost of living. A Thursday poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of Trump's handling of the cost of living. Just 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, marking a new low. U.S. consumer confidence dropped this month to the lowest level in more than a decade, according to an index published by the Conference Board. One reason: More than 28% of the respondents told the business think tank that they expect fewer jobs to be available in six months, double the 14% who expect more. The online jobs site Glassdoor reports that its employee confidence index, based on how workers view prospects for their own companies, dropped last month to the lowest level in records going back to the beginning of 2016, a period that includes a global pandemic. It was the index's third record low this year. "Employee confidence has been continuously grinding downward over the last year as workers grow increasingly anxious about everything from layoffs to AI," said Glassdoor chief economist Daniel Zhao. The public's misgivings about jobs partly reflect an odd feature of the current labor market: Employers aren't laying off many workers, but they aren't hiring many either. A Labor Department measure of gross hiring – before subtracting those who quit or lose their jobs – has been stuck in a rut for more than two years. So economists describe a "low-hire, low-fire" job market in which those who have jobs are mostly secure, but jobseekers struggle to find work. In August, the average unemployed person had been out of work for more than six months, the longest average stretch of joblessness since February 2022. "People know that being laid off is unusually costly right now," said Glassdoor's Zhao. "They hear from their friends how long they've been out of work and had such a difficult time finding a job. That does make layoffs even more scary than usual." In that chilly environment, fewer workers are willing to quit their jobs. "They often feel stuck," Zhao said. "Workers aren't finding there's opportunity on the open market to find a better job – one that pays more or offers better work-life balance." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema used his first trip abroad since his re-election last month to tell Gulf investors to fully comply with the countryâs local procurement rules, he said.
Zambia is Africaâs second-largest producer of copper, whose prices have soared as demand rises for metals used in electric vehicles and power grids. Hichilemaâs stance matches that of regional rivals who are trying to use the scramble for critical minerals to drive economic development.

dfe8ea3ded2c.text: The Supreme Court on Monday will hear arguments in a case that could determine the fate of state-court lawsuits nationwide seeking climate damages from oil giants. Why it matters: Billions and billions of dollars are at stake for the oil industry in dozens of cases brought by state and local governments. Governments face mounting costs from climate change that litigants link directly to the companies' products. The big picture: SCOTUS is considering whether federal law blocks damage claims under state laws for the effects of interstate and global emissions. State of play: It's specifically about litigation against Exxon and Suncor that the city and county of Boulder filed in 2018. But dozens of state-court cases are active in California, Connecticut, New York, Massachusetts and beyond. The cases aren't identical. But overall they accuse oil giants of concealing risks or making deceptive statements, and seek damages for climate-related costs. Here are a few big themes and dynamics ahead of Monday morning: This is a blockbuster. The decision will be the culmination of an intense, years-long battle (unless it's not, but more on that in a moment). There's a high level of organizing, lobbying and advocacy among industry and climate advocates alike around these state cases. Industry and allied groups say the wave of cases threatens oil companies' very ability to operate. It's a sign that both sides see litigation as a critical battleground on climate. Take a spin through the case docket and you'll see what I mean. A kicked can is possible. SCOTUS might not decide the question of federal preemption. That's because it's also considering whether it even has jurisdiction right now. The question turns on whether a Colorado Supreme Court decision to let Boulder's case proceed in state court can be reviewed at this stage. Trump policies are a new(ish) wrinkle. U.S. and industry briefs argue that addressing an interstate and global topic with these state claims is preempted by federal law and the Constitution. But watch whether the White House attempt to repeal key Clean Air Act authority over greenhouse gases is used as a cudgel against federal preemption claims. This won't be the main argument — instead, the litigants against oil companies contend these cases are well within the bounds of traditional, longstanding state powers. But it could surface. There's an important absence on the bench. Justice Samuel Alito this week recused himself from the case. "Justice Alito's recusal is likely bad news to the petitioners as he is among the more preemption-friendly justices on the Court," writes environmental law scholar Jonathan Adler. There could be ripple effects. A ruling in favor of the oil companies could also jeopardize separate state climate policies. New York and Vermont have "climate superfund" laws that assess damages against fossil fuel companies to help fund climate adaptation. They're both tied up in court. Several states are considering some version of these laws. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

ccba07dc1e57.text: President Trump is expected to tap Jay Clayton , his director of national intelligence, for a new role as the White House's artificial intelligence — or in Trump's words, " super intelligence " — czar. Why it matters: Clayton, who Trump previously told Axios would be a good idea for AI czar, is expected to take on the second title, sources told Axios. Calls for government intervention into AI's rapid development are growing, but the president has repeatedly said he favors a light regulatory touch and has called fears about the tech's threat to humanity a hoax . Trump had been warming to the idea of tapping Clayton, who as DNI has shown that he sees the security threats AI poses as serious. Driving the news: Trump could make the announcement as soon as Friday, sources familiar confirmed to Axios. A White House official said in a statement to Axios that "[a]ny personnel announcement will be announced directly by the President. Any reporting until then is baseless speculation." Catch up quick: Asked by Axios earlier this week who he wants to be AI czar, Trump said: "I have somebody in mind." Clayton is "a good man. He's right here. That's a good idea," Trump added when prompted. Zoom out: Trump announced last month that he'd create an "AI Force" and would soon name a new AI czar, but offered few details on what the Force would do. Since then, he's huddled with several titans of the AI industry — some of whom have been key voices in advocating for a slowdown of the tech . Flashback: Clayton was elevated to be Trump's principle intelligence adviser atop the 18-agency intelligence community earlier this year after his prior DNI, Tulsi Gabbard, resigned in May. Previously the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Clayton's qualifications received bipartisan blessings. After sidestepping questions over who won the 2020 election during his confirmation, Clayton was confirmed on party lines, without Democratic support. Riot police have clashed with protesters as thousands of students demonstrating over education standards disrupted more than 560 schools in France on Friday.
Fires have burned in the streets as high school pupils and others objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.
The protests began last week in Paris and have spread across the country, with cities including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille affected.
French justice minister Gerald Darmanin said things had "gone from high-school student demonstrations to a public order disturbance".
On Friday, a 17-year-old was arrested on suspicion of attempted homicide after protests in Belfort, north-eastern France, where a police officer was targeted.
At least 65 staff members have been injured in the unrest, the education ministry said.
In the Paris suburb of Pantin police charged at protesters and made arrests after projectiles where thrown at officers.
Meanwhile, in Strasbourg tear gas was deployed as police feared conditions would become more hostile, according to the Reuters news agency.
Rubbish bins have also been set on fire in Rennes and Paris.
"As far as we're concerned, we've won - our school is closed this morning," Lola, a 16-year-old protester, told the AFP news agency on Friday.
She said police actions had made things worse.
"It makes us even angrier - the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us," she added.
In Marseille, fireworks were thrown at police and teachers were also inadvertently splashed with petrol at a school there, officials said.
"Significant damage" had been done to school facilities, the education ministry said.
Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes had suffered more than â¬2m (Â£1.7m) damage, according to the regional government.
The blockades and protests started last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.
Students say school hours are too long, classrooms too hot and too many members of staff are off work.
It comes at a crucial time for French President Emmanuel Macron, six months before next year's presidential election.
Budget cuts planned, which will impact on education funding, have infuriated the young protesters.
French Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray claimed on Friday that the movement had been hijacked by non-students.
He told French broadcaster BFMTV teachers had said "the people in front of me were not my students".
Parents have also been worried that their children have become caught up in a wave of violence and unrest.
At the Claude Monet school in southern Paris, 53-year-old Anya was looking for her son.
"We banned him from coming. I hope he isn't here, but he did leave the house, so," she told AFP.
"We're afraid the situation might escalate."
Darmanin, the justice minister, said prosecutors had been asked to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children and "pay for repairs".
He said since the start of the movement, about 2,000 people - most of who were children - had been taken into custody.
Many French unions have given their support to the protesting students.
Education union SNEP-FSU, public services union SNUEP-FSU and Solidaires have all called for members to support them.
Solidaires Trade Union Federation said in a statement: "Let's not let them fire on our children.
"Secondary school pupils have the freedom of assembly, association and demonstration."
