The panel found that she initially consented to sex with that man and one of his friends, though she later alleged in her lawsuit that she had been pressured into taking ketamine, marijuana and alcohol and was too intoxicated to consent. Then other men began showing up in the room, some drawn by a message one of the fraternity brothers sent to a Snapchat group at 1:42 a.m. using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman's body was freely available. Later, another person in the chat asked if the "shop" was still open. WATCH: New details intensify scrutiny of Cornell's handling of gang rape allegations The woman told investigators that her intoxication had rendered her partly defenseless. She said she remembered smoking marijuana and said she knew she took ketamine, her first time doing so, but didn't have an independent memory of it. The drug, she said, left her in a state of "vague consciousness." "You look like an operating human being," she told school investigators at a hearing in May of 2025. "You don't look dead or asleep necessarily. So, lights are on, but nobody's home. Your brain is not functioning at its proper level." She said some of the men inhaled drugs off her unclothed body. "I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me. It just was a totally debilitating place to be in," she told investigators. Accused student says he only entered room for a wellness check One of the men the woman accused of snorting drugs off her body — but not participating in other elements of the assault — denied her account. He told investigators he was in the room for no more than five minutes, and didn't go there for sex. "That was not our intentions at all. He said he sat on a couch and chatted for a few minutes, then left after the woman and another man there both indicated they were all right. A Cornell disciplinary panel later cleared him of sexual assault or exploitation allegations, but found him responsible for attempted sexual exploitation because it didn't believe his claim to have gone to the room for altruistic reasons. The fraternity member, who is challenging Cornell's disciplinary process in court, also posted in the Snapchat conversation, saying what was happening in the room was not a joke, adding: "Firsthand pov not a bit." 86cc59162556.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Saturday took a veiled shot at Anthropic and its work on the soul of AI, saying he was "very uncomfortable" with the idea of attributing some kind of religious power to models. Why it matters: It's yet another point of division between Altman and his former colleague Dario Amodei, whose company has reportedly pursued scholars across faiths to make the case for moral, conscious models. But some of the top voices in AI are starting to publicly line up against Anthropic's efforts to infuse consciousness into models. What they're saying: "I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue," Altman said in a post to X. Context: Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah has been meeting with religious leaders to consider questions of model consciousness — but also to figure out how to infuse morals and moral behavior into AI. At one point, the Times reported, Olah considered the possibility of models engaging in Catholic-style confession, not just to admit their mistakes but to shape their future behavior. The big picture: Spirituality is suddenly becoming something of a flashpoint around AI's future. On Friday Pope Leo, an outspoken AI critic, called on the church to ally with artists to preserve human creativity, saying: "Algorithms lack the spark of humanity." Between the lines: The pope's stance put renewed focus on a fundamental question: Do models have souls and feelings? The Times reported that Olah, before a Vatican event in May, tried to persuade the pope's advisers that they should take the prospect of conscious models more seriously. So far, other top scientists seem to be lining up against the idea. "I am disturbed by how some of my fellow AI researchers keep trying to elevate the moral standing of checkpoints and harnesses," Google DeepMind principal research scientist Jon Barron posted to X. "I hope the rest of us on Team Meatbag reject this movement and stay focused on solving real problems and helping actual humans." For the record: Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic immediately responded to requests for comment on Altman's post. The bottom line: The AI safety debate largely focuses on things like cybersecurity and bioweapons. The real problem may be more spiritual than that.

f95a14c2bfa2.text: By — Ed White, Associated Press Ed White, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/governor-says-tennessees-prisons-chief-is-resigning-after-failed-execution-of-christa-pike Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Tennessee's prisons chief is resigning after the failed execution of Christa Pike Nation Updated on Oct 3, 2026 3:30 PM EDT — Published on Oct 3, 2026 11:41 AM EDT The head of Tennessee's prison system is resigning, Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday, the first major staff shake-up since Christa Pike's stunning failed execution left her unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital. Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, will step down this month, Lee said. Some of the governor's fellow Republicans and other elected officials had been urging a change in leadership. It was the second time since May that Tennessee has not been able to execute a prisoner who was seemingly moments away from death. READ MORE: Christa Gail Pike wasn't Tennessee's first failed execution this year. Here's what to know Strada said in a statement that resigning was "in the best interest of Tennesseans" while an independent review determines what happened Wednesday when the state failed to execute Pike despite administering two doses of a lethal drug, pentobarbital. "I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary, and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred," Strada said. Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row. Strada defends execution protocol There was no immediate response from Pike's lawyers for an update Saturday on her condition at a hospital. They had disclosed Friday that she was on a ventilator and unconscious in the hours following the execution attempt and that hospital staff were trying to clear the two doses of pentobarbital. The shocking failure has left both sides of the death penalty debate demanding answers. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted any new executions. Strada said he believes the state "carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol." Pike's legal team welcomed Strada's departure but said "it does nothing to help Christa now." "What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," the four-lawyer team said. "We hope the governor's call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee's entire death penalty system." Second failed execution since May Pike's attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream. In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm but couldn't get a secondary IV line. The governor ordered officials to wait at least a year before trying to execute him again. READ MORE: Many states have backup execution plans, but failures still happen Strada took over the Correction Department in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections. In late 2024, he announced that Tennessee was changing its lethal injection protocol and would use only pentobarbital. Four people have been executed in Tennessee since 2025, according to the Correction Department. Some Arizona executions had snags When Strada was in Arizona, that state in 2022 resumed executions after a nearly eight-year break, following criticism about an execution that took about two hours as well as difficulties obtaining certain drugs. Clarence Dixon was the first that year. The medical team had trouble finding a vein to administer the lethal drugs and finally made an incision in his groin area. The process took about 25 minutes. That same year in Arizona, medical staff preparing Frank Atwood for execution initially could not locate a vein in his right arm but inserted the IV in his right hand — at Atwood's suggestion, said Henry Brean, an Arizona Daily Star reporter who was a witness. Strada announced Murray Hooper's execution by lethal injection, the third in 2022. There was an unsuccessful attempt to insert an IV line in his right arm. The IV in Hooper's leg was inserted into his femoral artery. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 710b3b32a158.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/dual-uk-iranian-national-released-on-bail-over-suspected-plot-against-u-s-run-military-base Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Dual UK-Iranian national released on bail over suspected plot against U.S.-run military base World Oct 3, 2026 11:33 AM EDT LONDON (AP) — A dual U.K.-Iranian national arrested on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England has been released on bail, authorities said Saturday. The 25-year-old man was arrested Thursday in London on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. He was the sixth person taken into custody and then released on bail as detectives investigate the incident. WATCH: UK-Iranian citizen arrested over air base terror plot British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. The five other men were not named, but police said they are all British nationals in their 20s and from London. Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base early Sunday as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swooped on the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant – gasoline – in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the U.K. sees "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident. He did not provide details about what the suspects were planning or why the U.K. thinks Iran was involved. Iran has denied involvement. It has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target. RAF Fairford, 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year's war with Iran. READ MORE: UK police say 5 men arrested near a U.S.-run air base will be released on bail Top U.S. officials have criticized the decision to grant the five suspects bail, with President Donald Trump saying "I wouldn't have done that" and Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying a lot of people were "disturbed" by the move. The arrests came at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British security services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on U.K. soil. British officials have said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states, including Iran, increased by 50% in the six months to December 2025. U.K. officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 309de39e5f96.text: By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press By — Sam Mednick, Associated Press Sam Mednick, Associated Press By — Cara Anna, Associated Press Cara Anna, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ap-report-axe-wielding-flydubai-co-pilot-had-been-flagged-over-extremism-concerns Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AP report: Ax-wielding FlyDubai co-pilot had been flagged over extremism concerns World Updated on Oct 3, 2026 3:25 PM EDT — Published on Oct 3, 2026 11:15 AM EDT CAIRO (AP) — The co-pilot accused of attacking the captain of an Israel-bound flight with an ax and trying to seize the controls was an Omani national who had been barred from flying on his country's airline because of concerns about extremist views, officials said Saturday. The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, according to three people with knowledge of the situation, including a Gulf and a Western diplomat, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. The United Arab Emirates, which is leading the investigation, said the co-pilot attacked with the cockpit's crash ax and tried to take control of the plummeting plane in a "terrorist attack" Wednesday. His actions nearly crashed the flight with 182 people on board before passengers and others rushed in and subdued him. WATCH: Investigators search for motive after alleged attack by FlyDubai co-pilot The new details raised questions about how thoroughly FlyDubai vets potential employees, and how the co-pilot's presence on a flight filled with Israeli passengers got past Israel's strict security protocols. Israel has said it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots of nations without diplomatic ties from flying there. Israel and Oman don't have formal diplomatic relations. The UAE government has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses. The incident occurred at a sensitive time for Israel, a week before the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, that sparked the war in Gaza. It also came weeks before a highly contentious election in which security, and Oct. 7 security failures, have been central issues. FlyDubai hired the co-pilot after Oman Air barred him Separately, a regional official and a person familiar with the matter said the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns that he had adopted extremist views. The official said he was moved to an administrative job at Oman Air. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. They gave no details about the alleged extremist views. The co-pilot was later hired by UAE-based airline FlyDubai, the person said. It wasn't immediately clear to what extent the co-pilot was vetted. The Gulf diplomat said he had undergone standard security checks before being hired, but it appears that the checks focused on whether he had been convicted of criminal charges and didn't go deeper into examining his background for potential signs of radicalization. READ MORE: Pilot stabbing further unsettles region shaken by U.S.-Iran war The regional official also said security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot's motives, aided by the United States and other Western governments. The Gulf diplomat said the investigation, which hasn't concluded, hasn't found any connections with militant groups, suggesting that the co-pilot acted on his own. The regional official said the co-pilot was born in the UAE and his mother is Syrian. He obtained Omani nationality from his father, also an Omani national. The regional official also said the co-pilot had traveled to Syria, with no details. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone "Islamist radicalization," but provided no evidence. There was no immediate comment Saturday from Israel's government. A social media account was deleted the day of the flight A FlyDubai spokesperson said in an email that the airline could not comment beyond its official statements and acknowledged "there are many questions at this stage." There was no immediate comment from Oman Air, and Oman's government has said nothing publicly in response to repeated questions since the incident. In a statement to The Associated Press, Royal Air Maroc, Morocco's national carrier, said the co-pilot "completed a three-month theoretical training period with the airline in 2025, as part of the pre-employment process. At the end of this training period, his application was not selected for employment." There were no details. WATCH: Passengers describe stopping pilot's alleged attempt to crash Israel-bound flight Keith Coles, a spokesperson for Buckinghamshire New University in England, told the AP that al-Hammami previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management there but "did not undertake any pilot training." There were no details on the timing. Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot's background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted. Captain and passengers have described drama on board Airlines are generally required to carry crash axes in the cockpit that could be used in an emergency to break open a window to escape or break open a panel to access a fire. The captain, who was badly wounded, has said he used his remaining energy while being attacked to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed alarming sounds to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilize the flight while passengers screamed. In a phone call with Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday, the flight's captain, Smit Machchhar, said that before the attack, the co-pilot wanted to pray, and that he turned away out of respect. He said he felt a blow to the back of his head a few minutes later,

Cornell University's president says the school "must do better" after a woman alleged she was drugged and raped by a group of men at a fraternity house.
In an eight-minute video statement released on Saturday night, Michael Kotlikoff described the allegations raised by the woman, identified as Jane Doe, as "deeply disturbing".
The alleged incident has raised questions around the culture on campus of drug and alcohol use, and the way investigations were conducted in the case, Kotlikoff said.
Jane Doe was a 20-year-old student at the university when she says seven men from its Chi Phi fraternity assaulted her for hours in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine on 19 October 2024.
She said she had reported the incident two weeks after it happened to Cornell University police, which investigated, but no charges were laid.
Last month, Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university, in which she alleged Cornell had failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved.
Kotlikoff said Cornell was "committed to investigating" the way the case was handled, and said the school administration and community "must do better".
"We must foster a culture in which sexual assault is inexcusable and ensure our community is empowered and understands informed consent," he said.
He added that university leaders need to create an environment where victims of sexual assault "feel safe coming forward and are treated with compassion and dignity".
Kotlikoff said it is a "defining moment" in the university's history.
"We must lead the way, we owe it to Jane Doe and to survivors of assault to get this right. And we must keep each other safe," he said.
On the university's campus this week, the BBC saw growing frustration about the situation.
At a public hearing for students to speak about the alleged gang rape, many told the BBC they were ashamed of what happened and said the university had failed Jane Doe.
"Our administration needs to change and it needs to change drastically and it needs to change fast," one student told the BBC. "Something like this never should have happened, this is a disgrace."
As part of "broader work" that needs to happen, Kotlikoff said in his video statement that there should be a "serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life".
"Being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility for our own actions, for how we treat others, or for speaking up when someone may be at risk," he said.
The university president also said that at the "appropriate time", the school would speak about how Cornell will "use this moment, this conversation, this anger, to help lead the broader effort to combat sexual assault not only on our campus, but beyond it".
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled, and has appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to lead a review of the case.
Kotlikoff said he supported the decision to appoint James to lead a criminal investigation, and welcomed an independent review by a law firm of how Cornell has handled the matter.
Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and could not provide consent.

Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (Â£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion.
Noting the risk was low and the likelihood highly improbable, he told the New York Times he had a responsibility to consider all possibilities as the US-Canada relationship is redefined under the Donald Trump presidency.
"That's just risk management," Carney said.
Trump's global tariffs and his often-repeated desire to make Canada the 51st state has led Canada to war game an attack by the Americans.
In 2025, the US president said it was "highly unlikely" that the US would ever use force against Canada. Instead he said, he would continue to exert economic pressures to obtain political aims.
"President Trump has done more than anyone to protect the great people of Canada," the White House told the BBC in a statement this week.
Military experts who spoke to the BBC also think an invasion is a long shot, pointing to the multiple ways the two countries work together on defence.
But the issue is clearly weighing on Canadians' minds.
In January, after the US captured NicolÃ¡s Maduro in Venezuela, a Leger poll suggested that over 30% of Canadians believed that a US invasion was likely.
Why it is unlikely to happen
A war between Canada and the US would be complicated and almost difficult to imagine, said Lt-Gen Christopher Coates, a former military officer of 34 years with the Royal Canadian Air Force who held various senior positions.
"I was involved in military operations for my whole career, and we never considered the possibility that there would be a military attack coming from US territory," he told the BBC.
Coates, who had served on Nato missions, noted that Canada and the US collaborate on many aspects of military defence.
They are both members of the north Atlantic defence alliance, which mandates members to defend a fellow member-nation should they be attacked.
The two countries also conduct joint Arctic defence missions under the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD), and frequently share intelligence.
Because of this, Coates said he believes an attack by the US on Canada would not begin with an armed assault, but rather with more discreet means like cyberwarfare.
Not always the best of friends
After World War II, Canada and the US became natural allies for the latter part of the 20th Century, and have become heavily integrated economically, militarily and culturally.
But it wasn't always this way. In fact, a core tenet of Canada's identity is its resistance of US expansionism in the 18th and 19th Centuries, said Tim Foran, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum.
"Fear of the United States is foundational to the political project that is Canada," he said.
Canada was formed as a collection of British North American colonies who remained loyal to the British Crown when the colonies in the modern-day US rebelled.
Before the formation of Canada, the US had attempted to invade British North American colonies, taking control of Montreal in 1775 and nearly conquering Quebec City.
In the war of 1812, the Americans invaded what was known then as Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime colonies repeatedly, resulting in a stalemate. During that war, British troops famously burned down the White House in retaliation.
Foran said that at the time, the colonies that later became Canada relied on Great Britain and its Royal Navy for its defence, as well as indigenous peoples who served as generals in major battles.
Canada again contemplated war with the US post-World War I in response to its growing power and influence.
It drafted a plan that was informed by secret trips to border cities made by Canadian army generals, who would pose as tourists and snap photos of bridges and highways for intelligence.
They also spoke to local residents to better understand their enemy.
A war was an unlikely scenario then, said Andrew Burtch, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum with expertise on Canada in the 20th Century, but the Canadians still wanted to be prepared.
"That's part of what militaries do," he said. "They envisage all sorts of different scenarios."
What a US invasion could look like
Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.
He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way.
"It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.
Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.
So what would it be like if it happened?
The first phase of a war could be quite short.
According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a week
Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.
Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.
The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.
The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.
He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.

bf73b62c6247.text: By — Gene Johnson, Associated Press Gene Johnson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/a-28-billion-hemp-thc-industry-is-fighting-to-save-itself-from-a-looming-federal-ban Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A $28 billion hemp THC industry is fighting to save itself from a looming federal ban Economy Oct 3, 2026 6:06 PM EDT In a commercial kitchen outside Raleigh, North Carolina, Nicholas Hohns spreads a blue-green goo into a gridded mold, making one of his company's signature products: potent THC gummies, featuring the primary intoxicating compound found in marijuana. It's a business he might soon have to give up. America's multibillion-dollar market for impairing hemp products — from THC seltzers sold at some Target stores to smokable cannabis flowers, and different from the regulated legal marijuana industry — faces potential elimination after Congress voted to close a loophole in federal law that has allowed it to flourish. WATCH: How a small law change could have a huge impact on the U.S. hemp industry Advocates for the industry, along with some lawmakers, are fighting to save it. The short-term government-funding bill signed by President Donald Trump last month delayed the effective date of the "hemp THC ban" from Nov. 12 to Dec. 11, giving Congress more time to consider regulating the products rather than banning them. "It's such a weird spot to be in," said Hohns. "You worked 100 hours a week for the past four years, and, yeah, you made some money. But now you might have nothing to show for it." Sen. Mitch McConnell closed a loophole in the hemp law he championed Marijuana and hemp are the same plant — cannabis. Marijuana is cultivated for high levels of THC in its flowers. Low-THC hemp has historically been grown for its sturdy fibers, food or wellness products. "Rope, not dope" was long the motto of farmers who supported legalizing hemp. To give farmers a new cash crop, Kentucky Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell successfully pushed the legalization of industrial hemp in the 2018 farm bill. But the way that law defined hemp — as having less than 0.3% of a specific type of THC, called delta-9, by weight — opened a huge loophole. Beverages or snacks could meet that threshold and still contain more than enough THC to get people high. READ MORE: What to know about the looming federal ban on THC-infused drinks and snacks Vape oil, gummy candies, chips, sodas and other unregulated, untested products laden with hemp-derived THC spread around the country, including in gas stations or convenience stores, where they were available even to teens. Some businesses started selling marijuana under the theory that raw marijuana's THC is in a form called THC-A, which only turns into impairing delta-9 when heated or burned. The products evaded state prohibitions on recreational weed or undercut heavily taxed and regulated cannabis where it is legal. Dozens of states responded by regulating or banning impairing hemp products. McConnell finally closed the loophole late last year by inserting a hemp THC ban into a measure that ended the longest government shutdown in history. The ban, which limits the amount of THC in hemp products to 0.4 milligrams per container, wouldn't take effect for a year. An industry tries to save itself The ban "threatens to reduce retail revenues by $28.3 billion, displacing 225,000 jobs and reducing state sales tax potential by $2.1 billion," according to a report last month from Whitney Economics, which studies the market. The industry hopes to save itself by restricting impairing products to people 21 and older, limiting how much THC can be in a package, and banning imported cannabis compounds. The owners of Kentucky's Cornbread Hemp, Eric Zipperle and Jim Higdon, are prepared to cap their products at, say, 5 milligrams if that's what it takes to win support from lawmakers. But the 0.4 milligram limit would destroy their business, they said. "If it goes through in December, this place is toast — it's gone," Zipperle said. They have 105 employees, sell hemp beverages in 18 states and expect to bring in $65 million this year. The 0.4-milligram cap is so low that it would ban even some non-impairing CBD products, such as topical lotions, said Jonathan Miller, general counsel of the industry group U.S. Hemp Roundtable. Some consider other work Hohns, who runs Deutermann Farms in Clayton, North Carolina, entered the hemp industry after losing his job as a personal trainer during the COVID-19 pandemic. North Carolina has not legalized either medical or recreational marijuana, but many of the edibles Hohns makes are more potent than what's available in states that have. "When I started seeing THC edibles being sold … I was like, I got 18 months to two years to make money in this industry," Hohns said. "No way is the government just going to sit here and let us do this when this was supposed to be for fiber, plastics, building materials, rope." WATCH: How the bill that ended the shutdown could threaten the U.S. hemp industry's future That was more than four years ago. Hohns kept his capital investments minimal, fearing a shutdown. He has considered making other products, such as creatine gummies, if he has to get out of the hemp THC business. Things have been more stressful for others. Drinkin' Buds, a cannabis beverage company in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, has mothballed production. Co-founder Matt Swanson took himself off the payroll on Thursday. "There's just so much uncertainty," Swanson said. "I'm actively looking for employment." Allies and opponents line up Among those who have come to the defense of the hemp industry are alcohol retailers, including Total Wine & More. Sales of cannabis seltzers have helped offset falling alcohol sales. Opponents include people who say the products are dangerous. d7900e70a080.text: By — Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-rallies-in-ohio-to-boost-jon-husted-in-a-tight-senate-race-against-sherrod-brown Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump rallies in Ohio to boost Jon Husted in a tight Senate race against Sherrod Brown Politics Updated on Oct 3, 2026 6:11 PM EDT — Published on Oct 3, 2026 4:53 PM EDT VANDALIA, Ohio (AP) — After a few days campaigning in safe conservative territory, President Donald Trump on Saturday is taking his midterm tour into Ohio, a battleground state that's home to one of the top-tier Senate races this cycle. Trump has embarked on what he says will be a 32-day blitz ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, hitting the deep red states of Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama this week. Saturday's rally is just outside Dayton, Ohio, where he is stumping for key candidates in competitive races for the House, Senate and the governor's mansion in Columbus. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Perhaps the most pivotal of these races is the Senate race. GOP Sen. Jon Husted — who was appointed to fill the Senate vacancy left by now-Vice President JD Vance — is running to win the seat outright. There is likely no path to a Senate majority for Democrats without flipping Ohio, where former three-term Sen. Sherrod Brown is trying to return to the Senate after losing to Republican Bernie Moreno two years ago. "They threw him out of the Senate once before. He's horrible," Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Ohio. Since last year, Democrats have listed Ohio, along with states such as North Carolina and Maine, as key races to win control of the Senate. And this week, the head of the Senate GOP's campaign arm said Ohio is among 10 battleground races that are "within striking distance." "The good news for us is that Jon Husted is a closer," Sen. Tim Scott, the chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told reporters. "We're seeing the gap that was there between the two candidates, which was just a few points, now it is right at a dead-even race. So this is as tight as ticks, as we say in South Carolina." Data centers are a hot issue in the Ohio race At his rallies, Trump has been trying to convince voters that the economy is better than they feel it is, even though polls show Americans are frustrated with the way he's handled it. The high cost of living, including gas prices elevated by Trump's war on Iran, is a top issue in the Dayton area, too. And just days before Trump's rally, nearly 1,400 people were laid off from a truck factory in nearby Springfield. Trump's rally comes as Republicans worry that Husted's campaign has failed to adequately catch fire with voters in the Republican-dominated state. Brown and allied groups have hammered Husted for his role in attracting data centers to the state when he was lieutenant governor, and the NRSC has pinpointed it as a political vulnerability. READ MORE: A gut punch in Ohio: Nearly 1,400 laid off at truck factory just days before Trump rally The massive warehouse campuses powering artificial intelligence projects have become a toxic political issue, drawing bipartisan opposition in races across the country, with voters concerned about their impact on electricity prices, farmland and water supplies. The GOP-controlled Senate tried to advance legislation this week sponsored by Husted that would ask utility regulators to effectively charge large power users more, as consumers struggle with high energy costs. But it was blocked by nearly all Democrats. "You got to remember, Sherrod Brown was for data centers, and Jon Husted is for data centers being responsible," Scott told reporters this week. "If a community doesn't want them, he doesn't want them either." But Trump has become one of data centers' most vocal proponents, shrugging aside voter concerns and arguing that the U.S. cannot cede advancements in AI to China. READ MORE: A fact-checked guide to Trump's talking points and falsehoods at midterm rallies "Senator Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centers in Ohio," Brown wrote on X on Friday, ahead of Trump's visit. "Now, he's making Ohioans foot the bill." Brown's campaign also has hammered Husted for donations he's received from retail magnate Les Wexner, who once employed the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Husted has donated remaining Wexner contributions to an anti-human trafficking charity. Meanwhile, in the governor's race, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy faces Democrat Dr. Amy Acton, the state's former COVID-era health director. A wealthy biotech entrepreneur and 2024 presidential candidate, Ramaswamy's star appeal among conservatives led to quick backing by Ohio Republicans and hopes of an easy victory in the Republican-dominated state. However, despite a massive fundraising lead and more than $12 million spent in campaign advertising, he is now locked in a close fight with Acton with weeks to go until Election Day. AP Congressional Correspondent Lisa Mascaro in Washington and AP writer Julie Carr Smyth in Columbus, Ohio, contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 11ded76a44c2.text: By — Constant Same Bagalwa, Associated Press Constant Same Bagalwa, Associated Press By — Eve Brennan, Associated Press Eve Brennan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/inside-the-study-for-a-remedy-to-fight-congos-deadliest-ebola-outbreak Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Inside the study for a remedy to fight Congo's deadliest Ebola outbreak Health Oct 3, 2026 4:40 PM EDT RWAMPARA, Congo (AP) — More than 250 participants have been enrolled in a trial for a drug that could stop them from contracting Ebola in Congo, in what experts have described as a critical step to try to fight the deadliest outbreak of the disease in the Central African country. The drug is targeted at Bundibugyo virus, which is responsible for the fast-moving outbreak and is without an approved vaccine or treatment. The trial began in July and is one of several studies launched to find some protection and another way of at least slowing the outbreak. READ MORE: Congo faces health worker shortage as Ebola remains out of control, WHO says The Associated Press spoke this week to participants and doctors at the health center where the trial is taking place in the eastern province of Ituri, the epicenter of the outbreak. The participants include people who have been exposed to the disease in this outbreak, among them health workers and patients' relatives. At least 8,300 confirmed cases, including 4,000 deaths, have been recorded since this Ebola outbreak was declared in mid-May in eastern Congo. It has spread to seven provinces and continues to outpace efforts to track and slow it, authorities say. The trial is testing Gilead's experimental antiviral pill, called obeldesivir, which is given soon after suspected contact with the virus to prevent the disease from developing. That approach is called post-exposure prophylaxis, or PEP. The drug aims to stop the disease before it spreads One participant in the trial known as EBO-PEP told AP that she enrolled in the study in August after her husband tested positive for Ebola. She says so far no one from her family developed symptoms. She and other trial participants requested anonymity to protect their privacy due to the sensitive nature of the Ebola outbreak and the medical protocol involved. "I realized that if I even touched my husband — and I did touch him, his vomit, everything — (it meant that) I was a direct contact. I could have also passed on this contagious disease. I could have been contaminated," the participant said. READ MORE: Congo begins Ebola vaccinations for health workers in the epicenter of the outbreak She said she knew of entire households which had become infected after a family member tested positive for Ebola. But so far no one from her family has developed symptoms, she says. Ebola disease only spreads once symptoms begin. People exposed to infected patients have to wait to see if they get sick. Finding people at high risk of incubating the Bundibugyo virus — also known as contact tracing — has proved difficult in Congo. Another participant said two of their family members had caught Ebola, and one of them had died. "This disease is killing. It's better to take precautions," he said. How the trial works The trial, coordinated by ALIMA, a medical nonprofit, aims to recruit nearly 1,000 adults or children over the age of 12 who have come into contact with a confirmed case within the last five days but have no symptoms. Half will get a placebo. Participants are monitored in person every day for 21 days, with a final phone call after 42 days, according to Dr. Godefroid Basara, who is working on the trial. ALIMA said that if trial participants begin to develop symptoms, they will immediately receive supportive treatment, which has been shown to be helpful when symptoms are caught early. If the pill proves effective, it could help break the infection chain. READ MORE: Congo's fast-moving Ebola outbreak started month before it was declared, WHO says "It differs from a vaccine, which may take days or weeks to provide protection. It is also different from curative treatment because it is intended for people who are not yet showing symptoms," ALIMA research coordinator Dr. Guilavogui Jean Paul Yassa said. Dr. Jacques Zawadi, an investigating physician working with ALIMA at the trial center, said most participants are happy to take part in the study, but it had been challenging encouraging some people who live far from the center to sign up. He said the study is sometimes disrupted when participants find out their family members have died from the disease. "This is the biggest challenge we face. When a person is emotionally affected, it is not easy to reason with them and ensure they return to the study," he said. The trial partners also include Congo's National Institute of Biomedical Research and the French institute ANRS Emerging Infectious Diseases. Front-line health workers are also at high risk As new vaccines are under development elsewhere, Congo started vaccinating health workers with the Ervebo vaccine which was effective during previous Ebola outbreaks caused by a different, more common virus. Authorities have said Ervebo could offer some protection against Bundibugyo, but whether the vaccine can actually prevent illness is still being studied. On Thursday, humanitarian organization Doctors Without Borders said a staff member had tested positive for Ebola and was being evacuated to the Netherlands. In June, a humanitarian physician with ALIMA also tested positive after returning to France from one of the virus hot spots. The World Health Organization has said the outbreak continues to outpace efforts to track and slow the spread, and is set to exceed West Africa's regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016 — the deadliest on record — which killed 11,000 people. Brennan reported from Dakar, Senegal. Lauran Neergaard contributed from Washington, D.C. The Associated Press rece

4c023d6ca2fc.text: By — Martha Bellisle, Associated Press Martha Bellisle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/what-to-know-about-the-kelvin-wave-raising-the-sea-level-along-the-west-coast Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about the Kelvin wave raising the sea level along the West Coast Science Oct 3, 2026 3:45 PM EDT SEATTLE (AP) — Sea levels along the West Coast will begin to rise by up to a foot this month as a series of pulses of warm water called Kelvin waves hit the shoreline and move north, sparking concerns about beach erosion and flooding in areas already impacted by climate change and El Niño. Kelvin waves are not like tsunamis, and they don't curl over and crash on the beach. A better image is water sloshing in the bathtub or a swimming pool during an earthquake. In the ocean, they are bulges of water that lift the sea level as they move along the coast. They're common during El Niño events, but this year's super El Niño could intensify the impacts, experts say. Over the next week, the 6-inch to foot-tall surge will move north along the California coast at about 6 miles per hour (9.6 kilometers per hour), or 150 miles per day (241 kilometers per day), bringing higher sea levels to Oregon and Washington state. Experts predict the waves will continue to pass through from October until February. "It's not that this Kelvin wave is going to come and flood anything on its own," said Michael Jacox, a research oceanographer with National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Fisheries' Ecosystem Science Division. Instead, it raises the baseline. If you start with sea levels that are 6 inches higher than normal, when you have really high tides, big storms or storm surges, the water levels are now 6 inches higher, he said. "The effects can be amplified," he said. The waves also increase ocean temperatures and push cold, nutrient-rich waters deeper below the surface, which has an impact on marine life. Here's what to know about Kelvin waves. How does a Kelvin wave form? Kelvin waves are a "fact of life" during an El Niño, a naturally occurring climate pattern involving the warming ocean waters, said Dillon Amaya, an assistant professor in the Department of Marine, Earth, and Atmospheric Sciences at North Carolina State University. They form when the trade winds along the equator change direction. WATCH: How a super El Niño is fueling extreme weather patterns Winds blowing east to west along the equator push water in the Pacific Ocean west toward Asia, Jacox said. When those winds weaken or reverse direction, that bulge of water gets pushed back toward the east along the equator until it hits South America. When the surge of water hits the coastline at the equator, it moves north and south along the North and South American coasts. The wave isn't visible to the naked eye and they won't cause boats to go up and down, Amaya said. It's more like a big pancake. It's wider than it's deep: The bulge extends 12 to 20 miles (19 to 32 kilometers) off the coast and about 200 meters deep, Amaya said. What are the potential impacts of Kelvin waves? Many coastal communities are already grappling with the impacts of rising sea levels, like the coastal erosion eating away at the beach in San Clemente, California. Waves are also getting bigger, experts say. The higher sea levels could exacerbate those problems. "People are on edge," Amaya said. "They think about more flooding happening, more beach erosion so when you hear elevated sea states coastal inundation risk, I think that raises a lot of anxiety." The higher sea level combined with larger than average waves from North Pacific swell, which are expected during the El Niño, plus large spring tides from October to February, can cause exceptional erosion on the West Coast, said Sean Vitousek, a research oceanographer with the U.S. Geological Survey. WATCH: Ocean at the front door: Coastal communities battle erosion Generally, the largest El Niño events of 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16 caused West Coast beaches to experience their worst erosion on record, Vitousek said. "The loss of protective beaches also increases wave impacts and coastal flooding on property and infrastructure," he said. Things could intensify over time as more waves arrive over the winter. Typically El Niños are associated with five or six of these waves, Amaya said. During the last major El Niño in 2015-2016 there were five Kelvin waves. One already came through in May or June and there's evidence of a third Kelvin wave forming, he said. Experts expect it to continue up the coast over the next month or so. How are states responding to concerns about higher sea levels? There's concern the waves could worsen challenges along the Southern California coast, said Alyssa Napuri, deputy chief of staff for Orange County Supervisor Katrina Foley. Already, waves are approaching a seaside rail line and oceanfront homes were damaged during swells last month tied to Hurricane Marie. Authorities are placing emergency sand on beaches as quickly as possible, Napuri said, adding that forecasts show the Kelvin Wave could send water levels between six to 12 inches higher. "We're already struggling as it is," Napuri said. California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, proclaimed a state of emergency in late September to prepare the state for what will likely be a historic El Niño season. The proclamation will help the state "move faster to protect communities, stage critical resources, and strengthen readiness before severe weather intensifies," the governor said in a statement. Could a robot designed by young engineering students from Northern Ireland end up on the Moon?
A team, from Queen's University Belfast (QUB), are heading to Florida later this month to take part in a Nasa 'lunabotics' competition.
Lunabotics is a university-level competition for teams to use the Nasa systems engineering process to design, build, and operate a lunar robot.
The students created a lab-built robot that they will bring to the competition to find out how it would deal with future moon missions.
The robots will be expected to dig up lunar material, drive over obstacles and use the material to form a wall.
Jack Fitzpatrick, who's studying for a PhD in mechanical engineering, said "it's a great feeling" to have been invited and they're looking forward to the opportunity to take part.
The team of 10 QUB students made it to the competition following their win at the competition earlier this year.
They'll be competing at the University of Central Florida against university teams from Australia, India and the US.
Jamie Smith is a third-year electrical and electronic engineering student.
He explained that the team was divided into three groups for software, electronics and mechanical.
Jamie was the software team lead for this project. He said their main task was to control the rover then provide the autonomous capabilities towards it.
And, they had to build rover simulations to test their software before they actually got one.
Jack, however, is part of the mechanical side.
"We analyse that something is physically strong enough, it's well built enough to survive this environment, it's going to have the traction to drive in this environment," he explained.
Jamie explained they designed the 52 kg aluminium frame robot rover and took it compete at a competition in Milton Keynes.
"We got on very well. We ended up winning the competition and had great fun," he said.
Then a few weeks later, they were invited to compete at Nasa's international Lunabotics competition.
Jack said that being asked to go was a "great feeling" and "a real opportunity to demonstrate everything that you've learned".
"It's just a great opportunity to represent Northern Ireland, the UK and really Europe abroad as we are the only European team that will be there," Jack explained.
Both of the students said their success was a reflection of both themselves and also the university and the School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering.
What does the robot actually do?
Jamie explained that the main objective of the rover is that should be able to drive itself around a lunar-simulated room.
"That means it should start at a point, figure out where it is within this room, travel to an excavation point, so in that point, it will pick up then some sand which is meant to be lunar-simulant.
"It'll pick up the sand and then deposit it at another location, and it's meant to do this all by itself."
Jack explained that the purpose of this is to simulate how real rovers carry out these kind of tasks on the moon.
"It's being able to autonomously operate on the moon and build environments for humans to later habitat. And that's the real drive behind why this competition exists," he explained.
So are they feeling confident they can bring home another win?
Jack explained that there have been several precursor competitions in different countries and this competition takes the top tier of those competitions and brings them together "to really showcase the talent" that there is internationally.
"We are the winning team from the United Kingdom competition and we will be representing the UK and, by extension, Europe at this competition."
"We may not win the competition this year but we're building a base upon which we can improve year on year and maybe come back in a few years and really come through with a winning design," he said.
CaolÃ¡n Boyle, Head of Robotics at QPL, said the team is "exceptionally proud and excited".
He said "hundreds of hours have gone into making the rover mission ready for the event".

Rare tornado whips through small Australian town
Several people in Ulladulla, New South Wales, filmed the moment a rare tornado came through the town on 3 October.
The Australian Bureau of Meteorology said the phenomenon was caused by "severe" thunderstorms and that it was "very uncommon to see one in such a populated place".
The weather incident caused damage to properties and knocked over some trees, it added.

Rebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said its decision to relocate was made because of concerns about risks to civilians.
Two residents in Mekelle told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF forces have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services appear to have resumed in parts of the city.
Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and federal government forces alongside allied fighters in parts of Ethiopia's northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.
The development marks a major shift in the conflict and raises concerns among observers that the fighting could further destabilise the Horn of Africa, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries.
The US Department of State called for "restraint" and "dialogue" on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting about the conflict in Egypt on Sunday with leaders from some of Ethiopia's neighbours.
Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides.
However, in the last six months there has been a worsening of relations, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement.
Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.
The civil war was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
On Friday, neighbours Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with each other after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting a new rebel alliance - an allegation that it denied.
Ethiopia has also accused Egypt of supporting the rebels, leading to the expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, which Cairo responded to by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period.
The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

abada82e52ec.text: LOS ANGELES — Voters could make history next month by giving the two largest U.S. cities something in common: South Asian immigrant democratic socialist mayors. Why it matters: Such a pairing would capture two forces reshaping urban America — its growing diversity and the Democratic Party's shifting ideological boundaries. New York, the nation's largest city, is already led by democratic socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani . The challenger in Los Angeles is Nithya Raman, an Indian-born urban planner and two-term City Council member who is trying to unseat Democratic Mayor Karen Bass on Nov. 3. Bass, elected in 2022, is the first woman to serve as mayor of Los Angeles. State of play: Raman became the first Asian American woman and first South Asian elected to the L.A. City Council in 2020. A Harvard and MIT graduate, she entered politics after working on homelessness and neighborhood organizing. A September Berkeley IGS/L.A. Times poll found Raman at 39% among likely voters, Bass at 28% and 33% undecided. The intrigue: The Berkeley poll had Raman ahead 66%-4% among likely voters under 30, while 56% rated Bass' response to the Palisades Fire poor or very poor. It also found an even wider gap among likely Latino voters : Raman led Bass 45%-21%, with 34% undecided. What they're saying: "I'm getting a little emotional thinking about it," Raman told Axios and Noticias Telemundo on Wednesday at Visionarios when asked what it would mean if she and Mamdani led the country's two largest cities. Raman, who immigrated to the U.S. as a child, said her family came to America seeking opportunities they didn't have in India. She contrasted the welcome her family received with what she sees as a harsher moment for immigrants today under the Trump administration. "The idea of this city welcoming an immigrant as its mayor ... is just so deeply moving to me at this moment." The other side: Bass strategist Julie Chavez Rodriguez told Axios and Noticias Telemundo that voters are talking about rent, affordable housing, public safety and whether they can afford to raise families in Los Angeles. Rodriguez credited Bass with accelerating nearly 47,000 affordable housing units, a figure also cited by the mayor's office for units in the city's pipeline. She also defended Bass' response to federal immigration raids, pointing to lawsuits and restrictions on using city property to assist immigration enforcement. Zoom in: Raman's version of democratic socialism sounds less revolutionary than municipal. She told Axios that Americans are pushing back against an establishment they believe favors wealthy and politically connected interests. Her alternative: make City Hall deliver basic services and prove government can work for ordinary people. Raman called it "sewer socialism" or "pothole politics," adding: "I just want government to work for the people." Zoom out: Mamdani has made a similar ideological bet in New York, declaring at his inauguration that he was elected as a democratic socialist and would govern as one. Yes, but: Raman isn't simply the West Coast version of Mamdani. She calls herself an independent leader and has repeatedly split with Democratic Socialists of America-LA — accepting a pro-Israel group's endorsement that earned her a DSA censure . She also backed Jim McDonnell for LAPD chief over the group's objections and sought changes to L.A.'s voter-approved mansion tax that housing activists opposed.

0eebba796caa.text: A closely watched Nvidia-backed startup called Reflection is preparing to shake up the AI race with a powerful open-weight system that could threaten Chinese upstarts and U.S. AI giants alike. Why it matters : The marriage of an American open-weight model and Nvidia GPUs would give individuals and companies a new, cheaper alternative to Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. Open models, designed to compete with Chinese rivals, can be harder to monitor and regulate than the Big Three so-called frontier models. Supporters of such ecosystems say their widespread availability and transparency also bring security advantages. Reflection's first model is set to be joined by other open-weight models from other Western players this month, sources tell Axios. That will bring a new competitive dimension to the AI boom. State of play : Reflection's model, set to be released soon, is expected to initially lag behind the most cutting-edge U.S. models and be competitive with top Chinese open-weight models. Sources tell Axios it will still boast powerful intelligence — capable enough to help companies build their own proprietary, low-cost AI systems. Combining a lower-tier open model with high-quality company data can yield results that rival the most expensive frontier AI systems in certain situations. A Reflection spokesperson declined to comment. The big picture : Open-weight models, the most powerful of which are almost uniformly made in China, have taken Silicon Valley by storm. As opposed to closed models like Claude and ChatGPT, open-weight models like Reflection's are generally available to be downloaded freely and can be used and customized by anyone. On platforms that serve many models, their combined market share at times has surged to take up a majority of usage. However, in the far higher-spending arena of enterprise use, which is typically handled through API and corporate billing, open-weight models account for a small proportion of usage, AI execs and analysts say. Zoom in : Reflection's ultimate goal is to pioneer the "AI factory" — a product allowing institutions to spin up their own localized AI ecosystems. A company, for example, would take its own proprietary data, use Reflection's models and secure its own computing firepower to build a highly customized, cheap AI system. Some institutions, particularly hedge funds and trading firms, are already eager to build proprietary AI systems using their own highly guarded data. The startup has already begun testing this concept, announcing a sovereign AI factory partnership with Shinsegae Group in South Korea. Behind the scenes : In preparation for the launch, Reflection has held discussions with interested parties in Washington and elsewhere in recent weeks to detail its model release and explain how the AI factory will work, sources told Axios. It is also aggressively locking up the compute capacity required to scale. In recent weeks, the startup signed massive deals with Nebius and SpaceX to rent Nvidia AI servers. What they're saying : Reflection CEO Misha Laskin has indicated it will take time for its models to reach the most advanced capabilities. "They're kind of like rocket ships," Laskin, a Russian–Israeli researcher who previously worked at Google, told CNBC . "To build a big rocket ship, it takes time." The Nvidia factor : The AI factory has been a core vision of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for years. He has described a scenario combining computing hardware with open-source models, allowing enterprises to retain ownership of their data. Top AI users in Western business and government, such as banks or the Pentagon, balk at using highly capable Chinese models due to security risks. Reflection and other Western players are trying to fill that void. For years, Huang has sought to strengthen the open AI ecosystem and has been strongly supportive of Reflection's move toward building a top open system, according to stories in The Wall Street Journal and The Information . The bottom line : Reflection's release, and the startup's close ties to Nvidia, will bring a renewed focus on open-weight models, combining with other coming offerings to shake up the AI race.

Major bridges in Kyiv have been hit by Russian drone strikes for four consecutive days, as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine's capital.
Two people were injured when the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge was struck on Sunday morning for the second day in a row, while the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times earlier in the week.
The latest attack came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a surprise visit to Kyiv in a show of support against Russia's continuing full-scale invasion.
Russia's military said it would be intensifying strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions. It earlier said it had hit the two bridges used to transfer Ukrainian troops.
Video footage of Sunday's strike, verified by the BBC, shows cars moving on Pivnichnyi Bridge as a drone crashes into it before exploding, creating a ball of fire. A cloud of black smoke can be seen rising above the bridge.
Other videos and pictures have emerged on social media showing a gaping hole in the middle of a traffic lane on the bridge.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were injured in the latest Russian attack. He earlier said that the Pivnichnyi Bridge's roadway was hit.
Kyiv's eight bridges across the wide Dnipro River link the western (right) and eastern (left) parts, and many of the capital's estimated three million residents rely heavily on the metro lines and trains to travel across the city.
Some 500,000 vehicles use the bridges every day.
The two struck bridges are still standing - but the damage and restrictions to traffic and public transport have caused gridlock in parts of the capital at times.
"To get from the left bank to the right one and back - it's just hell," Kyiv resident Roman told the BBC on Sunday.
Large numbers of commuters cross the river, especially on weekdays. Repair teams are working to fix the damage and officials say they are planning temporary pontoon bridges, ferry services and even a tunnel under the river to keep Kyiv connected.
Klitschko also said a separate Russian drone strike had damaged a heating main, adding that there would be a temporary lack of hot water in the north-eastern Desnyanskyi district as a result.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenksy said on Sunday morning Russian drones had also attacked a warehouse in the north-eastern region of Sumy, killing one person.
Meanwhile, in the central city of Dnipro, six people were injured after a communications facility was struck, he said.
Ukraine's Air Force said that overnight Russia had launched 135 drones, including 52 jet-powered ones. It said that 125 projectiles had been shot down.
As emergency services responded to the incidents, Germany's Merz met Zelenksy in Kyiv. They laid wreaths to Ukrainian soldiers who have been killed in the war.
Merz reaffirmed his country's support for Ukraine, writing on X: "Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I travelled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us.
"Germany's security also depends on the outcome of this war. That is why we are helping out of our own self-interest as well."
Zelensky later said that a new aid package worth more than â¬1.3bn (Â£1.1bn; $1.5bn) had been agreed with Germany.
"These are weapons that will help [us] right now, as well as support for our energy sector ahead of winter," he said.
As Merz was visiting Ukraine's Academy of Sciences building badly damaged in a Russian drone attack earlier this week, fresh air alert sirens were heard across the city. Two people were killed in that drone attack.
Since Merz became chancellor in May 2025, Germany has become the single largest donor to Ukraine.
He said the country "needs all our support in the coming weeks", adding: "If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us."
Zelensky said there would be "important agreements" made between Ukraine and Germany.
The Ukrainian president has made repeated appeals for Western allies to provide more military support to the country, including supplying advanced interceptors that can shoot down new jet-powered Russian drones and also ballistic missiles.
The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier this week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had earlier said his military was carrying out retaliatory attacks following Ukraine's strikes on Moscow's energy facilities, despite the fact that it was the Kremlin that had first launched such attacks.
Putin began a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
The Russian foreign ministry on Saturday repeated a warning for foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv.
Responding to the warning, EU ambassador KatarÃna MathernovÃ¡ wrote on X on Sunday: "The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe's support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!"
German ambassador to Ukraine, Boris Ruge, reacted to Mathernova's post with: "Amen - we're staying".
Earlier attacks on the Pivdennyi Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday.
Klitschko warned that the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities.
Experts say Russian drones are unlikely to bring down the bridges - but repeated attacks will force their closure and risk weakening their structure, making them unusable.

Conservationists have said they are planning to buy a field to extend a "green lung" in one of Jersey's most built-up parishes.
The National Trust for Jersey said it had secured the rights to acquire the land near Maupertuis Farm in St Clement and hoped to complete the purchase shortly.
A green lung is an area of fields, parkland or vegetation within an otherwise urban area, providing space for wildlife and helping to reduce pollution.
The trust previously raised Â£50,000 in 37 days to buy a nearby field on Samares Lane in 2021.
The trust said the latest acquisition would help preserve the agricultural heritage of Maupertuis Farm and the surrounding area.
Chief executive Alan Le Maistre said green spaces were becoming "ever more precious" and protecting them was particularly important in densely developed parts of the island.
"It is a privilege to have the opportunity to extend this green lung for both the wildlife and people of the area," he said.
The National Trust for Jersey, which celebrated its 90th anniversary in August, manages about 1,800 vergÃ©es of land across the island.
It invited people who want to support the latest acquisition to contact the charity directly.

Here's what you need to know.
The man not on the ballot
Jair Bolsonaro, the right-wing former army captain who governed Brazil from 2019 to 2023, will not be running for president in this election.
Not only is the 71-year-old barred from standing for office, he is also serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula.
Due to recurrent health problems, he is currently under house arrest rather than in a cell, but he has had restrictions imposed on him prohibiting him from posting on social media or making public statements.
Despite these restrictions, his shadow - and sometimes his moving and talking image - looms large over this election.
At the event where FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro officially launched his presidential campaign, an AI-generated avatar of Jair Bolsonaro endorsed his son's candidacy.
When pressed by the Supreme Court about the deepfake, Jair Bolsonaro's lawyers may have denied he had given his permission for its use, but there is nevertheless little doubt that FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro has the backing of his father.
What do the polls say?
While there are 12 candidates running for the presidency, there are only two who have reached double figures in the opinion polls, and they are LuÃz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva and FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro.
BBC Brasil's poll tracker shows them both hovering around the 40% mark, with Lula slightly ahead of Bolsonaro.
The other 11 candidates are polling at 4% or less.
If none of the candidates gains 50% of valid votes in the first round on 4 October, the top two contenders will proceed to a run-off election on 25 October.
The opinion polls suggest a run-off is highly likely - but with a relatively high number of voters still undecided just days before the election, an outright win cannot be entirely ruled out.
BBC Brasil's poll aggregator suggests that at the end of September, 9% of voters were either still undecided, or planning to spoil their ballot, cast a blank ballot or not go to the polls at all.
Brazilians who are 16 years of age or older are entitled to vote and it is compulsory for those aged between 18 and 70 who are literate, with a fine imposed on those who do not cast a ballot.
Almost 160 million Brazilians are eligible to vote in this election and, with polls typically surveying just thousands of people, the end result can differ considerably from the indications given by surveys.
