The former metalworker left office with record approval ratings of over 80%, but his party was later rocked by huge corruption scandals.
Lula himself spent more than 18 months in prison between 2018 and 2019 after being convicted of corruption and money laundering, charges he has always denied.
Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for the presidency in the 2022 election, in which he beat Jair Bolsonaro by 1.8 percentage points.
When he started his third term in office, he vowed it would be his last, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 later this month.
There is no doubt he remains a towering figure in the left. But while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions.
His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism.
Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy.

ALTADENA, Calif.—Sylvie Andrews walks among the brilliant white poppies, purple California grapes and olive-green thorns surrounding her yard’s blackened pizza oven—one of the only things that survived last year’s devastating Eaton Fire. But her eyes scan the block beyond, ever-aware of changes to her neighborhood.
Andrews says virtually all of her neighbors have received unsolicited offers for the empty plots of land where their homes burned as part of a recent push from developers moving into the wildfire-ravaged area.
She hasn’t herself yet, and Senate Bill 1090—the Keep Altadena Land in Altadena Hands Act—signed by California Gov. Gavin Newsom Wednesday, will make it less likely that she does.
But that doesn’t address the developments that have already been approved.
Will Andrews rebuild the home she lost in the blaze—completed in 2018 with Nick Wright, her partner at the time—in the place she has loved all her life?
“We don’t know,” the 46-year-old told Inside Climate News.
“We have to factor in questions about what our neighborhood will look like in five years. Will I rebuild my bungalow only to find that a developer buys the lot across the street, builds out to the property line and up two stories and blocks my view?” said Andrews, who is determined to never sell to a developer.
Andrews supports affordable housing and multi-family homes but doesn’t want her neighbor “to be some private-equity LLC shell corporation.”
The worry is not unfounded. Outside parties have advanced development more quickly in Altadena than owners of homes that burned have, interviews, local permitting records and data reviewed by Inside Climate News showed. While projects are also moving fast in the Pacific Palisades, Altadena’s older housing stock, historic layout and relatively lower fire risk have attracted droves of developers to an area with already strained infrastructure in the wake of the Eaton Fire.
“There’s too many question marks right now,” said Andrews, who works helping businesses and seniors, mostly in Altadena, with computer tasks. “Like a lot of people, we’re waiting for the [Southern California] Edison lawsuit to settle, so we find out how much money we’re looking at. But that’s not the only factor.”
Another is how long it will take Altadena’s infrastructure to recover to make living tenable and affordable after the Eaton Fire. The wildfire, which officials reported was sparked by an old Southern California Edison transmission line, burned over 14,000 acres, resulted in 19 deaths, destroyed more than 9,000 structures and damaged over 1,000 others.
Los Angeles County has issued more than 3,600 building permits within the Eaton Fire burn scar between February 2025 and late September 2026.
SB 1090, signed by Newsom as the legislative session came to a close last week, limits controversial high-density development in two Altadena zip codes. In a letter accompanying his signing, Newsom said he recognized the community’s “desire for stability” as it charts its recovery.
But homeowners say plenty of projects have already slipped through the cracks. Inside Climate News has learned that as many as 60 new housing proposals—the vast majority from developers outside of the community, representing between 200 and 300 new structures—have already been approved in Altadena. SB 1090 does not affect any proposed developments with plans submitted prior to Oct. 1.
Laws to Ease Housing Crisis Complicate Rebuilding
Local government officials and families allege that developers have seized on other state legislation, taking advantage of the development opportunities provided by Senate Bill 1123 and Senate Bill 9, in a community still in recovery.
SB 9, passed in 2021, allows lots to be split and additional residential development on qualifying single-family lots. SB 1123, which took effect four years later, allows for construction of up to 10 small homes on plots zoned for single-family homes.
The bills, created to help alleviate California’s crippling housing shortage, also make it more feasible for a property to be split into smaller parcels that can then be individually sold to multiple businesses or people.
Various proposals for duplexes and bungalow courts have moved forward in Altadena despite criticism from residents still getting back on their feet. They worry that new units will add strain to the already limited parking options and stray from the craftsman homes that traditionally dotted the community.
These projects also deviate from a development plan the community itself had worked on just before the Eaton Fire and “welcome wholeheartedly,” said Shawna Dawson Beer, a longtime community organizer and one of the founding members of grassroots group Altadena for Accountability. The West San Gabriel Valley plan already included adding more housing, creating mixed-used corridors and walkable dense residential neighborhoods with infrastructure to support them.
Elizabeth Vazquez, a spokesperson for Los Angeles County Public Works—citing ongoing litigation—did not comment on permits issued under the senate bills passed to increase housing density before the Eaton Fire.
She defended the county’s pace of advancing projects for ordinary homeowners, which some residents have called too slow.
“Our permitting departments have shortened review turnaround timelines and deferred or refunded more than $33 million in permitting fees for wildfire impacted residents,” Vazquez said in an email, noting the county has also piloted new programs to make the process smoother.
Vazquez said work to preserve and restore Altadena’s historic look and character “will inherently require more time and planning to rebuild.”
Matthew Lewis, a spokesman for California YIMBY, argues that SB 1090’s three-year pause on dense development will speed up the displacement it’s meant to prevent. He pointed to LA Times analysis of permits from California fire zones, which found that only 38 percent of burned homes were rebuilt five years later.

Water regulators and farmers in Colorado’s San Luis Valley are in a lose-lose situation.
Either they adopt a plan to aggressively manage the use of groundwater from their rapidly declining aquifer, likely forcing a contraction of the local agricultural economy, or continue overpumping and further lower the water table, which will likely force mass shutoffs of well water in the future.
“It’s really draconian,” Colorado state Sen. Cleave Simpson, a fourth-generation valley farmer and general manager of the Rio Grande Water Conservation District, said in an interview in March. “I don’t know how my community is going to survive.”
But Simpson sees no other option.
San Luis Valley groundwater provides roughly 800,000 acre-feet of irrigation water annually in the highly productive agricultural region. But after decades of overpumping and persistent drought conditions, the aquifer reached a record low in August.
Simpson estimates the district has spent roughly $100 million over 14 years trying to reduce groundwater pumping, which fell by about one-third over the past decade. Despite those efforts, officials say the aquifer’s long-term storage is getting “worse and worse.”
“Everything we’ve tried to do is failing, just because we don’t have snowpack, we don’t have inflow,” said Simpson.
Now, a proposed groundwater management plan would dramatically increase the fee thousands of well users pay for pumping from the aquifer.
That would deal a blow to the local agricultural industry, with some producers saying the additional cost will put them out of business. But if the region does not meet aquifer restoration goals soon, state engineers can shut down the valley’s wells entirely—a situation that would devastate its economy.
The groundwater plan was the subject of a weeks-long Colorado water court trial this summer, with a ruling expected later this year. Regardless of the outcome, the case is likely to be appealed to the Colorado Supreme Court, Judge Michael Gonzales said.
Water managers, farmers and lawyers largely agree that the aquifer must be brought back to sustainable levels. The case will help determine how that happens and how its economic impacts are distributed.
A Shrinking Supply
An extensive canal system spreads surface water from the Rio Grande through the valley. But across the river’s headwaters, snowmelt rates decreased by 20 percent per decade from 1984 to 2017, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
Fourth-generation farmer Michael Jones has seen that firsthand. When his grandfather was farming in the valley, their irrigation ditch had a flow until sometime in September. “We’re lucky to even get water into July now on our ditch systems,” said Jones. “And that’s in my lifetime I’ve seen that change.”
The earlier the ditches turn off, the greater the imbalance between how much is pumped from and recharged into the valley’s aquifer system.
The valley has both a deep, confined aquifer, and an unconfined aquifer closer to the surface that is unique—contained by multi-layer, permeable components so that one user’s well pumping can alter water availability elsewhere in the system. Water storage in the unconfined aquifer, which supplies most irrigation wells, has fallen dramatically, losing an estimated 1.3 million acre-feet of water since 1976, when tracking began.
With that in mind, regulators created groundwater subdistricts in the early 2000s to manage resources more collectively.
“This very complex hydrology will essentially be threatened without some additional layer of collective management, as opposed to the operation of individual decrees that you see in less hydrologically complex areas,” said Gregor MacGregor, water attorney and faculty fellow at the University of Colorado Law School.
Groundwater Subdistrict No. 1, a highly agricultural area at the center of the mitigation effort, created and scrapped multiple plans to halt the unconfined aquifer’s decline over nearly two decades. After severe drought in 2018 wiped out much of the district’s hard-earned progress, Simpson received a warning.
State Engineer Kevin Rein wrote that he “will be put in the unenviable but required position of curtailing groundwater diversions” if the subdistrict’s sustainability goals are not met by 2031, a deadline set by its Colorado Supreme Court-approved plan for water management in 2011. And this could occur earlier if it becomes “undeniable” at any point that the goals won’t be met.
In other words, if the district didn’t act fast, the state could shut down its wells.
Today, producers in Subdistrict 1 pay a fee for every acre-foot of water they pump—equivalent to covering one acre in one foot of water. Many earn groundwater pumping credits by using their surface water allotments to recharge the aquifer, then pay the pumping fee for any additional water that’s needed. The district’s latest plan would raise the fee for groundwater pumping beyond a producer’s surface-water rights from $150 to $500 per acre-foot, an intentionally prohibitive price designed to force pumping reductions. However, those with unused surface-water rights can instead sell them to those without rights, with the price set by the market.
The goal is to reach a 1-to-1 system: For every acre-foot of groundwater pumped, an acre-foot of water is returned to the aquifer.
Contracting an Economy
At the trial, there was broad agreement that the unconfined aquifer must be raised and kept at sustainable levels, said Heather Dutton, manager of the San Luis Valley Water Conservancy District: “They weren’t necessarily arguing about the science and the facts of the hydrology … Nobody disagreed that we have to take action and that the aquifer is at these historic levels.”
But how that should be done is a point of contention. In the valley, “many a barbecue has been ruined” talking about the “overall state of the water in the region,” said farmer Jones.

Protecting all heritage sites from the impact of climate change "just may not be possible," according to a National Trust manager.
Justin Scully, manager of Fountains Abbey and Studley Royal, said extreme heat, heavy rainfall and wildfire risk were already affecting gardens, moorland and historic structures.
He said heavy rain could overwhelm drainage systems and penetrate walls, causing damp and erosion, while repeated cycles of wetting, drying, freezing and thawing could harm stonework.
Flooding could also undermine foundations, while hotter, dry conditions could increase the risk of subsidence and wildfires.
Scully said the organisation may have to accept it cannot save everything as it is today.
"These last two summers have really brought this home to ourselves and to our visitors," he said.
"Climate change isn't a thing that's happening out there to other people, it's actually impacting ourselves and the places we love. The threat is tangible."
The National Trust is planning for more extreme weather by looking at what could happen to the properties and landscapes it manages over the next 40 years.
"We've got to think about what could be the worst possible outcome and then work backwards from that," Scully said.
At Fountains Abbey, this could include increasing drainage capacity and gutters to cope with heavier rainfall.
It could also result in changing the appearance of the gardens.
Scully said the trust needed to be "more open to how we would adapt," with gardens potentially becoming "less manicured".
"People expect things to look perfect and crisp," he said.
The trust looks after properties including Beningbrough Hall, Nunnington Hall and Treasurer's House in York, as well as miles of coastline from Loftus to Filey.
It said coastal sites were among those facing the greatest climate pressures, including erosion and rising sea levels.
A National Trust spokesperson said: "Climate change is affecting many of the places we care for, and our conservation work has to evolve with it."
Conservation decisions would consider the significance of a place, the benefit it brings to people and whether an approach is sustainable long term, they added.
The National Trust is a charity and receives no guaranteed government money, although it can apply for project grants from public bodies and lottery funds.
Scully said some adaptation processes could be "very expensive".
The trust did not give a figure for those costs, but said it would continue to invest significantly in conservation.
It also called for climate resilience to become a national priority, led by a Cabinet-level minister coordinating preparedness across government and supporting long-term investment.
Scully said people should not despair.
"There are small things that we can do as communities [such as reducing carbon footprints] that will make a big difference over the longer term."

Australian authorities are investigating the links between the country and a Flydubai co-pilot who attempted to take control of a plane travelling to Israel.
The co-pilot is alleged to have attacked the captain with a crash axe during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv before passengers managed to overpower him and successfully take control of the plane.
The Australian authorities have not identified the co-pilot, who has been named by multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times as Hamam al-Hammami.
The prosecutor in the UAE has said it is investigating the incident and any possible motives.
In a statement to the BBC, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed its investigation into "the man's links to Australia".
The investigation involves state police and the country's security agency, it said, adding that an update would be "provided at the appropriate time".
Sources familiar with the case, who have spoken to Australian media, have said the co-pilot was issued a student visa in 2014, and studied in Australia between 2015 and 2017, until he left the country.
The Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) said the co-pilot's student visa was cancelled in 2019 as he was no longer enrolled in a course, making him ineligible for it.
Counter-terrorism officials will look at whether the man was radicalised in Australia, the ABC reported.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he was an Omani national.
The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on 30 September was carrying more than 170 passengers to Israel.
Two and a half hours into its journey, the plane plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) when the Omani co-pilot attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.
The pilot flying the plane, Capt Smit Machchhar, described how he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.
Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.
Machchhar, an Indian national, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.
The co-pilot was arrested after the emergency landing and is being questioned by Saudi authorities, according to Netanyahu.
The UAE's attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said on Saturday investigations were under way to establish the circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident.
He said investigations into the incident revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act", according to the country's state news agency.
In the days since the attack more details have come to light about the co-pilot's employment history.
While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.
It is also known that, from 2020, he was studying on a distance-learning course run by Buckinghamshire New University in the UK.
He graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.

A father and son who worked at a Mississippi smoke shop have been arrested and charged in connection with the death of at least one university student who died from a suspected overdose of kratom, sometimes called "gas station heroin" in the US.
The pair worked at a shop that allegedly sold derivatives of the substance to University of Mississippi students.
US prosecutors charged Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, 51, and Islam Yahya Mosleh, 18, for possession with the intent to distribute controlled substances in connection with the death investigation of two Ole Miss students last month.
Although their deaths have not officially been attributed to kratom, officials afterward issued warnings about consuming kratom.
The criminal complaint alleges that on 21 September, an Ole Miss student was found dead in his dorm room. The apparent cause of death "appeared to be consistent with a drug overdose", the US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Mississippi said in a press release.
Law enforcement found packages - with some tablets missing - of suspected kratom derivatives.
About an hour later, a second student was found dead from a suspected overdose in another location, also with packages of suspected kratom derivatives.
Officials connected the packages with the local vape, tobacco and beer store, the US Attorney's statement said.
Law enforcement executed search warrants and seized suspected kratom derivative controlled substances from the store. The Mosleh's, father and son, were later arrested.
The two students' deaths have sparked alarm and warnings from officials about the plant-based drug referred to as "gas station heroin".
Kratom - a herb with opioid-like effects - has grown in popularity in the US over the last decade, and is typically purchased over the counter and consumed in pill or liquid form.
For years, anti-kratom advocates have pushed for bans, and in some countries, like the UK, it is illegal. But Kratom is not regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration and is legal in some states, including Mississippi.
The Mississippi prosecutors said that kratom derivatives, such as MGPI, MGM-15 and MGM-16, are now schedule I controlled substances in the US and can be significantly more potent than natural kratom leaf products and morphine.

ba10b62b716c.text: By — Catherine A. Sanderson, The Conversation Catherine A. Sanderson, The Conversation Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/the-misperception-that-keeps-bystanders-from-intervening-and-how-to-short%e2%80%91circuit-it Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter The misperception that keeps bystanders from intervening and how to short‑circuit it Nation Oct 4, 2026 3:02 PM EDT This article originally appeared on The Conversation. As an undergrad student decades ago, I attended a dorm presentation describing the importance of giving and receiving sexual consent. The workshop leaders explained that if your partner said "no" or "stop" but you proceeded to have sex anyway, it was considered rape. A high-profile athlete on campus raised his hand and said, in utter disbelief, "That can't be right. By that definition, everyone I've ever had sex with I've raped." I was horrified by his comment, but most students laughed. He clearly saw nothing wrong with the view he'd expressed, presumably believing it was widely shared. READ MORE: Cornell president calls alleged gang rape 'deeply disturbing,' pledges greater transparency I immediately thought of this experience when I heard about the alleged sexual assault committed by seven fraternity members at Cornell University. As a social psychologist, and the author of a book examining why so-called good people stay silent in the face of problematic behavior, what I find most tragic about the events at Cornell is that reportedly over 50 men on a group chat learned about the assault as it was happening. Yet there's been no public report that any of them tried to stop the assault, help the victim or contact campus or local police departments. This type of inaction is very common. In about one-third of sexual assaults, at least one other person is present who potentially could intervene but in most instances chooses not to. Why? Misperceiving that you're the only one Data suggests a minority of men actually commit sexual assault. Researchers estimate about 6.5% of male college students in the United States and Canada have committed rape. Yet many men who find sexual violence offensive mistakenly believe that other men do not. Undergraduate men in one study reported their beliefs about common rape myths, such as "If a girl doesn't physically fight back, you can't really say it was rape," and "If a girl goes to a room alone with a guy at a party, it is her own fault if she is raped." Researchers then asked participants how they thought both their close friends and average male college students would answer these same questions. READ MORE: Woman told Cornell investigators she 'felt like bait' during alleged gang rape The results provided clear evidence that college men have skewed views of what those around them are thinking. Most students saw their classmates and friends as more supportive of rape myths than they themselves were. Unfortunately, believing that other men generally accept sexual violence — even when this belief is wrong — inhibits their willingness to intervene to stop such behavior when they encounter it. In fact, men's beliefs about their peers' attitudes are a stronger predictor of their willingness to intervene than their own stated attitudes about sexual aggression. What's behind these mistaken beliefs Men who underestimate their peers' discomfort with sexually aggressive behavior often fear the consequences of calling out problematic views or intervening in the face of inappropriate behavior. The most common reason male college students give for failing to intervene in situations involving sexual violence is a fear of being laughed at or ridiculed — in particular, a desire not to appear weak to other men. Men who actually commit assault also tend to overestimate support for such behavior. Not surprisingly, men who report having committed sexual assault believe that other men are more accepting of such behavior and have engaged in such behavior themselves. This assumed support leads them to feel comfortable describing problematic behavior, which leads other men to believe that sexual violence is more common, and more accepted, than it actually is. Resetting a social norm Given the consistent evidence that men wrongly believe that most men are more comfortable with sexual violence than they themselves are, the challenge is not to change the social norm. It's getting people to see what it actually already is. Correcting such misperceptions can go a long way toward reducing sexual violence. First-year male college students who participate in a 90-minute sexual assault prevention program — focused on refuting rape myths, increasing awareness of the importance of consent, and correcting misperceptions about other men's attitudes and behaviors — report reduced levels of sexual aggression themselves four months later. WATCH: Appointing Cornell sex assault special prosector, Hochul says she won't let anyone 'sweep this case under the rug' These programs work in two ways. First, men who receive accurate information about what other men actually believe are less inhibited about speaking out and intervening. Second, men who are at risk of engaging in sexual aggression may change their intentions after learning that their peers do not support such behavior. At the same time, men in tight-knit groups feel considerable pressure to show loyalty to other group members, which may lead to ignoring bad behavior committed by their peers. But the underlying dynamics of peer influence can help shift group norms from protecting group members by staying silent to stepping in to prevent bad behavior. One college football player described looking out for his teammates, even if that meant interrupting a potential sexual encounter: "Maybe you don't get the girl, but you'll keep your scholarship and still be on the team." A 12-year-old girl was killed in Baltimore over the weekend during an apparent disagreement over a parking space, police in the US city said.
The girl was caught in the crossfire of bullets between two men who police said were allegedly fighting over a parking space in a park where children were playing American football.
In addition to the young girl, another woman was also found with gunshot wounds when police arrived on the scene. Two men also visited area hospitals for injuries related to the shooting, police said.
Police are now searching for at least two suspects, Baltimore Police Commissioner Richard Worley said at a news conference.
"What we know is there was some type of argument between two cowards," Worley said. "They both opened fire on each other. In the crossfire, a 12-year-old little girl, who was probably down there watching football, was shot and killed."
Worley said the girl, who police have not named, was not a target of the shooting.
The girl was pronounced dead in hospital. The other three individuals who were injured have non-life-threatening injuries, Worley said.
The incident happened after 18:00 EDT (23:00 BST) on Saturday.
Authorities are still investigating the shooting and have asked any witnesses to bring information to police.
It remains unclear how many shots were fired, Worley said.
"Two grown men got into an argument, and now a 12-year-old is gone," Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott said at the news conference.
"We never should have to say something like that. What happened out here today is one of the most disgusting things I've ever seen in my life."

a8455072f62a.text: By — John Raby, Associated Press John Raby, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/search-ongoing-for-missing-medical-flight-from-bermuda-to-boston-as-crews-plan-to-scour-ocean-floor Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Search ongoing for missing medical flight from Bermuda to Boston as crews plan to scour ocean floor Nation Oct 4, 2026 1:53 PM EDT A search continued Sunday off the Massachusetts coast for an air ambulance carrying six people that disappeared during a flight from Bermuda to Boston as authorities planned to comb the seabed floor, the U.S. Coast Guard said. The Federal Aviation Administration contacted the Coast Guard at 2 a.m. Saturday that it had lost contact with the Gulfstream G100 carrying four Canadians and two Bermudian nationals over the Atlantic Ocean. Searchers later Saturday found a "debris field" off the coast of Nantucket, Coast Guard Northeast District Rear Adm. Matt Lake said at a news conference Sunday. READ MORE: Air traffic control calamity disrupts hundreds of U.S. flights, spotlighting the aging system Coast Guard crews along with the New York National Guard's Air Rescue Wing and Massachusetts authorities have since searched an area encompassing 2,840 square miles (7,356 square kilometers) using fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, boats and cutters. "This is a large and demanding search area," Lake said. The depth of the water around the debris field was 80 to 90 feet (about 24 to 27 meters). The Coast Guard was in the process of deploying sonar to search the seabed floor, he said. The Coast Guard has been updating the next of kin of those aboard the Canadian-registered air ambulance jet with the progress of the search, Lake said. Weather has not been a factor in the search efforts, said Coast Guard Capt. John McTamney, chief of response for the northeast district. "We'll continue to search and saturate the area until we're at the point where we are confident that if there were any survivors remaining on the surface of the water, we would have found them," McTamney said. The plane had four crew members and two passengers aboard when it departed Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport for the nighttime flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport's operator, Skyport. Air traffic audio indicates that the plane may have been "coming in blind" when a storm loomed ahead shortly before it vanished. The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net. "Roger, you said you're coming in blind. Is that what you said?" a controller can be heard asking the pilot. That makes Mary Schiavo, who is a former Inspector General of the Transportation Department, think the plane may have lost its navigational instruments just as a storm moved across its path on radar. The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 24,000 feet to around 10,000 feet, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24. "Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm. It's a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind," said Schiavo, who is an aviation attorney. "It's very easy to get disoriented and not know if you're turning, climbing, descending, etc." Transport Canada was closely monitoring and working with authorities on search and rescue efforts, the country's Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon said on the social platform X. AP Transportation Writer Josh Funk and Associated Press reporter Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas, a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative, contributed to this report. Three female journalists have accused police officers in India of sexual harassment during street protests in the capital Delhi.
The claims were made on Saturday after the force detained scores of young people calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner.
In a post on social media, Delhi Police said its New Delhi District had received the complaint, and it had been transferred to its crime branch for a "fair and impartial" inquiry.
Thousands of protesters gathered in Delhi and Mumbai cities for a third day on Sunday demanding that Gyanesh Kumar step down over large-scale changes to voter rolls.
The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.
Videos online show people being physically dragged away from the Jantar Mantar protest site in central Delhi.
The accusations by the women journalists include inappropriate touching by some police.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said women fear for their safety and the home ministry must "answer for this".
"Police dragged me by my hair," Aahna Singh, an activist and student at Jawaharlal Nehru University told Reuters news agency during the protests.
She said the police were resorting to "brutality".
The Press Club of India has demanded immediate action on the complaints against police officers, saying it was "shocked and dismayed" by the treatment of journalists.
"Behaviour of this kind cannot be normalised in a democracy. Journalists must be allowed to work freely, without fear, and document those who gather to raise various issues," it said in a statement.
The protesters say the voter-roll revision will benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.
It says the last revision was done nearly a quarter of a century ago and the voters' list needs to be updated to account for those who have died, left the country or are registered in more than one place as they've moved to a new address.
But the exercise has been mired in controversy from the start with the opposition parties accusing Kumar of manipulating voters' list to favour the BJP during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.
The protesters have included supporters of the influential Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) that began as an online satirical movement.
The pressure group recorded its first major victory in July when it forced the then Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign after weeks of protests calling for education reforms.
The CJP called for the latest protest after a report in The Indian Express, external said that Kumar's two fellow election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had formally objected at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders they said had been issued without their knowledge.
The differences were reported to be mostly over the controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year.
The Election Commission has defended its way of working and said in a statement that "differing views" were part of the "decision-making process" and that all the decisions were taken unanimously.
But the revelations sparked a furore, with opposition leaders demanding Kumar's resignation.

The head of Yemen's internationally recognised government has announced it will wage an all out war in an effort to take all territory held by the Houthis.
It follows an exchange of strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition in recent days.
The Iran-backed group said it had struck sites belonging to Saudi national oil company Aramco, in response to what it described as 50 Saudi-led coalition strikes in 12 hours. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment.
The Yemeni government's fierce statement was expected after the Houthis' offensive last month, which saw them seize control of the country's coastline, including the vital shipping lane of the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
On Sunday, Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address: "Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory."
Yemen's capital, Sanaa, which has been held by the Houthis for more than a decade, has come under sustained attack as government forces try to weaken the group's military capabilities.
Attacks on the Houthis have also spread across Yemen, including to the Saada region, the group's northern heartland.
But security sources say the Iran-backed Houthis have continued to make gains.
The frontline in Yemen remains focused around the key city of Taiz, which is still controlled by the internationally recognised government.
On Sunday, the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden, the interim capital of the Yemeni government, AFP news agency reports.
Citing three Yemeni military sources, AFP also reports that the Houthis now control the area and supply route, effectively encircling Taiz.
"They've achieved the military objective of isolating Taiz from Aden, even if they haven't fully taken control of it," Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at the Chatham House think tank, told AFP.
Al-Alimi was unlikely to have made the fierce announcement without the green light from Saudi Arabia, which remains the key backer of his government.
Saudi Arabia has been under constant attack as the Houthis try to target the country's economic lifeblood - oil.
On Sunday, Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched a ballistic missile and drone attack on Aramco sites in the capital, Riyadh, and the oil-rich Khurais area in the kingdom's east.
"Both operations successfully achieved their objectives," the spokesman said in a statement. "The strikes were precise, causing large fires at the targeted sites."
It is not the first time the group has said it has hit Saudi oil sites. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on Sunday's claimed attack, but has previously dismissed some claims as misleading, mocking the Houthis for "chasing imaginary victories".
But it has once again shown the price Saudi Arabia - and, as a consequence, the global economy - could pay if it launched a new all-out war against the Houthis.
In retaliation, Saudi Arabia has also been striking Houthi targets, according to the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel. It said at least two people had been wounded in strikes on Sunday.
On Saturday, Yemen's government also said its forces had hit Houthi targets across the country, including in Sanaa, Saada and the group's positions near Taiz in the south-west.
Yemen is one of the poorest countries in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis.
A war erupted in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital city from the Saudi-backed government, before going on to take control of swathes of the country's north.
Riyadh intervened in the war the following year, leading an international coalition.
After several years of relative calm, the war reignited in July amid the widening conflict in the Middle East.
Last month, a lightning offensive enabled the Houthis to seize the country's entire Red Sea coast, stopping Saudi Arabia from using it as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz.
The strategy benefited the Houthis' main sponsor, Iran. But it has also forced Saudi Arabia back into direct military confrontation with the Houthis.

1687427f1dc8.text: By — Eldar Emric, Associated Press Eldar Emric, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/bosnia-votes-as-pro-russian-politician-looms-large-and-ethnic-tensions-simmer Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Serb separatist Dodik declares victory in Bosnia vote as ethnic tensions and EU hopes collide World Updated on Oct 4, 2026 4:03 PM EDT — Published on Oct 4, 2026 12:42 PM EDT SARAJEVO, Bosnia-Herzegovina (AP) — Bosnian Serb nationalist politician Milorad Dodik has declared victory for his party in an election in Bosnia on Sunday that was shaped by economic pressures, the prospect of the Balkan nation joining the European Union, and ethnic tensions that have divided the country since its brutal 1992-95 war. Dodik is a staunchly pro-Russia politician who, despite not appearing on the ballot, has dominated the campaign and inflamed divisions with separatist rhetoric that have sparked fears of renewed instability in Bosnia. Formerly the president of the country's Serb-majority entity of Republika Srpska, Dodik was banned from holding public office after being convicted last year of defying decisions by the international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace agreement that ended the war. READ MORE: Brazil's presidential vote pits Trump ally against incumbent Lula With nearly 90% of votes counted, Dodik's ally Zeljka Cvijanovic of the right-wing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats had more than 55% of votes to take one of the three seats in the country's tripartite presidency, leading her nearest opponent by around 30 percentage points. Speaking at a news conference late Sunday, Dodik said his nationalist party would also hold a "vast majority" in Republika Srpska's assembly, and credited U.S. President Donald Trump's "magnificent victory" in 2024 and Russian President Vladimir Putin's support for the election win. "No one should ask us to change our politics," Dodik said. "We will not give up, but continue for our people ... I cannot believe that we smashed it like this." Election marked by low turnout Around 3.4 million voters were eligible to choose the three members of the country's multi-ethnic presidency, lawmakers for the national parliament and heads of institutions for the country's two entities: the Muslim-majority Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, which is dominated by ethnic Serbs. With over 94% of votes counted on Sunday, Darijana Filipovic of the nationalist Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina held a commanding lead for the Croat seat on the presidency, while incumbent Bosniak member of the presidency Denis Becirovic of the Social Democratic Party led his nearest opponent, Bakir Izetbegovic, by fewer than three percentage points. Both Filipovic and Becirovic declared victory in their races late Sunday before all votes were counted. Bosnia's Central Election Commission said that 1,432,269 votes were cast in total, a turnout of 42% that was down by around 8% from Bosnia's last election in 2022. READ MORE: Main Kremlin party keeps control of Russian parliament after a carefully orchestrated vote Bosnia has a complex web of governing institutions that were created by a U.S.-brokered peace agreement in 1995 in an effort to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the war. Yet Dodik has consistently tested those limits, openly defying Bosnia's national government in the capital Sarajevo and making moves for Republika Srpska to separate from the country. At his party's final election rally Friday night in Banja Luka, Republika Srpska's administrative capital, Dodik told supporters that Bosnia "is dead." "It is an impossible country. It doesn't make any sense," Dodik said at the rally, which was also attended by Russian Ambassador Igor Khalabukov. Such political and ethnic divisions — in which the country's Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats largely vote along ethnic lines — have blocked Bosnia's progress toward joining the EU despite the bloc's efforts to encourage the country's divided leaders to work together for reform. Dragan Bursac, an analyst, said that despite Dodik not appearing on the ballot for the first time in nearly 30 years, he "is still in command. He is everywhere." "It is obvious that these measures to ban him from political life are not working, and he is using them," Bursac said. Vote took place as ethnic tensions simmer One of the poorest countries in Europe, Bosnia is still struggling to recover decades after the war that started in 1992, after the country declared independence from the Serb-led former Yugoslavia and ethnic Serbs took up arms to carve out their own state and join Serbia. The conflict killed more than 100,000 people and displaced millions. Bosnia's wartime wounds were recently revived by a public homage in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs to the wartime army commander Ratko Mladic, who died in late August while serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes. Bosnian Serbs view Mladic as a hero despite his conviction by a U.N. court over the massacre of more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995, and other atrocities. Electronic election security introduced Sunday's election was the first time Bosnia used electronic identification of voters and ballot scanners to prevent irregularities or organized voter manipulation, which have cast doubt on the fairness of previous elections. On Sunday morning, Associated Press journalists reported seeing multiple polling places where voting couldn't begin on time because of difficulties with the new digital technology. Bosnia's election commission announced late Sunday that some polling stations that had experienced disruptions earlier in the day would be permitted to remain open past the 7 p.m. cutoff. On Sunday, some voters in Banja Luka expressed concern that the new digital systems could confuse older voters. Republika Srpsk

US murderer Christa Pike remains critically ill in hospital and her prognosis is still unclear following her failed execution, her lawyer has said on Sunday.
Speaking to CNN on Sunday morning, Pike's lawyer Stephen Ferrell said doctors were still trying to clear two doses of pentobarbital from her body.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death following her conviction for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995.
She survived two execution attempts on Wednesday, and was transferred to a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee.
Ferrell said: "She's still in the hospital, on a ventilator, critically ill, we really don't know the prognosis yet, and may not know for several days."
He didn't believe she had regained consciousness at any point, adding that he has been receiving updates through her medical power of attorney rather than consulting directly with doctors.
He has not been in to see her. "She is guarded. I'm not sure who may have seen her," he said.
Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong. But Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state said he would resign on Saturday.
"If she recovers - she may not fully recover - and there may be issues about her competence. I mean, we just don't know any of this," Ferrell said. "We have had no discussions about this. The Tennessee attorney general's office so far has not given us any indications of what their intentions will be."
He called on the governor to commute her death sentence to a life sentence "at the very least". "She has endured a torturous attempt at executing her," he said. "She's spent over 30 years in prison, most of that in solitary confinement."
"We don't know right now - and we may never know - what sort of torture she endured during [her failed execution]."
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer in 1995.
She was sentenced to death the following year after a media frenzy around the killing in Knoxville, Tennessee.
Slemmer's mother May Martinez travelled to Nashville for the execution, which moved ahead despite last-minute legal challenges.
Martinez, who supported Pike's death sentence, told local news outlet WJXX that she "broke down in tears" after finding out it was not successful.
"I think that the state owes me a big apology," she said.
The state's Department of Correction has defended the use of lethal injections, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".
Pike's lawyers previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins - meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection.

6bbe7a01a87e.text: By — Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Melanie Lidman, Associated Press By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ap-report-uae-had-shared-details-about-flydubai-flight-with-israel-including-pilots-names-and-nationalities Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AP report: UAE had shared details about FlyDubai flight with Israel, including pilots' names and nationalities World Updated on Oct 4, 2026 2:37 PM EDT — Published on Oct 4, 2026 12:14 PM EDT TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Authorities in the United Arab Emirates shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of the FlyDubai flight on which a pilot attempted to seize control of the Israel-bound aircraft and crash it, regional officials said Sunday, raising new questions over how the attacker evaded detection. WATCH: Investigators search for motive after alleged attack by FlyDubai co-pilot Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later told the head of the National Security Council to appoint an examiner to review "all security aspects regarding foreign civil aviation to Israel." With the investigation into the FlyDubai incident underway, preliminary details have highlighted several major security lapses. Officials already have said the Omani co-pilot had been barred from flying by his own country because of concerns about his extremist views. It also remains unclear how a citizen of Oman, an Arab country that has no diplomatic relations with Israel, was allowed to fly a planeload of Israelis to Tel Aviv. The UAE, which is leading the investigation, said the co-pilot attacked the flight's captain with the cockpit's crash ax and tried to take control of the plummeting plane in a "terrorist attack" Wednesday. His actions nearly crashed the flight with 182 people on board before the Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and others to rush in and subdue the attacker. Israel did not raise concerns about passengers and crew The regional officials said Emirati authorities had shared information about the passengers and crew, including their nationalities. Israel hadn't raised red flags on any passenger or member of the crew, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters about the probe. The Shin Bet, Israel's domestic security agency, said the Transportation Ministry is responsible for vetting passenger lists from foreign flights. Transportation Minister Miri Regev on X said the security agencies are responsible for flight security and that her ministry wasn't given a list of passengers or any warnings. READ MORE: AP report: Ax-wielding FlyDubai co-pilot had been flagged over extremism concerns Sharing the list is standard aviation procedure. But the head of aviation security at the Transportation Ministry, Dvir Rubenstien, told Army Radio that the ministry relies on local security checks and does not have the tools or the ability to run checks on each passenger on every flight. Netanyahu said Thursday that Israel has long-standing agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don't maintain diplomatic relations with Israel. Australian police said Sunday that counterterrorism investigators were looking into the attacker's possible connections to Australia. The passengers who halted the attack and helped regain control of the aircraft have been hailed as heroes in Israel. Questions being raised about security failures But as the initial euphoria of the rescue has subsided, officials have begun to raise difficult questions and trade accusations about the security blunders that could have led to a major disaster. Ahead of the elections at the end of the month, some opposition candidates have seized on the security failures to highlight what they perceive as negligence on the part of Netanyahu and his supporters. Transportation Minister Regev is a member of Netanyahu's Likud party and a staunch supporter. "This is exactly what system collapse looks like," Yair Golan, head of the opposition Democrats party, wrote on X. "A transportation minister who completely abandons our skies, and a prime minister who abandons national security." READ MORE: Pilot stabbing further unsettles region shaken by U.S.-Iran war It also remains unclear how FlyDubai, a low-cost Emirati airline that operates flights between Israel and the UAE, had failed to identify the Omani pilot as a security risk. Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England who wrote a book about aircraft hijackings and bombings, said background check systems differ from country to country and there are limits on what types of information can be shared. "In terms of aviation security itself, obviously we want to have as robust background checks as possible. But there are huge limitations on doing background checks in any case, especially in cross-border checks," he said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. bfde7647fe2a.text: By — Jeffrey Collins, Associated Press Jeffrey Collins, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/christa-pikes-lawyer-says-she-has-not-regained-consciousness-since-her-failed-tennessee-execution Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Christa Pike's lawyer says she has not regained consciousness since her failed Tennessee execution Nation Updated on Oct 4, 2026 1:41 PM EDT — Published on Oct 4, 2026 11:56 AM EDT Christa Pike has remained unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital in the four days since her failed execution in Tennessee, and her prognosis might not be known for days more, one of her lawyers said Sunday. READ MORE: Christa Gail Pike wasn't Tennessee's first failed execution this year. Here's what to know Little has been released about Pike's condition since Wednesday night's execution attempt. She has since remained hospitalized under guard as doctors try to get the massive dose of the barbiturate pentobarbital out of her system. When asked whether she ever regained consciousness after the execution attempt, Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell, Pike's lawyer, said on CNN's "State of the Union": "Not that I am aware of." Lawyer says Pike's medical decisions are being decided by someone else Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row. Tennessee prison officials gave Pike two doses of the lethal injection drug on Wednesday night. The pentobarbital didn't kill her, but her lawyers said her arms were burned and blistered from the caustic drugs. Pike gave someone her medical power of attorney and that person is protecting her privacy, Ferrell said. READ MORE: Tennessee's prisons chief is resigning after the failed execution of Christa Pike "I'm not sure what all they may have told that person," Ferrell said. Pike's attorneys have not identified who is making Pike's medical decisions. They said they may not know for several more days whether or not she can recover. "We don't know right now, and we may never know what sort of torture she endured during that process, where her consciousness was, what physical pain there was — what mental torture she went through," Ferrell said. A spokeswoman for Pike's defense team said in a statement early Sunday that "we appreciate all respect for Christa's rightful privacy." Pike's lawyer says Tennessee needs to be more open about executions Pike's execution was delayed for more than eight hours Wednesday as the U.S. Supreme Court considered, and ultimately overturned, a federal appeals court ruling to halt her lethal injection so judges could thoroughly review whether the jury that sentenced her to death should have considered sexual abuse she said she suffered as a child. Her attorneys asked a court Friday to order Tennessee prison officials to preserve any written records, communication, images or video from the execution. Tennessee, like many other states with capital punishment, keeps many details about executions secret from the people involved to details about how the drugs are manufactured or obtained or any tests done on their quality. "The state of Tennessee has got to start telling its people exactly what it is doing so that in the democratic process, the people of Tennessee can decide if that's what they want to be done in their name," Ferrell told CNN. Tennessee has struggled with executions before This was the second time this year Tennessee has not been able to execute a prisoner who was seemingly moments away from death. In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm but couldn't get a secondary IV line. Commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Correction Frank Strada announced Saturday he was resigning. WATCH: What we know about Tennessee's botched execution of Christa Pike Gov. Bill Lee has ordered an independent investigation into the state's capital punishment system conducted by former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton. He also reviewed Tennessee's execution procedures after Lee called off a different execution in 2022 and found the state did not comply with its own lethal injection process. Prison officials and the Tennessee Attorney General's Office have said little since Pike was taken to the hospital. Future of Pike's death penalty case is unclear It is unclear what will happen in her death penalty case. Pike's lawyers have asked the governor to commute her punishment to a life sentence. "If she recovers, she may not fully recover. And there may be issues about her competence," Ferrell said. Pike didn't deny she killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995. The two were classmates at Knoxville Job Corps. Prosecutors said Pike feared Slemmer was a romantic rival and lured her to a secluded area where she and her boyfriend slashed Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. The case got widespread attention because of the brutality of the killing, the ages of the people involved and because a satanic symbol was carved into the victim's body. 12e7f3e93601.text: By — Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press By — Eléonore Hughes, Associated Press Eléonore Hughes, Associated Press By — Anna-Catherine Brigida, Associated Press Anna-Catherine Brigida, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/brazils-presidential-vote-pits-trump-ally-against-incumbent-lula Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Brazilians vote for next president as Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro hope for first round victory World Updated on Oct 4, 2026 4:13 PM EDT — Published on Oct 4, 2026 11:40 AM EDT SAO PAULO (AP) — Brazilians voted Sunday in a high-stakes presidential election pitting incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro at a moment when the region is shifting to the right in line with the Trump administration. Bolsonaro, 45, is the son of far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year sentence for a coup attempt and an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump. Lula, who at 80 is one of the world's oldest heads of state, is running in his seventh presidential election and has strengthened Brazil's ties with Beijing. READ MORE: Brazil's Lula warns against foreign interference in elections, urges leaders to respond to global conflicts Trump allies have fared well in recent elections in Latin America, including in Argentina, Colombia, Honduras and Peru. If none of the 12 presidential candidates gets more than 50% of the vote, the top two will head to a runoff on Oct. 25 in Latin America's economic powerhouse. Brazil's nearly 159 million eligible voters will also elect 27 state governors, members of state legislatures, all 513 federal members of the lower house of congress and 54 of the country's 81 senators in Sunday's vote. Polls closed at 5 p.m. Sunday with those still in line able to vote and a count expected within hours. Lula promises to stand up to Trump A person throws campaign leaflets in the air outside a polling station during the general election in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on Oct. 4, 2026. And he still enjoys a strong base of supporters who credit his social policies for improving millions of Brazilians' lives. The incumbent president has often spoken about risks of U.S. intervention in the Brazilian elections after the Trump administration imposed high tariffs against Brazilian exports, revoked the visa of the country's ambassador and sanctioned a Supreme Court justice who chaired the investigation that eventually sentenced Jair Bolsonaro, Lula's predecessor. Lula told journalists after voting Sunday that he needs "to do double of what we have done" if reelected, and expressed confidence in a first-round win. But the incumbent faces a tough battle because of an affordability crisis and a corruption scandal that ensnared the same justice who led the investigation into Bolsonaro. "Many in the Lula campaign were not expecting such a difficult election a few weeks ago, and it is clear to them that the present election is a tough battle and the next ones, without Lula, could be even more so," said Carlos Melo, a political science professor at Insper University in Sao Paulo. Bolsonaro embraces Trump alliance Flávio Bolsonaro has touted his proximity to the White House, although he denies his campaign received help from the U.S. government. He has promised to crack down on Brazilian criminal groups and insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare minerals economy, second only to China. Bolsonaro also has campaigned on releasing his father and bringing him back to politics. "Brazil needs change. Brazil can't stand so much suffering," he told reporters at the Rio de Janeiro voting center, where he cast his vote Sunday. The senator faces his own challenges. He has seen his political career tainted by several corruption accusations, including receiving millions of dollars from a disgraced banker to allegedly produce a movie on his father's life. Voters choose between incumbent or return to right Rosane Wink, 67, a retired engineer, is a lifelong conservative voter who supports Bolsonaro and his promise to classify criminal groups as terrorist organizations. "It's a kind of terrorism that they're doing with us," said Wink as she voted in Rio de Janeiro. Last month she had a gun held to her stomach as a criminal bit her hand and removed her wedding ring, she said. Maria Ribeiro, a 50-year-old cellphone vendor from Brasilia, said she voted for Bolsonaro because she wants freedom to express her Evangelical religion. She hopes he follows in his father's footsteps. "I voted for his father, and I don't regret it," she said. "That crazy guy wants to come in here to buy our country, so that our country will be like it is over there," she said at a voting center in Brasilia. "He won't succeed if Lula wins." Even for those outside the country, Lula's social programs, including his flagship welfare program Bolsa Familia, drove many to continue supporting him. "Thank God I do not need (the help of) social programs, but I vote for those that need them: health, education, basic sanitation, housing, food," said Catia Oliveira, a 61-year-old Brazilian who cast her vote from Portugal. 1f157838511c.text: By — Leah Willingham, Associated Press Leah Willingham, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/education/cornell-president-calls-alleged-gang-rape-deeply-disturbing-pledges-greater-transparency Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Cornell president calls alleged gang rape 'deeply disturbing,' pledges greater transparency Education Oct 4, 2026 11:17 AM EDT Cornell's president called the alleged gang rape of a student at a fraternity house in 2024 "deeply disturbing" Saturday, said it would weigh on the university for years to come and pledged greater transparency amid mounting outrage over the school's handling of the case. In an eight-minute video message to the Cornell community, Michael Kotlikoff described the past week as one of the most difficult in the university's history and acknowledged troubling questions about the investigations that followed the allegations. "My heart aches when I think of what she experienced," Kotlikoff said. "It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use." READ MORE: Woman told Cornell investigators she 'felt like bait' during alleged gang rape Kotlikoff reaffirmed his commitment to supporting an independent review of Cornell's handling of the case called for by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and said the school's Board of Trustees would announce details next week. He also expressed support for Hochul's decision to turn the criminal investigation over to the state attorney general. "I want to acknowledge something that can be difficult for an institution to say," Kotlikoff said. "We don't have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves." Scrutiny has mounted in recent days over Cornell's response to allegations that the woman was sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members in 2024. The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, has sued the university and seven former students. During a student assembly hearing Thursday that gave students an opportunity to voice concerns and discuss proposals to improve Cornell's response to sexual assault, several speakers called for Kotlikoff's resignation. Hochul, asked at a news conference Friday whether she believed Kotlikoff should resign over the university's handling of the case, declined to take a position, saying she did not yet have enough information. Kotlikoff acknowledged frustration that Cornell has not communicated enough, saying that has led to distrust. While citing "real legal and privacy limits" on what the university can disclose, he pledged greater transparency and more opportunities for students, parents and others to engage with university leaders. He also committed Cornell's support to legislative efforts to change New York's sexual assault laws. WATCH: Appointing Cornell sex assault special prosector, Hochul says she won't let anyone 'sweep this case under the rug' The case has renewed scrutiny of a state law that makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults involving people who voluntarily consume alcohol or drugs, even if they became too intoxicated to consent. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten cited the law in defending his initial decision not to pursue charges, saying the woman's original statement to police described voluntary drug use and sexual activity. Critics have long sought to close what they call the "voluntary intoxication loophole," which distinguishes between people incapacitated by drugs administered without their consent and those who voluntarily became intoxicated. Hochul has pledged to push for changes to the law. Kotlikoff also called for a "serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life," saying Cornell would engage students, alumni and others in examining how to preserve the benefits of Greek life while strengthening accountability and transparency. "Being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility for our own actions, for how we treat others or for speaking up when someone may be at risk," he said. a519d79464c5.text: Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis on Sunday in an effort to win back territory from the rebel group, the head of Yemen's presidential council said in a speech. "We have exhausted all opportunities for deescalation with the Houthi militias," Rashad al-Alimi said . Why it matters: One of the key objectives of the operation is to regain control over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports. When the Houthis took over territory on the Red Sea coast close to the strait, it gave them — and Iran, which backs them — powerful leverage over the U.S., its Gulf allies and the world economy. Despite pleas from Saudi Arabia, the U.S. is not getting involved in direct combat against the Houthis for now. It is providing intelligence and targeting support, U.S. officials say. Driving the news: The counteroffensive has been planned for many weeks by Yemen's internationally recognized government and Saudi Arabia. Tens of thousands of ground troops loyal to the Yemeni government are participating. The Saudi military is mainly providing air cover for Yemeni forces and conducting airstrikes against Houthi targets. The goal is to retake the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control for several years. The Houthis continued launching missiles at Saudi targets over the weekend, including at facilities of state-owned oil giant Aramco. The intrigue: President Trump is caught between wanting to help Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, his friend and ally, and avoiding getting entangled in a new front in the Middle East. U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also had serious reservations about launching strikes in Yemen, viewing it as a distraction from its focus on Iran, a U.S. official said. On Thursday, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to brief him on the planned operation and ask again for U.S. airstrikes against Houthi targets, the official said. A second U.S. official said that the U.S. "is not going to take kinetic action for now," but stressed that could change if the operation runs into problems. What to watch: On Friday, Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the conflict in Yemen, Axios first reported. It's unclear whether the meeting ended with new policy recommendations for the president regarding Yemen.

A US Marine has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a woman's body was found in a hotel in Okinawa, Japan, local officials say.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described the crime as a "brutal and heinous" robbery and murder. She said she had urged the US to "enforce stricter discipline" of its personnel.
Japan's public broadcaster NHK identified the victim as Yagi Anna, 39, and the suspect as Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma.
"We are actively cooperating with Japanese authorities, in response to allegations of serious criminal actions by a Marine," the Marine Corps said on social media, extending condolences to the victim's family.
Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said the woman's body was discovered early Saturday morning in a hotel in Naha City, the capital of the Okinawa prefecture.
"Such an incident is utterly inexcusable and fills me with strong indignation," Koizumi wrote on social media, adding that "incidents and accidents involving U.S. military personnel cause significant anxiety to the local community and must never occur".
The US Embassy in Tokyo said that it was fully cooperating with the Japanese government and local police. Japan's foreign ministry said it summoned US ambassador George Glass to discuss the incident on Sunday.
Okinawa is home to several US military bases and tens of thousands of American troops.
Okinawa Governor Genta Koja says the prefecture has repeatedly demanded that the US take action to prevent such incidents, and said he sees the alleged crime as a sign of a lack of discipline.
"The fact that this kind of event has happened again leaves us no choice but to conclude that the US military's efforts in maintaining discipline, educating personnel, and other such measures are completely ineffective," he said.

The US has withdrawn all of its bombers from RAF Fairford, the British military base at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter terror police.
A statement from a US department official confirmed on Sunday it had removed all of its bombers from the base back to their home stations in America.
The US did not give a reason for the withdrawal, but it follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences near the base and subsequently released on police bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
Days after the incident, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.
Initially, five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF). All five were UK nationals from London.
They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".
The sixth man, aged 25, was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts. Counter terror police confirmed on Saturday he had also been released on bail.
RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

Polls have closed in Brazil's general election, after voters queued in long lines for a tight first round of the presidential race.
After casting his ballot, 80-year-old left-wing President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva warned that the choice was between democracy and "barbarism".
His challenger, right-winger FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, 45, said he wanted to "free the Brazilian people".
The result is forecast to be close. BBC Brazil's poll aggregator shows that the gap between Lula and Bolsonaro is only two points. If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, the election will go to a run-off on 25 October.
According to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE), more than 158.7 million Brazilians, including one million people abroad, are eligible to vote in the election.
Lula is challenged by 11 candidates, although BBC Brazil's poll aggregator shows that candidates other than Lula and Bolsonaro will get only about 10% of the vote.
The TSE has not set a fixed time for the release of the official results, but they are expected within hours because voting is electronic and experience from previous elections shows that results tend to come quickly.
A victory for Bolsonaro would extend a wave of wins across Latin America by right-wing candidates aligned with US President Donald Trump, while Lula's re-election would create problems for Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.
Some countries, from which Brazilians living overseas are able to vote, have already released preliminary vote count data.
In China, Lula won 56.63% of the votes, while Bolsonaro came in second with 31.33%. Lula also won in countries including South Korea, New Zealand and Saudi Arabia.
In Israel, however, Bolsonaro won 74.40% of the valid votes. He also won 71.59% of the valid votes in Japan.
Today's result will also determine the composition of the Senate from February 2027 onwards, as 54 of the Senate's 81 seats are being contested, representing two-thirds of the chamber.
Currently, the largest bloc in the Senate is Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL), followed by the Social Democratic Party (PSD), which has served in a coalition government under Lula.
In the last election four years ago, Lula narrowly defeated FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro's father, Jair. But the tumultuous aftermath of the election, which saw Jair Bolsonaro convicted of plotting a coup after thousands of his supporters stormed the Brazilian Congress, has had a lasting impact on the nation's political life and this election.
Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup and is barred from standing for office.
Because of recurrent health problems, he is currently under house arrest rather than in a cell, but he has been prohibited from posting on social media or making public statements.
Despite these restrictions, there is little doubt that FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro has his father's backing.
