874dc10b0824.text: By — Jacqueline Ganun, Associated Press Jacqueline Ganun, Associated Press By — Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/education/despair-over-future-fuels-political-anxiety-for-college-students-on-the-cusp-of-adulthood Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Despair over future fuels political anxiety for college students on the cusp of adulthood Education Oct 4, 2026 4:30 PM EDT EAST LANSING, Mich. (AP) — Frankie Llerandi, 21, has been unable to land a single internship in his three years at Michigan State University. He will graduate in the spring with an economics degree and an interest in data analytics, but true adulthood seems maddeningly far away. Most of his cousins have not been able to buy a house or start a family deep into their 30s. Kira Saiti, a 19-year-old sophomore, is more upset about the broader world than her own future. Every time she looks at her phone she sees images of violence and horror, both in the Middle East and closer to home. "It's kind of hard to look at that and say, 'This world is a great place,'" she said. READ MORE: Some states are helping graduate students pay for school. Here's what borrowers should know Julian Bautista, 20, saw his chosen profession of environmental work decimated by Trump administration cuts, pushing the junior to decide he will leave the United States to find work in the Netherlands when he graduates. He considers what remains his home country for the next 18 months to be a failure of democracy led by what he sees as corrupt politicians. "Throughout my life, we've either stagnated or declined, we haven't improved," Bautista said. For many of their classmates on campus and elsewhere around the country, the present looks bleak and the future uncertain at best. Their anxiety is fueling a restlessness with a national political system that they worry is no longer capable of improving their lives or no longer interested in helping. Two years ago, grim economic vibes helped Donald Trump win a far larger share of young voters than is typical for a Republican — 47%, according to AP VoteCast, an extensive survey of the electorate. Now, anxiety about artificial intelligence and the Iran war has been added to the mix, powering a wave of disruptive candidates on the opposite end of the political spectrum who have been embraced by college students. Llerandi, Saiti and Bautista all support a slate of progressive, antiestablishment Democratic candidates in Michigan who are pledging to shake up the status quo. Among them are Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official running for U.S. Senate, and Will Lawrence, a liberal activist trying to unseat Tom Barrett, the Republican congressman who represents the swing district that includes the university. The future looks bleak for many students Anxieties about the job market, homeownership and adulthood are widespread across the campus, even among those who are not deeply involved in politics. "It's just something to laugh at, but, you know, I really do want a house when I'm older," said Praveen Amunugama, a 21-year-old biochemistry major who plans to go to graduate school in hopes the job market improves over the next two years. His friends feel the same way. "They want to be able to afford things, raise a good family," he said. Despite the economic angst among young people, at first blush the picture does not look that bad for them. The unemployment rate for those age 22 to 27 is 7.2%, higher than the broader rate of 4.1% but lower than some other moments of economic calm. A 2024 study found members of the younger generation known as Generation Z are poised to be wealthier than millennials, who themselves are wealthier than the prior generation despite the persistent sense of economic doom that accompanied their entry into the job market during the Great Recession. Kevin Corinth, the economist who co-authored that study, said he understands Gen Z angst, given modern uncertainties, especially the prospect of AI reshaping various industries and data showing younger people are taking longer to leave home and start families. "For previous generations, if you took certain paths you were likely to succeed, to do better than your parents," said Corinth, who is at the American Enterprise Institute, a center-right think tank. For young people now, he acknowledged, that path is not as clear. WATCH: Degree in three: Why more colleges are speeding up graduation timelines Kathryn Edwards, a Texas-based economist, noted that unemployment among recent college graduates is at 5.6%, higher than at most other times in recent history other than the Great Recession. Combined with historically high housing prices and rising costs for essentials such as food and healthcare, that is a challenging environment for young people. "It's pretty bad for them," Edwards said, adding that young people are picking up on broader warning signs in the economy. "So many aspects of our current economy, I think young people have gotten right." They are also fully exposed to the new form of job hunting: AI-powered, digital and done almost exclusively online, where it is hard to discern real job openings from fake ones. "Think about the amount they get spammed and scammed, and there are tons of fake jobs out there," said Marla McGraw, assistant dean of career management in Michigan State's business school. "They're always coming in here going, 'Is this real?'" She spends a lot of time trying to buck up disenchanted students. "Our message right now is the job market is tough, but you're tougher," McGraw said. Students say political leaders are falling short Young Americans' optimism about the job market has plummeted since 2024 and the gap between their view of the economy and those of their elders is greater than almost anywhere in the world, according to a Gallup survey earlier this year. b8a50431ef54.text: The White House is monitoring reports of a suspected plague case and a related quarantines in Russia, a Trump administration official told Axios on Sunday. Driving the news: Russian health authorities have taken precautionary measures in response to the death of a woman who worked at an anti-plague research factility, but have not confirmed that she contracted plague. What they're saying: The Trump administration "is aware, monitoring the outbreak, and assessing options," the administration official said. The backstory: On Sept. 25, 28-year-old Daria Shipilova, who worked at an anti-plague research institute in Russia's Irkutsk region, broke a test tube containing the pneumonic plague pathogen, local reports said. Shipilova was admitted to a hospital on Sept. 29 with symptoms of severe pneumonia and died overnight between Oct. 1 and Oct. 2. After her death, authorities imposed quarantines at several medical facilities in the region and placed nearly 200 people who had come into contact with Shiplova under medical observation. Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev said those being monitored showed no signs of illness and had tested negative. Russian media reports suggested Shipilova may have contracted pneumonic plague, but health authorities have not confirmed the diagnosis. Russia's public health agency said Shipilova had "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that further testing found no microorganisms linked to her work. The agency said the epidemiological situation in the region remains stable. Zoom out: Plague is a potentially life-threatening bacterial disease but can be cured with antibiotics when treated promptly, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . White House spokespeople referred questions to the State Department, which did not respond to a request for comment.

a5387537c755.text: By — Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ap-report-u-s-air-force-removes-all-bombers-from-british-air-base-targeted-by-a-suspected-terror-attack Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AP report: U.S. Air Force removes all bombers from British air base targeted by a suspected terror attack World Oct 4, 2026 5:37 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. Air Force has brought home its bombers stationed at a U.S.-run military air base in England used to strike Iran following an investigation into a planned terror attack at the RAF Fairford base. The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the United States, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorized to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke Sunday on condition of anonymity. READ MORE: Dual UK-Iranian national released on bail over suspected plot against U.S.-run military base Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war. Observers noticed a host of B-1 bombers fly out of the base on Sunday. The move comes as President Donald Trump weighs options for his war on Iran — including new strikes — despite his initial promises to Americans that the campaign would last a matter of weeks. "We have decisions that I'll make about Iran. Iran's been decimated. So the only question is — it'll either be the easy way, or the hard way," Trump told reporters on Saturday as he left the White House for a rally in Ohio. A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and then released on bail during the investigation. British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement. RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East. The U.S. military still maintains a sizable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a U.S. official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier, as well as the USS Malkin Island amphibious readiness group — a group of ships that together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines — are heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers in the region as early as the end of October. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The News
One of the Democratic Partyâs most prolific lawyers also is becoming one of its most prolific posters.
Marc Elias has argued dozens of cases around mail-in balloting and election access across the country and in front of the Supreme Court over the last decade. But he has also moonlighted as an election law content creator and advisor for Democracy Docket, a digital media company he founded in 2020 to focus on redistricting, gerrymandering, and voting access.
What began as a hobby to help explain complex redistricting cases more effectively has grown into a serious media operation. Last month, Democracy Docket surpassed 500,000 free email subscribers, the company first told Semafor, including 70,000 subscribers paying $10 a month or $120 per year. The company also has a YouTube channel with more than 800,000 subscribers, a following that has grown significantly in recent months (the account has added half a million subscribers on the platform since January 2025).
âIn this era where so many political disputes, so many public controversies really wind up in court, and oftentimes the court arguments frame the public debate â I think lawyers have an obligation to speak directly and plainly in language that everyone, non-lawyers and lawyers alike, can understand,â he said. âThat is something Iâve tried to do, particularly in the area of voting and elections, but really more broadly, in the area of democracy.â
Elias told Semafor that he founded the outlet for a fairly prosaic reason: Heâd maxed out the number of people he could send emails to on a private email listserv that heâd previously used to send election and redistricting law updates to a few hundred Democratic policymakers, executives, and officials across the country.
The timing turned out to be convenient: COVID-19 lockdowns prompted a wave of court cases around mail-in balloting, an issue which Elias knew well and was, at times, directly involved in. Democracy Docket began posting public legal documents before many news outlets, gaining email subscribers and direct online traffic through Twitter and Facebook.
Elias told Semafor that his readership is a mix of DC insiders, #Resistance liberals who watch Eliasâ interviews on MS NOW, and legal and political professionals interested in keeping up with the ins and outs of election laws and voting access issues.
While Elias told Semafor he dedicates just a few days a month to the management side, he acknowledged Democracy Docket has become a profitable enterprise. Asked how much money the company brought in each year, Elias declined to elaborate but said that the vast majority of the companyâs revenue came from basic subscriptions, with a small but growing VIP tier of supporters paying $500 a year. Those projections would likely put the company in the ballpark of $9 million to $11 million in annual revenue.
Maxâs view
Democracy Docket is part of a wave of new digital news outlets founded in the Trump era that have surged during the Republican presidentâs second term.
While liberal and left-of-center audiences channeled their interest (and horror) with Trump during his first term by tuning into MSNBC, CNN, The New York Times, and The Washington Post, this go around, shares of those audiences have seemed to abandon traditional outlets for more ideological new media outlets positioned against traditional media.
Outlets like Zeteo, The Bulwark, Crooked Media, and More Perfect Union have added millions of readers, listeners, and YouTube subscribers, even as cable news viewership continues to slide. Some of the movement appears to be ideological: Elias told me that some of the best days of membership for the site have come in the wake of blow-ups at major news outlets like CBS News, which he argues shows viewers were upset with what they saw as media ownersâ capitulation to Donald Trump.
But perhaps more interesting, Democracy Docketâs real innovation is in the continued erosion of the wall between real political players and the media that cover them. The proximity between Eliasâ legal work and journalistic output is likely a bit too close for those who prefer a more traditional separation of church and state, though Elias insists that heâs fairly hands-off when it comes to the newsroomâs coverage. He said that he has occasionally disagreed with Democracy Docketâs stories and opinions.
âSometimes youâll see they report it one way and then I write an opinion piece and I donât correct them in my opinion piece, I just like say âthis is what I think about the case, and if you want to know what I think the outcome of the case is, you know, become a premium member,ââ he said.
Notable
- Older outlets like the Guardian and The Atlantic have similarly benefited from increased left-of-center interest by explicitly positioning themselves as checks on the current administration â and even on some of their less-aggressive peers.

d700e3d026eb.text:
The Scoop
Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson was talking about the media business on Voxâs Channels podcast last month when host Peter Kafka asked him: How was the magazineâs editor-in-chief, Jeffrey Goldberg, feeling about the growing success of Thompsonâs personal podcast?
âWe make a lot of money on the stuff I do,â he said. âJeff likes when we make money.â
Thompsonâs response ricocheted around The Atlanticâs newsroom. Thompsonâs podcast, The Most Interesting Thing in AI, has emerged as a source of tension between the magazineâs business and editorial teams. Journalists have complained that the lucrative and high-profile show is not subject to The Atlanticâs editorial rules, input, or oversight â yet a casual listener could easily take it for an Atlantic editorial product.
Thompsonâs show is made by the magazineâs business side, and âÂ like any number of contemporary podcasts âÂ features interviews with technologists and business leaders, interspersed with sponsored content. When the podcast launched in 2024, the newsroom raised no objections; The Atlantic has featured a robust paid content arm for years through its creative marketing studio and custom events business.
But as the showâs profile has risen in recent months, the podcast has caused increasing consternation internally. Thompson, despite his commercial role, is a well-known former tech reporter and former editor-in-chief of Wired. Last year, when he published a well-received memoir of his family and time as an elite long-distance runner, The Atlantic ran an excerpt. On Most Interesting Thing, he has booked and interviewed top-tier guests, including OpenAI founder Sam Altman âÂ leading staff to complain that the CEOâs bookings are, intentionally or not, undercutting the newsroomâs own efforts.
According to four people familiar with the situation, the podcast has been a particular source of friction between Thompson and Goldberg. Goldberg, who also has a close relationship with Atlantic owner Laurene Powell Jobs, does not report to the CEO and instead reports directly to the Atlanticâs board of directors. (Goldberg had formally reported to Thompsonâs predecessor, Bob Cohn.)
Dissolving Lines
The traditional separation between news outletsâ editorial and business halves has been facing pressure from both sides of that line. Axel Springer CEO Mathias Dopfnerâs podcast has drawn world leaders, cultural figures, and executives. Axios CEO Jim VandeHei regularly writes columns and occasionally breaks news on the companyâs site, in addition to steering its business. The growth of independent media in the Substack era has also created a generation of journalists who run both the business and editorial arms of their own small media outlets.
In this media environment, Thompsonâs sponsored podcast is hardly an outlier. But itâs the latest instance in which Thompsonâs attempts to nudge the newsroom on the business side have run up against a more skeptical and traditionalist editorial staff.
Deepening the tension are differing views about the substance of the AI story. Thompson inked a content-licensing deal between The Atlantic and OpenAI in 2024, angering newsroom staffers, some of whom view the frontier AI labs as having stolen journalistsâ work for training.
The publicationâs editorial union publicly expressed skepticism of the deal and the publicationâs policies around AI. The magazineâs tech editor published an op-ed saying publishers like The Atlantic were making a âdevilâs bargain.â In an August 2024 letter first reported by Semafor, editorial staff said OpenAI was hallucinating Atlantic stories and linking to aggregation of the publicationâs reporting. And while The Atlantic has published largely skeptical coverage of major AI companies and their productsâ impact on society, Thompsonâs tone, in his podcasts and LinkedIn posts, has been more optimistic.
The View From The Atlantic
The Atlantic declined to comment. But one senior company source stressed that there are clear disclaimers demarcating content made by the business side of the company, even if the content itself can feel journalistic in tone â perhaps unsurprising in the case of The Most Interesting Thing, as Thompson is a former journalist.
Maxâs view
The Atlantic is one of the clear media success stories of the second Trump term, fueled by Signalgate and other critical reporting and commentary on the Trump administration, a successful events business, and shrewd moves to capitalize on the public stumbles of its DC neighbor, The Washington Post. The 168-year-old magazineâs breakout journalism, its digital success, and a bit of good timing have given both Goldberg and Thompson plenty to brag about on the media podcast circuit.
But strains at the top of the organization over its brand and direction reflect many premium news outletsâ dilemmas about survival and profit in a post-traffic, AI-ascendant media age. Marketers have infinite options for buying ads, meaning publishers no longer have the leverage they did when they controlled much of their own distribution. Meanwhile, independent journalists are developing direct relationships with advertisers and marketers, creating more fluidity between the editorial and business sides of their brands.
Still, the old boundaries existed for a reason. Fragmentation has allowed many powerful figures to get their message across by circumventing traditional media outlets whose questions many CEOs and politicians donât want to answer. Itâs not surprising that Altman was willing to sit down with The Atlanticâs CEO on a sponsored business-side podcast, but not with the magazineâs tech journalists.
Room for Disagreement
Readers and audiences understand that when someone runs or owns a news outlet, they have the right to make it publish their opinions and thoughts, Kafka told Thompson. âItâs not against the law, but itâs also a little creepy.â

ef5223a59670.text:
The Scoop
A Silicon Valley nonprofit close to the AI safety movement is pledging $10 million by the end of 2027 to fund mainstream and independent coverage of artificial intelligence.
The Tarbell Center for AI Journalism plans to announce that it is launching an institutional grantmaking fund, which executive director Cillian Crosson said will provide grants to newsrooms and other ambitious AI reporting projects.
The first recipient of the grant is Machine Gods, NPRâs new video podcast from former Hard Fork hosts Kevin Roose and Casey Newton, which is receiving a $480,000 grant from the organization. Tarbell is also separately backing NPRâs âPower and Influenceâ desk, giving the public media outlet $250,000 to help expand its coverage of how AI intersects with politics, money, and power.
âWe think that having resources at newsrooms is an important part of ensuring strong coverage,â Crosson told Semafor. The new fund will âincrease our support but it also allows us to more easily support a more diverse range of perspectives.â
The organization, which is backed by groups including the deep-pocketed nonprofit Coefficient Giving, said it plans to fund investigative teams, AI verticals at national outlets, and other large-scale initiatives in new and legacy media. In particular, the organization is focused on expanding reporting and on frontier companies and the ways that AI companies and aligned political action groups are influencing American politics and tech regulations.
Itâs a significant expansion from the organizationâs previous commitments, which have totaled $400,000 over four years. Tarbellâs previous grants focused on backing early-career journalists inside established newsrooms, offering media organizations reporting grants ranging from $1,000 to $20,000 to work on individual stories on AI.
With increased monetary backing, the organization said it planned to issue grants between $50,000 and $500,000, but could make multimillion-dollar grants for the right projects.
Funding and AI safety
In recent years, Tarbell fellows have fanned out across several major news outlets, breaking stories that have often exposed reckless or aggressive actions by AI companies and frontier labs.
Though Tarbell offers funding with no formal strings attached, it has drawn criticism from some in the AI industry and on the political right who see it as fueling what they view as exaggerated safety concerns. The subjects of some of Tarbellâs journalism, including OpenAI, have complained about the reporting and financial support from some organizations aligned with effective altruism, a loose philosophical movement whose concerns include an AI-driven apocalypse.
As Semafor previously reported, cash-strapped news organizations have balanced concerns about optics of outside groups funding journalism with the much-needed financial support and aggressive journalists who have broken legitimate stories about AI and safety concerns. Semafor has not found instances where Tarbell interfered directly in any stories, and the organization is quick to point out that not all of the projects it backs are AI skeptics or strong AI safety proponents.
In a telephone interview last week, Crosson reminded Semafor that the organization has two editorial firewalls: One between itself and its backers, and another between Tarbell and the media organizations it supports. It discloses its donors over $10,000, its fellows maintain complete autonomy over their reporting, and the organization asks news outlets it partners with to disclose when it has provided funding to support a journalist or project.
In an interview with Semafor, Roose noted that Newton had worked with Tarbell at Platformer in recent years, and found the organization to be a strong supporter of independent journalism, and did not interfere or insert itself into any editorial content.
âTheir funding has been very useful in helping us get started,â Roose said. âIt was a way for us to de-risk going out on our own. Weâre feeling quite good about it and weâre grateful.â

Environmental groups have criticised a pilot scheme that aims to make housing developers pay a new nature levy.
The government wants parts of Norfolk to be the first areas subject to its Environmental Delivery Plan (EDP).
In order to unlock space for thousands of homes, developers would pay money that could create new wetlands, fund deer culls and restore rivers.
But ecology experts fear that it would fail to tackle the sources of pollution, leaving vulnerable chalk streams still at risk.
Sally Haines, chief executive of the Chartered Institute of Ecology and Environmental Management, said: "While [actions outlined in the plan] would improve ecological habitats in the area, they won't necessarily address the pollution that will be going into the water.
"Unless you do that, you are not going to get good nature recovery."
The EDP, which would apply to much of central Norfolk and parts of The Broads, would pool cash from housebuilders.
It would be spent on measures to help offset pollution from new homes.
Norfolk's rare chalk streams, often described as England's rainforests, are particularly vulnerable.
Environment Secretary Angela Eagle calls it a "win-win" for development and nature, claiming it would unlock space for 15,780 homes that are currently stalled because of rules protecting rivers.
With developers paying Â£2,675 per house, it is hoped the levy will raise about Â£42m.
The scheme is designed to replace the more complicated nutrient neutrality rules that are in place, which were blamed for blocking the regeneration plan for the former Colman's Mustard Factory at Carrow Works in Norwich.
A government spokesperson said the introduction of a single levy would make life easier for developers.
Natural England is leading on the project and chief executive Marian Spain said: "Instead of tackling pollution piecemeal, site by site, we can now deliver conservation measures that make a real difference for rivers, wetlands and wildlife across Norfolk."
However, Haines said it was a "fallacy" to blame environmental concerns as the main stumbling block when building houses - pointing instead to a myriad of issues such as the availability of materials and labour, and land prices.
Under the proposals, restoration projects would be put together for the River Wensum, the Bure broads and marshes, and the River Yare catchment area.
One eye-catching policy is to put some of the cash towards deer management, including targeted culling.
Booming deer populations in The Broads are becoming a growing issue as the animals can cause damage to the environment through grazing.
People can submit their views as part of a consultation, external - which opened on 17 September and runs until 27 October - before Natural England submits its final plans to Eagle and her department.
Natural England hopes to roll out EDPs in other parts of England in the future.
The chief executive of Norfolk Wildlife Trust, Eliot Lyne, said his organisation needed more time to review the proposals.
But he said it was worried about wider changes to planning rules and how they affected natural habitats.
"We are concerned that it weakens existing protections for Norfolk's nationally and globally important wildlife sites such as chalk streams, wetlands and valley fens," he added.
Mark Dye, a chalk stream campaigner for the Gaywood River Revival group in west Norfolk, said: "Fundamentally, if you are polluting a chalk stream or a river and you're putting more and more pollution into that river, and not seeking to address the underlying causes of that, then it's only going to get worse."
Steve Turner, executive director of the Home Builders Federation, claimed pollution from farmers was a bigger issue than new homes and he criticised water companies for not investing in infrastructure to stop sewage entering rivers.

Thousands of supporters of Pakistan's jailed ex-prime minister Imran Khan are marching to the capital Islamabad as they call for his release.
Concerns over the 73-year-old's health have grown louder in recent months. His family claims he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.
The cricket star-turned-politician, who faces charges in more than 100 cases, was jailed for 17 years over corruption last year. Khan said all the cases against him are politically motivated.
Even behind bars, he remains a force in Pakistani politics, and demonstrations in support for him have led to deadly violence and crackdowns in the past.
Sunday's march, which began in Lakki Marwat, a city 275km away from Islamabad, had paused for the night and is expected to resume around midday local time on Monday.
Originally scheduled for last week, it was postponed to allow for talks between the government and Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party but the talks ended in a deadlock.
Khan, who faces charges ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts, was first imprisoned in August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year.
Sohail Afridi, chief minister for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province ruled by PTI, expects that the march will make its way to a town about 80km (50 miles) west of Islamabad by Thursday.
"[By then] this movement will have reached every corner of the country and every square will have become a centre of activity," he said on Sunday, urging the people to "play an active role in the political process".
Authorities in Islamabad have stacked up shipping containers to block key access routes to the capital city.
The PTI said talks with government failed because authorities rejected the party's request for access to Khan so that its leaders could consult him on national and political issues.
The party also said it had demanded that Khan be given an immediate medical examination and treatment.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi meanwhile accused Afridi of "sabotaging" negotiations, saying the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government had backed out of earlier commitments on counter-terrorism issues, according to Pakistan's local media reports.
In August, Khan was briefly transferred from jail to a state-run hospital for medical examination and treatment following complaints about his deteriorating health. The doctors later deemed him "medically fit".
The intervention was the most significant relief Khan has received from the courts since he was imprisoned in 2023 on corruption charges, which he says were politically motivated.
Khan's family and the PTI, however, criticised the authorities for defying a court order that he be examined by physicians at a specific private hospital.
On 20 September, Khan's sister Aleema Khanum was arrested in the eastern city of Lahore.
The arrest order said Khanum had been mobilising people to "create law and order situations" and "raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the Government".
Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as the country's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.
His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things.
At least eight people died in the protests and the army had to be called in to quell the violence.
Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif urging Khan be accorded proper medical care.

Up to 500 schools across France will be partially or totally closed on Monday after clashes between riot police and student protesters in recent days, the French education minister said on Sunday.
Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some "400 to 500" high schools as security conditions "have not been fulfilled", Ãdouard Geffray said.
He also said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the start of the protests.
Thousands of students have been demonstrating over education standards and the protests, which started last week, have spread from Paris to other cities, including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille.
High school pupils and others have objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.
On Friday, French Justice Minister GÃ©rald Darmanin said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been affected "one way or another" by violent protests.
The education minister warned the number of schools potentially affected on Monday could be comparable to Friday's figure but promised a "partial, progressive return to lessons".
"There are activists - particularly from the far-left - who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Ãdouard Geffray claimed.
"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he said. Geffray added that 78 staff members in education had been wounded, which he described as "something we have never seen before".
On Friday 1,747 people were arrested, according to French Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez.
Over 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according the AFP news agency, with around 85% of them minors.
Organisers of the protests have called for the demonstrations to continue on Tuesday after accusing the government of a lack of "concrete measures", according to AFP.
On Sunday, French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu said his government is taking further steps to "address the difficulties faced by high school students and educational staff".
He said this includes ensuring classes continue, improving facilities, better organising school days and making the French university admissions platform more transparent.
Lecornu also said the government is accelerating the review of its "vandal-pays" bill to ensure that people responsible for damage bear the cost of their actions.

Six people aboard a medical transport aircraft that went missing on Saturday while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston are presumed dead, according to a statement from the flight's operator.
On Sunday evening, the United States Coast Guard said it was ending its search for survivors off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island.
"We must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died," Latitude Air Ambulance said in a statement shortly thereafter.
"Our thoughts are first and foremost with their families, loved ones, friends, and colleagues."
The Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Saturday morning.
On Saturday evening, authorities located a "debris field" confirmed to be from the aircraft.
The plane had departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time on Friday night, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT).
Four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals were onboard.
"This is an unimaginable loss for our Latitude family and for everyone who loved the six people aboard Heartbeat 104," said Peter Byl, President of Latitude Air Ambulance, on Sunday evening.
"Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities. We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day."
Latitude Air Ambulance is a Canadian company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home.
Two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, had flown to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News.
FlightAware's tracker shows that the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft).
Radio transmissions show trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported, based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net.
"You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?"
The pilot's response was inaudible.
"You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe.
The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency.
An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue".
The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar".
Latitude said in its statement on Sunday evening that it would continue to cooperate with relevant authorities during ongoing recovery efforts and investigations.
"Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred," the company said.

US President Donald Trump says he has created a new taskforce focused on artificial intelligence, which will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.
The "Super Intelligence Force" will work to ensure that the US continues to lead in the technology's development and will coordinate the government's engagement with the public, Trump posted on Sunday.
It comes after the president signed an executive order on 29 September to rename AI as Super Intelligence, after previously saying the word artificial made it sound "fake".
Trump also said last week that he would set up a board to oversee AI safety after top tech bosses signed what he described as a "morally binding" pact.
"The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump wrote.
Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Undersecretary of Defense for Research, Engineering Emil Michael and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor will also be part of the taskforce.
It will report directly to the president and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.
The taskforce's chief, Clayton, took office as the US national intelligence director in August after Trump's original choice, Bill Pulte, was rejected by lawmakers.
On AI, Clayton has previously said: "When something's both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it."
Clayton previously served as US attorney for the Southern District of New York, overseeing several prominent cases, including the drug trafficking case against former Venezuelan President Nicholas Maduro.
The announcement of the taskforce follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry, including executives of OpenAI and Anthropic, to tighten regulation of the technology.
In an interview published on 4 October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of AI justify accepting some of its risks and argued that the technology should remain accessible to the public.
"The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this âtechnology and people having the agency," Altman told Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded.
Trump has dismissed calls for stronger oversight and largely left it to AI companies to regulate themselves.
The pact signed on 29 September includes the signatures of executives from top tech firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Google.
On the same day, the president signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence.
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.
Some experts have questioned the logic of the rebranding, arguing that the use of "super intelligence" could cause confusion as it refers to more advanced systems.
Some top tech leaders have already started to use the new name, including multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who said on social media on Sunday that he will rename his firm's AI platform SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI.
"SpaceX is a super intelligence company", Musk wrote.
The Tesla boss has recently been brought back into the US government to be part of a project to study the future of war.
Musk previously served in the Trump administration, heading the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, before his tenure ended in a public spat with Trump.

"I was hurting inside, so I came to tell my story."
These were Seo Mi-hyeon's first words to the police.
Seo, who has an intellectual disability, struggles to form long sentences and can only communicate through brief words and gestures. But her memories of the abuse inflicted upon her were clear.
She was one of three residents at a state-run care home in South Korea who were sexually assaulted by the home's director, in a case that has shocked the country and raised serious questions about state care for the disabled.
Earlier this month, a court in Seoul sentenced the director - who has only been identified by his surname Kim - to 15 years in prison. Kim is appealing the conviction.
The court had heard that some residents were made to call the director "Dad", which prosecutors said illustrated the unequal relationship between Kim and those in his care.
The ruling came nearly two years after Seo, who is in her 40s, first disclosed the abuse to her mother.
We have changed Seo's name and the names of another victim in this story to protect their identities.
'I just endured it'
Seo first began living in Saekdongwon, a care home for the intellectually disabled, in 2016.
The institute, located in the city of Incheon, is fully subsidised by the state and still houses some 33 residents, although it has been asked to close down in light of this case.
According to Seo, the abuse began shortly after she began living there, with Kim visiting her at night or in the early hours of the morning to rape her.
Speaking through her lawyer Ko Eun-young, Seo said there was no adult at the facility she could speak to about the abuse, adding that she felt that other staff members would not help her. The care home has not responded to this allegation.
That was her life for almost 10 years, until the case came to light in February 2025, when Seo suffered a head injury.
She said it happened one of the times Kim tried to sexually assault her. She had blocked him with her hands, causing him to throw a glass at her.
Her lawyer told the court that the care home took Seo to hospital and informed her mother about the incident only after the wound on her head had been stitched up.
According to Seo's lawyer, Seo's mother had asked to see CCTV footage to establish how her daughter had been injured, but the facility refused, saying they were not authorised to release it.
As a result, her mother brought her home and decided to withdraw her from the facility. It was only after Seo was told that she would not have to return to the home that she disclosed the sexual abuse to her mum, who then reported it to the police.
"I thought it was safe to speak because I was told I didn't have to go back to Saekdongwon," Seo told the BBC via her lawyer.
When asked how she had managed on her own for so many years, she said: "I just endured it."
A police investigation into Seo's account was then widened to other residents.
They found at least two other alleged victims, including Lee Mi-Na, who said that she was also raped by Kim.
Earlier this month, a judge found all three victims' testimony credible.
He was sentenced to 15 years in jail for raping Lee and Seo, five years less than the original sentence prosecutors were asking for. He has denied all allegations and has since appealed the ruling.
For the third victim, Kim was found guilty of a lesser charge of sexual violence, with the judge saying the charge of rape against her was dropped as they could not find conclusive evidence that "force or threats [were used] that rendered the victim unable to resist".
A joint response committee made up of disability rights and other civic groups have criticsed this ruling, saying a victim's ability to resist an assault should not impact the verdict they receive.
The committee has also criticised the investigation process, saying there was a failure to identify more potential victims.
In November last year, following the initial allegations of abuse, local authorities from Ganghwa County had commissioned a team from Woosuk University to conduct an in-depth assessment of Saekdongwon's residents.
The report, which was submitted to the court as evidence, found indications that many more residents - at least 10 - could have been sexually assaulted by Kim.
But during the trial, the court did not address this finding.
According to local media reports, police had struggled to establish details of alleged abuse when interviewing residents, because most of them had severe disabilities and faced difficulties communicating. Some residents reportedly gave answers unrelated to the questions or did not respond at all.
Kim has not responded to allegations that he may have abused more residents.
Jeon Ji-su, the professor who led the Woosuk research team, told the BBC that investigators had accepted "only the accounts of people who could describe the abuse in complete sentences".
But activists said that this reliance on verbal testimony meant the police failed to recognise residents with greater communication difficulties as victims.
"If victims express their experiences differently from the way we expect, shouldn't the state make a greater effort to hear their voices?" said Baek In-seong, of Hansahoe, a counselling centre for survivors of sexual violence with disabilities.
Police have said that "while there may have been shortcomings in individual instances, these should not be taken as representative of the investigation as a whole".
Rights groups have also criticised others who have sought leniency for Kim.
Ahead of the verdict, a total of 13 petitions seeking leniency were said to have been submitted to the court. One of them, from a social welfare organisation, asked the court to take into account the defendant's "contribution to the welfare sector".
Welfare advocacy group Gyeol condemned the petitioning organisations, saying: "Past service in the welfare sector does not exempt anyone from accountability."
